Current versions of the Lambek Calculus used in computational linguistics are expanded upon using unary modalities to govern structural rules affecting sentence order and phrasing. This incorporation of controlled structural operations yields derivational ambiguities missed by the original Lambek Calculus and its simplification in pregroups. To enable the compositional interpretation of the extended calculus, a compact category has been proposed; however, these proposals neglect the modalities' control aspect, limiting them to purely syntactic roles. To remedy this, our approach elevates modalities to first-class entities within the vectorial interpretation, drawing from the directional density matrix semantics. By introducing an extra spin density matrix space to the type system's interpretation, our method results in the expression of multiple co-existing interpretations for ambiguous sentences through their tensoring with orthogonal spin states. This method offers a unified framework for handling both lexical and derivational ambiguity within a sentence's interpretation. Furthermore, this method enables the expression of a sentence's polysemy by rotating its interpretation and is applicable across various sentence orders and phrasings, revealing the sentence's word order and syntactic tree independence. To demonstrate this, we apply this method to a part-of-speech system consisting of verbs with diverse meanings. The proposed method also facilitates the extension of computational linguistics to address more complex forms of ambiguity, such as semantic ambiguity in polysemous words. To illustrate this, we consider the word "dog", which can refer to either an animal or a shape, to demonstrate its applicability to this type of ambiguity. In this study, we examine Cotton solitons within the context of almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Initially, we establish the incompatibility of such solitons when the potential vector field is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field. Then, assuming the potential vector field is perpendicular to the Reeb vector field, we demonstrate that on non-Kenmotsu almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a steady Cotton soliton emerges, characterizing a manifold that is locally identical in geometry to the warped product space $\mathbb{H}^2(-4) \times \mathbb{R}$. Furthermore, this soliton is a gradient soliton when the potential vector field has a specific relationship with the Reeb vector field. Additionally, we show that on Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with $\lambda \neq 0$, such solitons cannot exist. This research builds upon and clarifies previous findings concerning Cotton solitons in [7] and [8].

Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. To address this challenge, we present PyFDH - a Python-based framework that can handle the integration of PDF predictions and experimental data for further analysis. By leveraging established tools such as Apache Arrow and PyArrow for high-performance data processing, PyFDH can handle large-scale datasets commonly encountered in particle physics. In addition to its core functionality, the package includes an intuitive API and a comprehensive set of commands that can be extended by researchers. To demonstrate its capabilities, we illustrate the integration of several PDF predictors and demonstrate its computational efficiency in comparing the gluon distribution across different PDF sets. Given its modular design and reliance on established performance libraries, PyFDH can handle even the most complex inputs and outputs, making it a valuable resource for the PDF community. The package is openly available for download at https://lhecentral.github.io/pyfdh. To utilize its features, users must execute "pip install pyfdh" or "pip install git+https://github.com/lhecentral/pyfdh.git" within their terminal commands. For users of the Drell-Yan fast estimator tool, we also provide PyFDH as an alternative data processor in https://github.com/SCArithmSC/pydylearn. To report any issues or contribute to the package, we invite users to submit their concerns and code at https://github.com/lhecentral/pyfdh. Despite the advancements made by research groups that rely on it, PyFDH remains largely a nascent project that can still benefit from input and feedback from the particle physics community. In the long term, the project aims to evolve into a full-fledged analysis framework that can be used for PDF fitting and related phenomenological studies. However, this goal will require a significant increase in computational power, better memory management, and more robust performance optimization techniques. Until then, PyFDH will continue to provide a unifying integration

This equivalence can be demonstrated through two related arguments, either by showing the superbosonization formula derives from the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, or by reverse-engineering the transformation using the superbosonization formula. Initial findings from a measurement of the spin asymmetry of the top quark, 
relevant to the top quark's polarization, have been reported for events 
resulting from $t$-channel single top quark production. The data were obtained 
from proton-proton collisions at 8 TeV and have a total luminosity of 19.7 fb^-1. 
The method involves counting the number of jets that are determined to originate 
from the hadronization of the top quark in relation to the overall number of 
events. The results show a spin asymmetry of 0.25, with a margin of error at 0.06, 
based on a theoretical spin asymmetry of 0.44. A more precise calculation, 
taking into account various theoretical and experimental factors, yields a value 
of 0.438±0.096 for the asymmetry. This measurement is relevant to studies of 
the top quark's polarization in events involving the decay of a $W$ boson to an 
electron and a missing particle, which could provide insight into the existence 
of new physics involving the top quark. Additionally, this measurement may 
contribute to the development of techniques for accurately measuring the spin 
polarization of other heavy particles, such as the $W$ boson. As a result, this 
research will contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the properties 
of heavy fundamental particles. This research has been performed by the CMS 
collaboration and the results will be presented at the 2014 LHCP workshop in
Sudbury.

We have conducted an in-depth examination of the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR within LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices of varying bilayer thickness. Our spin-lattice relaxation time and shift measurements in a 6.55 T magnetic field provided detailed insights into the electronic structure and relaxation mechanisms of LaNiO$_3$. Notably, the spin-lattice relaxation rate exhibited a straightforward temperature dependence in linear proportionality, deviating from the expected activated behavior commonly observed in transition metals and rare-earth materials. This unusual temperature dependence suggests the presence of a robust, temperature-independent contribution to relaxation, likely stemming from the interaction between LaNiO$_3$ and the adjacent LaAlO$_3$ layers through metal-insulator heterointerfaces. Furthermore, we observed a notable increase in the Knight shift at La sites bordering LaAlO$_3$ layers, amounting to $\sim$0.05$\%$ or 2$\%$ of the LaAlO$_3$ Knight shift, which may be associated with an unusual carrier state induced near the heterointerfaces. These unique features offer a fundamental perspective on the physics governing LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices and pave the way for comparative studies with other transition metal oxides and heterostructures. Moreover, this study highlights the unifying role of $\beta$-detected NMR in investigating the electronic states of correlated metals within heterostructures. Ultimately, this study positions LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ as an ideal testing ground for understanding the unique properties of correlated metals within heterostructures.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, effectively 
incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation 
tasks at various levels of conversational depth, utilizing text features derived 
automatically from pre-trained models. Ultimately, our primary challenge is a 
complex theory of mind problem that necessitates controlled text generation 
based on anticipated listener reactions. To tackle this, we propose a framework in 
which anticipated listener impacts are factored into text features that influence 
conversational direction. Our approach to this multi-step listening task is 
incremental, starting with simple branching and gradually increasing complexity 
through trial and error, backed by extensive experimentation on our dataset. 
Our findings on conversational dialogue generation highlight the significance of 
controlled text generation in relation to anticipated listener effects. We 
conclude by outlining potential applications and future research avenues for

To provide an accurate assessment, we take into consideration the impact of correlated signal weakening and a phenomenon in which the intensity and phase of the reflected signal are interconnected, often disregarded in theoretical studies. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We also show that stationary Gaussian free field-valued processes can be defined on the upper half-plane and the first orthant. Furthermore, we establish the relationship between these processes and multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. This relationship is made explicit by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals. Consequently, these connections yield domain projections and associated Gaussian free fields for multiple SLE. We also show that stationary Gaussian free field-valued processes can be defined on the upper half-plane and the first orthant. This allows us to define the loop-swap measure, which is a measure that arises from multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that this measure has a scaling property, similar to the stationary Gaussian free field-valued process. This property is used to prove the convergence of multiple SLE to a tracing process on these domains. We also show that these tracing processes have the same scaling limit as multiple SLE. This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, combustion models must be linearized, which is shown to be challenging using existing models such as LES and DNS. Nevertheless, RANS models prove to be effective alternatives due to their ability to avoid closure issues. To apply these models, the researchers used LES to obtain the average flow conditions of the jet flame. An analysis of the results showed that a linearized RANS-Eddy Break-Up model yields the most accurate representation of reaction rates compared to other models, while an analysis of the model's equations revealed that reaction rate oscillations result from the disruption of Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings within the jet flame. Furthermore, the results from the model matched the outcomes from the LES simulations, confirming its effectiveness. The most responsive parameters to acoustic vibrations were identified as reaction rate and temperature, which demonstrated a phase lag of approximately 0.25 lambda v / Uj. Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be confirmed through data. The purpose of this paper is to modify nonlocal gravity theory so that the nonlocal aspect relates directly to observable properties, similar to the approach in nonlocal electrodynamics. The reformulated theory results in a constitutive relation identical to one proposed recently by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl. The nonlocal gravity theory can be applied to show that de Sitter spacetime does not meet the theory's requirements. The modification of nonlocal gravity theory is also utilized to develop a novel model of scalar field propagation within a de Sitter spacetime. The proposed model includes a nontrivial, fixed boundary condition that can be characterized by a boundary nonlocal mass. The theoretical model predicts that the boundary nonlocal mass should result in a measurable effect on the scalar field's two-point function. The measurable effect could potentially be observed through experiments involving scalar fields in a de Sitter spacetime. The theoretical model of scalar field propagation also offers a novel explanation for the well-known issue of the cosmological constant. The problem might arise from a connection between the nonlocal mass of the boundary and the nonlocal mass of matter, as suggested by the theoretical model. The proposed modification of nonlocal gravity theory has the potential to provide a unifying explanation for various phenomena, including the behavior of scalar fields in a de Sitter spacetime and the nontrivial gravitational field of antihydrogen. The theoretical model of antihydrogen's gravitational field could potentially be verified or rejected through experiments involving antihydrogen in a de Sitter spacetime. The experimental evidence for nonlocal gravity theory could also be interpreted as indication for a nonlocal mass of antihydrogen itself. The theoretical model proposed in this paper offers a unique perspective on the fundamental aspects of nonlocal gravity theory and its applications. The potential for the model to be verified or rejected through experiments involving scalar fields and antihydrogen could provide a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory with a level of nonlocal aspect that can be confirmed through data from gravitational experiments. Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific conflict scenario occurs when updating a key that has been modified elsewhere, resulting in one update being overwritten with the other's changes. Existing conflict resolution protocols either compromise performance or coherence when dealing with such conflicts. This design piece introduces RWF, a high-performance conflict resolution framework that leverages replication to handle updates conflicting with concurrent changes. RWF employs a 'Remove-Win' approach, where the update with the most recent replication version is given precedence. We demonstrate that RWF achieves high performance by avoiding coordination and utilizing replication history, but may result in data being temporarily inconsistent. Furthermore, we show that RWF's conflict resolution ability allows it to coexist with systems lacking similar support, essentially making it an 'application-level' protocol. To facilitate easy integration with existing systems, RWF can be implemented at the storage level as well as within applications. Ultimately, our evaluation highlights that RWF-based systems can handle high-performance data access, even in conflict-prone environments, and can provide efficient conflict resolution when combined with specific update policies. We also explore possibilities for adapting this design to address conflicts in other distributed systems. This design piece aims to stimulate discussion and further research into conflict resolution strategies that prioritize performance, coherence, coordination, and domain-specific updates. This design piece is relevant to the field because conflict resolution is an ongoing concern in the development of distributed storage systems, and there is a clear need for strategies that prioritize performance above coherence, require minimal coordination above specific update domains, and allow for adaptation above all else. This design piece is unique in that it addresses these concerns through an innovative protocol that can be applied at both the storage and application levels. Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed an effective approach to pinpointing the functional genomic elements responsible for the effects of associated SNPs, combining data analysis with a novel statistical method called the Functional Annotation Sum. This strategy is particularly useful for identifying the pervasive influence of regulatory elements on multiple associated SNPs. Using The Functional Annotation Sum, we uncovered extensive tracks of open chromatin and enriched H3K4me1 marks associated with 99 out of 108 genome-wide association study summaries. Furthermore, we applied this approach to investigate SNPs associated with immune cell types in lung and skin tissues, uncovering novel aspects of immune cell epigenomics. In lung tissue, for example, our findings revealed distinct subsets of open chromatin sites, H3K4me1-enriched regions, and super-enhancers associated with different immune cell types. Additionally, we identified enhancers linked to cell-type-specific promoters across 5.6 megabases of genomic sequence in lung tissue and pinpointed 434 cell-type-specific super-enhancers associated with 312 promoters in lung tissue. With further analysis, we found that 39% of lung tissue-associated SNPs from genome-wide association studies lie within 500 kilobases of these cell-type-specific super-enhancers. By examining lung and skin tissues, we have demonstrated the utility of The Functional Annotation Sum in identifying functional genomic elements influencing the effects of associated SNPs and shedding light on the cellular origins of genetic disorders. This approach can be applied to any genome-wide association study to uncover the functional genomic elements responsible for associated SNPs. We have made this approach available online at https://github.com/raelya/FAS.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to address the question of whether a large population of black holes exists in the galaxy's center, researchers need accurate information about the ratio of LMXB systems hosting black holes or neutron stars. Although the current study does not provide a precise answer to that question, it does offer a crucial step in the investigation. By analyzing the properties of a neutron star and its host system derived from radio and optical observations, researchers can model the binary's past, including the birth of the binary, but this process is highly computationally intensive and previously could only be done for a small number of systems. By using a method called "N-body simulations" in combination with a machine learning algorithm called "Gaussian Process", it's now possible to do this for a larger number of systems. For example, this study models the past of 29 systems that include the famous binary system PSR B1620-26b. Models indicate that about 7 of these 29 systems were born from the merger of two neutron stars, 4 were born from a neutron star and a white dwarf, and the remaining 18 were born from two white dwarfs. The research also predicts that there may be about 20-40 additional radio pulsars that are hidden within the galaxy's center due to their low brightness. To explore this possibility, we are conducting a statistical analysis of wide binary star velocity distributions in the second data release of the Galactic Star Gauge dataset. By comparing observed velocities to predicted values, we are estimating the velocity anisotropy parameters and mass density within the stellar population's spherical volume of influence. This process involves applying the Jeans equations with constant velocity anisotropy and a spherical mass density profile, assuming a stable and inertial stellar mass distribution. Our preliminary analysis of the stellar mass density within the radial distance of approximately 50,000 parsecs from the galaxy's center is consistent with the density profile defined by the stellar mass density map generated by the DESI and Pan-PPDr collaborations, based on near-infrared spectroscopic galaxy observations. We analyze the impact of acoustic waves on one-dimensional flows in general,
focusing particularly on massive stars experiencing outbursts exceeding the
Eddington limit. By leveraging approximate adiabatic invariants, we expand the
classical equal-area technique to include both integral and differential forms.
We model and simulate shock behavior within initially finite, sinusoidal wave
trains, identifying distinct patterns for internal shocks, and both head and tail
shocks, and confirming that our expressions align with numerical results. The
findings reveal that our integral theory accurately predicts the occurrence of
shock breaking or wave period reformation. Furthermore, we observe that our new
differential formula precisely tracks the evolution of shock fronts. Through
numerical simulations, we demonstrate that both integral and differential forms
of the theory effectively capture the behavior of waves by comparing them to exact solutions derived through matching procedures. The results also highlight a significant difference in the ability of head and tail shocks to maintain wave energy and eject matter. Additionally, we find that both types of massive stars and neutron stars experience shock breaking or shock reformation due to acoustic waves, and that this phenomenon may lead to periodic energy releases, given that the initial increase in luminosity does not significantly exceed the Eddington limit. This paper may also help to address puzzles arising from X-ray dips and super-Eddington outbursts observed in X-ray binaries.

THz radiation enables the precise stimulation of vibrational frequencies in molecules and crystals, leading to the introduction of inertial influences on electrons. By drawing a comparison to classical mechanics, where circular motion generates corotating frames, we identify analogous effect in quantum mechanics, where electron motion creates its own reference frames that rotate at the same speed as the vibrational motion. These frames can be used to reveal hidden periodic potentials and facilitate the diagnosis of electron behavior through the detection of vibrational motion-induced electrical currents. We apply this concept to the specific case of anharmonic vibrations in carbon nanotubes and demonstrate how it may provide a pathway to detecting coherent structural changes in solids through THz radiation. Furthermore, we propose that high-intensity THz fields could reveal the electron spin by inducing a potential for spin-dependent electron motion and potentially making the spin observable. Ultimately, this research suggests that quantum electron physics may be controllable and observable through the deliberate application of vibrational motion-induced periodic potentials in atoms and molecules, providing a foundation for a new area of research at the interface of quantum electron physics and vibrational electronics.

Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. It was discovered that the contradiction relation yields more precise results than the neutral relation in measuring diversity and integrating the NLI model's confidence achieves the highest performance to date. Secondly, this paper demonstrates a way to enhance the semantic variety of responses generated by the model through an iterative procedure called Diversity Threshold Generation, which, in comparison to standard generation methods, results in an average 137% improvement in NLI Diversity. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents select between two tasks of varying difficulty that require simultaneous fulfillment. It is essential to note that the system's structure and agent decision-making follow a linear rational expectations model. We demonstrate that in this scenario, a stable state of cooperation can be achieved through a method analogous to solving systems of polynomial equations. Furthermore, this approach allows us to establish conditions for cooperative equilibrium solutions by applying the Bezier curve construction. Additionally, our analysis identifies an intriguing connection between cooperative solutions and the geometry of Bezier curves. We also develop an algorithm to compute cooperative solutions efficiently. To illustrate the effectiveness of this method, we present an example where the structure of the system evokes the shape of a Klein bottle. Moreover, our research implies that complex cooperative solutions can be analyzed through geometric analysis methods.

As precision strategies advance for future colliders like HL-LHC, FCC-ee, FCC-hh, ILC, CLIC, CEPC, and CPPC, accurately controlling theoretical predictions becomes essential. We examine the potential role of amplitude-based resummation in achieving this level of control, with case studies at the LHC, future colliders, and even in quantum gravity. Our findings suggest that the method can significantly enhance the theoretical precision, likely leading to better alignment with experimental sensitivity in various processes. However, the implementation of this approach is computationally intensive and may not be feasible with current in-house computational capabilities for some of the most complex processes. Therefore, the development of new tools that can efficiently handle amplitude-based resummation, such as an extension to CutTools or a new on-demand tree-level amplitude generator, is necessary to make rapid progress in this area. We also highlight the importance of exploring new beyond-NLO resummation approaches, addressing uncontrolled scale variations at the NNLL/NNLLO accuracy, to further improve the theoretical precision in particle physics.

In the context of artificial intelligence, learning can take place without centralizing data among parties known as participants. There are two primary approaches to this decentralization: horizontal federated learning and vertical federated learning. While both methods learn from decentralized data, they differ significantly in terms of data representation and learning processes. This study focuses on vertical federated learning, a process in which participants learn from decentralized data by constructing a decision tree together. Although this method addresses concerns about data protection, it raises privacy risks associated with learning processes. In an effort to address these privacy risks, we developed a method for constructing decision trees without revealing participants' data to each other. This method enables multiple parties to construct a single decision tree by exchanging minimal amounts of encrypted data. Furthermore, this method allows multiple decision trees to be constructed, and these trees can be combined into an overall decision tree. We evaluated this approach using publicly available datasets and found that it can effectively prevent unauthorized access to participants' data and reduce the amount of data exchanged. This, in turn, improves learning accuracy and reduces the amount of data required for optimal performance. Compared to traditional vertical federated learning, this approach requires significantly fewer communication exchanges, which can lead to substantial cost savings in bandwidth-intensive applications. We also developed a cryptographic technique that can handle large datasets by breaking them into smaller, randomly selected samples. This technique, known as a single-data-point multi-party learning approach, enables a single decision tree to be constructed from exchanged datasets. We demonstrated the efficacy of this approach using a large dataset from the legal domain. This research offers a novel cryptographic technique for constructing decision trees in a decentralized setting and can serve as a foundation for future work on multi-level decision trees. This work is relevant to industries that handle large, sensitive datasets, such as healthcare and finance, and can contribute to the development of artificial intelligence systems that prioritize data confidentiality. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. This constraint is particularly significant when data sets are modern, high-dimensional, and sampled without a marginal weight - a common scenario in many research fields. To overcome this limitation, the use of random Fourier features has been proposed as a method to enlarge the capacity of kernel-based models while reducing computational costs. However, this method has a significant drawback: it significantly increases model parameters, requiring careful optimization to avoid significant performance degradation. In this research, we introduce a new technique that allows kernel-based models to be scaled up to modern, high-dimensional datasets through sampled evaluations of the kernel matrix, eliminating the need for parameter optimization. This technique leverages the mathematical properties of the kernel function and is demonstrated through a series of experiments across four diverse text classification datasets, resulting in consistent performance improvement of at least 10%. The code used in this research is openly accessible on the GitHub platform. 

Keywords: kernel methods, random fourier features, machine learning, without marginal weight.

In our study, we demonstrated how both a group that operates on a set in a recurring manner and a diagonal group are effectively incorporated into the wreath products under their combined, or product action, utilizing the Cartesian Decomposition technique. This integrated form, which we call $g \cdot \Gamma \cdot D$, precisely embodies the outcome of applying both the group operating in a recurring manner and the diagonal group simultaneously. Our method also clarifies that this combined form is attainable by applying the group operating in a recurring manner to the set in question and then subsequently applying the diagonal group. We then establish that this combined form operates in a recurring manner on the cross-product of the set in question and the set operated upon by the diagonal group, thereby identifying $g \cdot \Gamma \cdot D$ as an embodiment of the product action of the group operating in a recurring manner and the diagonal group, or their product action. This finding is particularly relevant when the group operating in a recurring manner is a monoid, in which case the product action is also a monoid. Our findings also facilitate an alternative expression for the cross-product of the group operating in a recurring manner and the diagonal group, leading to an innovative solution to a problem initially posed by A. Thron. Furthermore, this enables an additional general expression for the cross-product of two groups operating in a recurring manner when one of the groups is a monoid, and this results in an engaging mathematical exploration. For instance, this enables us to derive an intriguing formula for calculating the number of fixed points of the harmonic group operating in a recurring manner on the set of non-negative integers, which is equivalent to the harmonic group operating in a recurring manner on the set of positive integers. This understanding, derived from our method, is also applicable to polynomial groups operating in a recurring manner. In this context, we introduce a novel concept of "weak coherence" for polynomial groups operating in a recurring manner, which ensures the same behavior as "strong coherence" but is more broadly applicable. Ultimately, this enables us to tackle fundamental questions about wreath products and their fixed points in a more general framework. Our method is particularly versatile and can be employed in conjunction with other techniques to further explore the intricacies of group theory operating in a recurring manner. To illustrate this, we utilize our method to analyze the harmonic group operating in a recurring manner with various actions and demonstrate its effectiveness in this context. Consequently, our study is an initial step in a more comprehensive investigation of group theory operating in a recurring manner and its applications

This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. We start by classifying and describing these conformally flat hypersurfaces when they have constant M\"obius curvature under specific transformations. Next, we prove that a compact hypersurface with this constant M\"obius curvature, denoted R, is specifically equal to $(n-1)(n-2)r^2$ for values of r less than 1. Furthermore, if this hypersurface is compact, we establish that it is topologically equivalent to a torus defined by the union of a circle with a radius of $\sqrt{1-r^2}$ and a hypersphere with a radius of r in the space of n+1 dimensions. Conversely, any compact hypersurface that is topologically equivalent to this described shape and has a M\"obius curvature of r^2, where r is less than 1, can be obtained through a combination of these conformal transformations. Additionally, we demonstrate that these compact hypersurfaces are not globally minimised when their M\"obius curvature is greater than the M\"obius curvature of a hypersphere. Lastly, we derive an inequality relating the volume of the hypersurface to its M\"obius curvature, thereby establishing a lower bound for the M\"obius curvature when the volume is sufficiently large. We also discover an analogue of Brightman and Diver's result, demonstrating that the hypersurface is not minimised when its M\"obius curvature exceeds a certain threshold at least in certain cases. We conclude by posing several open questions for further research.

Optimally timing pulmonary valve replacement surgery in Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) patients primarily relies on heart volume and function criteria.  Our research aims to analyze decision-making processes for surgical intervention through a multi-criteria optimization approach, incorporating right ventricular volume and a specific functional index, the velocity image integration (VI).  By reviewing medical images from 1 to 19 years after initial surgery for 15 patients with TOF, our study identifies the critical point at which pulmonary valve replacement is needed to prevent right ventricular failure, as determined by both volume and VI metrics. A mathematical model derived from our data can predict the optimal timing of pulmonary valve replacement for each individual patient by considering both volume and VI factors. Object detectors, in particular those that utilize Feature Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in FPNs. This paper reexamines FPNs from a theoretical perspective and reveals that they inherently cannot handle objects across the entire image scale range seamlessly. It demonstrates that incorporating an auxiliary output over the entire image can significantly improve the accuracy of large-scale bounding boxes by leveraging additional scale information, but this only works when using simple backbone networks. Nevertheless, with complex backbone networks, the benefit disappears, and the method even results in a decline in precision. To resolve this issue, the proposed Spatially Adaptive Feature Pyramid (SPATIAN) significantly outperforms current best practices across a broad range of metrics on the MS COCO dataset. The main concept underlying this approach is the observation that using the auxiliary output with complex backbone networks results in a deterioration of precision due to the unnecessary computation of redundant feature map combinations. Consequently, the proposed method introduces an auxiliary output for each individual feature map, and this results in the method being at no additional computational cost compared to standard detectors. The method further improves detection accuracy by eliminating unnecessary feature map combinations that do not contribute to precision. This is achieved by determining a suitable combination of feature maps that can be used for accurate large-scale object detection through a systematic evaluation of all possible combinations. The results show that the proposed method delivers a substantial boost in large-scale object detection accuracy with no increase in computational cost. Complex, multi-dimensional data is often analyzed with conditionally specified models, which rely on implicit assumptions at their boundaries. Unfortunately, current methodologies lack a systematic approach to assess these extreme assumptions due to complex copula and marginal forms. In contrast, this research introduces novel tools to measure the implicit assumptions of conditional models concerning their boundaries. These tools allow us to derive explicit formulas for approximating extreme cases of a specific type of model, including the distribution of a tail event and a key metric of asymptotic independence. The method is then demonstrated with a widely used model, and an alternative condition is also introduced to address limitations in the original Heffernan-Tawn model's ability to capture certain cases of asymptotic independence. The proposed methods are validated through simulation and real-world data analysis. The newly introduced concepts and results provide a deeper understanding of conditional models' extreme assumptions and can be used to analyze multi-dimensional data, facilitating more effective identification of the causes of extreme events. The methods are available in the accompanying R package called THREPs. The research is ultimately aimed at enhancing conditional model building's ability to pinpoint the underlying reasons for rare events in complex, multi-dimensional data sets. The newly described techniques are also applicable to the analysis of tail events in statistical models beyond the Heffernan-Tawn model. The study is premised on the notion that rare events in complex systems often have a significant impact and require a high level of scrutiny. The developed tools can be used in risk management to identify the key factors that contribute to significant losses. The methods are novel and address a significant limitation in the current understanding of conditional models, particularly concerning their extreme assumptions. The research is a critical step towards building conditional models that can accurately identify the underlying causes of rare events in complex, multi-dimensional data sets. The developed tools can be used in risk management to provide detailed information about the key factors that contribute to significant losses. The methods are highly versatile and can be applied to any statistical model that contains the Heffernan-Tawn model as a special case. The research is an important milestone in the development of conditional models and will have a lasting impact on various fields, including risk management, finance, and multi-dimensional data analysis. The methods are now available in the THREPs R package, facilitating the implementation of the described techniques in real-world applications. The research is also accompanied by an R package that provides the method's implementation and several demonstration datasets, including the Swiss Temperature dataset. The package enables users to access the developed tools and reproduce the results presented in the research

We aim to tackle the Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) challenge, which poses a difficulty in language understanding where identical word forms convey different meanings based on context. Although humans naturally infer word meanings from their context, machines struggle with this task. In order to build upon and improve previous work, particularly Huang et al's. GlossBERT model, which addresses WSD (Huang et al.,2019), we plan to enhance their results through modifications to their dataset, ensemble techniques, and replacing BERT with alternative transformer architectures like BART and ALBERT. A corresponding GitHub repository contains our code and the modified dataset used for both single and ensemble-based experiments. Interestingly, our findings reveal that both applying ensemble techniques and replacing BERT yield similar performance increases when compared to the original results by Huang et al.,2019. Moreover, our results show no notable improvements from using the more recent Multi-Head Attention technique proposed by Huang et al.,2019. Furthermore, we observed that using the ALBERT transformer results in a similar performance when compared to BART. Ultimately, our most successful ensemble model surpasses the current state-of-the-art by achieving a 73.1% performance score according to the standard SecEval metric. We hope that both our code and the modifications to the dataset will contribute to advancements in WSD through both dataset and model improvements. Reasoning about and sequencing unordered events is a crucial skill to understand real-world procedures that involve various forms of communication. Sequential task comprehension typically requires reading extensive text and then executing the learned sequence of actions. Comprehending sequential tasks becomes increasingly difficult when task instructions are presented as unstructured and unordered lists of points. To investigate this challenge, our task, Unordered Sequence Execution (USE), asks a model to execute a sequence of actions based on unstructured and unordered instruction lists. Our evaluations show that current advanced language models perform worse than machine learning baselines when evaluating instruction execution, demonstrating the difficulty of this task. To enhance USE task performance, we suggest using an executive model that executes a sequence of actions learned from structured action lists and evaluate this approach with multiple executive model designs. Our research reveals that current executive models struggle with complex action sequences and that USE task results are negatively impacted by list format variations. To address this, we propose using an executive model that can process raw text and evaluate this approach with multiple USE task datasets. Our results indicate potential for further research in this area. Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization by removing nodes in a specific order, known as the avalanche method. However, the complexity of the immunization model increases significantly with large networks. To address this challenge, a new model called the "dynamical avalanche" was proposed, which utilizes a first-in-last-out approach to prioritize node removal. Although this model reduces the complexity of the immunization challenge, it's unclear whether it can lead to similar results as the traditional avalanche method. To answer this question, we analyze the complexity of the dynamical avalanche model and investigate its applicability to various network attack scenarios. Additionally, we propose a generalization of the model called the "general dynamical avalanche," which can be used to study immunization in temporal networks. To demonstrate the feasibility of this model, we apply it to an analysis of the spread of ideas in a social media network focused on the dissemination of fake news during the 2020 US presidential election. Due to the potential for rapid data collection through API access, we anticipate the general dynamical avalanche model to contribute significantly to the study of temporal networks.

Properties of semi-classical orthogonal polynomials relative to a generalized Airy weight and their corresponding zeros and recurrence coefficients are examined, where specific parameters apply. The study is extended to a symmetrized form of this weight known as the generalized sextic Freud weight to analyze the limiting case where the weights become equivalent. The focus then shifts towards characterizing the quasi-classical behavior of these polynomials and their associated properties. The characterization process involves the solution of a nonlinear discrete Painlevé equation, and the resulting formulas provide a foundation for studying the polynomial's properties, including its recurrence coefficients, potential values, and the relationships between its zeros and oscillatory characteristics. The study of the corresponding Hermite-Padé approximations is also an area of interest. The study is motivated by the observation that the classical and semi-classical orthogonal polynomials exhibit intricate connections with Hermite-Padé approximations and hypergeometric functions, which are then analyzed through the solution of a nonlinear discrete Painlevé equation and the associated properties derived therefrom. The developed formulas are the key to the study of the underlying polynomial properties, further extending the established connections between analytic and algebraic functions and the related polynomials and Hermite-Padé approximations. The focus of this paper is specifically on the generalized Airy weight and its symmetrized form, the generalized sextic Freud weight, which are the most broadly applicable cases given the method's suitability. The method is also shown to be an adaptable framework for any non-negative weight function $y(x)$ with isolated zeros for its orthogonal polynomials. The associated Hermite-Padé approximations are then a set of monic polynomials $p_{N}(x)$ such that $p_{N}(x)/\mathfrak{d}(x)^{N}$ provides a best fit to $e^{-\mathfrak{d}^2(x)}$ in the complex plane except at the branch points of $\mathfrak{d}(x)$. The study of these approximations is an area of ongoing research. The considered cases hold parameters that satisfy specific constraint sets, denoted as $\mathcal{S}_m$ for weights of degree $m$, where the constraints are such that the weight defines a set of non-degenerate semi-classical orthogonal polynomials. The method used to derive the formulas for the zeros, recurrence coefficients and the associated Hermite-Padé polynomials is the quasi-classical approach, a method that solves the Stieltjes-Wigert problem.

Recent large-scale MIMO systems are considered an exciting development, capable of providing rapid data transfer in crowded environments. As a result of their substantial size, MIMO arrays are subject to space-based disruptions and varying ranges that affect how data is transmitted. To study these systems, researchers use a technique where the environment is broken down into smaller parts, analyzed statistically, and then simulated numerically to assess their performance. This statistical approach allows researchers to investigate complex interactions between MIMO arrays and their surroundings but also incorporates assumptions that may not always reflect real-world conditions perfectly. To gain a more accurate understanding, researchers propose a new framework that uses empirical data to better capture the statistical properties of MIMO arrays in action. This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for larger numbers of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a system of up to 20 ions, achieving an average reduction of frequency errors of ion entanglement by a factor of 100, compared to conventional Molmer-Sorensen gates. We found that up to 7 extra photons can be tolerated before the gate's performance is noticeably impaired, a limitation set by motion mode decoherence and laser phase noise. This upscaling capability is shown to enable the development of a reliable quantum gate within a reasonable error tolerance in a system comprising 20 ions and 20 logical qubits. Additionally, this robustness enables the development of reliable molecular motion-based quantum parity gates and molecular motion-based conditional sign flips, essential components for trapped ion-based Shor codes. This study offers an efficient solution for addressing frequency errors, a pervasive issue in the development of quantum gates using trapped ions, and provides a crucial step towards the creation of fault-tolerant quantum gates on a larger scale. This approach can serve as a foundation for the development of large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum chemistry using trapped ions. This research can also be applied to other quantum systems prone to frequency drift, such as superconducting qubits, by utilizing the same-scaleable frequency compensation techniques used in this study. This breakthrough technology is anticipated to play a significant role in the acceleration of large-scale quantum development. This work is also accompanied by the open-source software necessary for its implementation. This software is built on top of the Python QI SDK and is freely available at https://github.com/QuantumIsolated/Molmer-Sorensen-robust. Using advanced computer simulations of atoms in motion, we've found that titanium in barium titanate maintains an unexpected position within its molecular structure even when it's not polarized. This discovery challenges the widely held assumption that certain simulations can be bypassed when modeling this phenomenon. To address this, we utilized machine learning to develop multiple accurate statistical models that capture the behavior of titanium in the presence or absence of polarization. Further, we identified that two simple underlying structures can effectively represent the polarization of titanium within a barium titanate structure, and that these models can be used to generate useful statistical predictions for other elements within similar structures. These predictions have the potential to enhance existing computer simulations of atoms in motion and may also be applied to other types of materials that possess a similar structural framework.

Lately, researchers have focused intensely on solid electronic theory's strongly correlated systems and graphene, yet the $sp^{2}$-electrons that form Dirac bands in graphene lack strong interactions. Consequently, novel, interaction-induced phenomena tied to Dirac points are underutilized. We propose GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ as a new material where Dirac electrons are paired with strong interactions and frustrated magnetism. Calculations indicate its crystallographic and electronic properties harbor symmetry-protected Dirac points at the Fermi level, allowing for multifaceted physics encompassing possible instabilities of charge, magnetism, or superconductivity. By merging various methods to assess its many-body behavior, researchers have observed potential transitions to Mott-Hubbard, magnetic or charge-orbital ordered states, along with $f$-wave superconductivity facilitated by spin-orbit coupling and nearby Fermi surfaces. This unique merging of Dirac electrons and strong interactions makes GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ an ideal candidate for researching interaction-induced phenomena in graphenoid materials. Additionally, researchers have proposed a method to adjust the material's properties through isoelectronic doping, an attribute essential to testing its proposed phases of matter. Due to its sensitivity, researchers strongly advise developing reliable doping techniques to ensure accurate, reliable results in future research.

Estimation is achieved via maximum likelihood, supported by a Monte Carlo simulation evaluating the efficacy of these estimators in finite samples. A real-world application illustrates the proposed distribution's aptitude in modeling data sets with bimodal patterns. The associated R package enables convenient implementation of the methods.

In a gyroscopic Sagnac interferometer, typically used for calibrating a gyroscope's angular momentum, a notable spectral shift around anomalies occurs. This spectral shift within the rotating gyroscope can be understood in relation to the longitudinal Doppler shift experienced by the opposing light beams in the Sagnac interferometer. A mathematical derivation, taking into consideration the rotation-induced phase difference, yields a key equation that connects the spectral shift to the rotation rate, carrier wavelength, and cavity dimensions. Through the application of this equation, accurate calibration of the angular momentum of a gyroscope can be achieved even in the presence of anomalies. Furthermore, this method may provide a means to measure rotation rates in a gyroscope-calibrated environment. A demonstration involving a diode laser was conducted to validate the proposed method, showing that calibration based on the derived formula is significantly more accurate (by a factor of at least 100) than the conventional method used for rotation rates below 10$^{\circ}$/s. A notable feature of this approach is its potential to provide rotation rate information without relying on the time it takes for the gyroscope to reach its initial state. Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we tested various strategies to combine the strengths of both models, resulting in a method that leverages $n$-gram-based language knowledge while utilizing neural models' efficient test-time inference. The proposed model showcases significant improvements in both task efficiency and performance on intrinsic evaluation tasks, ultimately providing valuable insights for the community to reevaluate the status of $n$-gram models in modern NLP. Our code has been made available for public use.

We've developed families of three-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial, non-toric terminal Fano varieties of considerable depth, corresponding to 54 distinct mutation classes in the realm of Laurent polynomials. From the perspective of mirror symmetry, these high-dimensional non-toric varieties establish the Fano/Landau-Ginzburg connection for our current knowledge limits. Building upon this foundation, 46 more $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds have been constructed, with their depth spanning between 10 and 19. Among these, certain examples will be expressed as toric complete intersections and others as Pfaffian varieties. Furthermore, we've derived 24 $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds of depth 10 and demonstrate their depth can be achieved by non-toric varieties alone. This breakthrough is accompanied by the presence of an LG model for each of these 54 $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds, thereby extending the current record in algebraic geometry. These discoveries were made possible by combining the techniques of [KKP20] and adapting them to the context of Fano varieties. As a result, 46 $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds with depth between 10 and 19 have been constructed. Among these, certain examples will be expressed as Pfaffian varieties and others as Picard rank 2 Fano varieties. As for the Picard rank 2 Fano 3-folds, our research reveals that their birational counterparts can be expressed as the hypersurfaces of forms analogous to $x^a + y^b + z^c = 0$, where the variables $x, y, z$ are replaced by sections of line bundles over $\mathbb{P}^3$. It's also shown that such varieties can be mutated to yield 18 distinct $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds. As a result, the previous limit of 5 for the non-toric depth of Fano 3-folds has been surpassed. As for the Picard rank 1 Fano 3-folds, our research constructs 24 $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano 3-folds of depth 10 and demonstrates that their depth can be achieved by non-toric varieties alone. These discoveries are accompanied by the derivation of LG models for each of these 54 $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds, thereby extending the current record in algebraic geometry.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Experimental evaluations on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets demonstrate notable improvements in both face alignment and reconstruction metrics. Moreover, our method achieves superior results compared to the current state-of-the-art approaches on the more recent AFW-3D and COFW-3D datasets. In informed ocular screening, an Informed OCR (iOCR) is a cutting-edge technology that excels conventional OCR by using visual feedback to guide text recognition. This innovative approach leverages the capabilities of computer vision and machine learning to create an immersive user interface where users can correct errors and inaccuracies in real-time. As a result, iOCR is distinguished from traditional OCR systems through its superior accuracy, error detection, and user engagement. This analysis looks to quantify the advantages of iOCR over traditional OCR by conducting a time--error diagram analysis of both systems. To accomplish this, a series of experiments are designed to measure the time it takes to complete each task using both iOCR and conventional OCR, along with corresponding error rates. These results in turn allow for a comparative assessment of the time--error costs of each system, ultimately demonstrating the superior performance of iOCR. This research is relevant to any application where optical character recognition is used to capture data, such as medical records, legal documents, and everyday user forms. As such, it is hoped that this analysis will contribute to a broader understanding of the benefits of using informed ocular screening in place of conventional OCR methods. This research is particularly salient within the context of automated document management systems, where even slight reductions in error rates can have substantial implications for data quality and system performance. As a byproduct of this analysis, suggestions are provided to system designers looking to optimize the integration of computer vision and machine learning components within iOCR systems. Deep neural networks (DNNs) benefit from being trained on optimal subsets of annotated data. Active learning algorithms effectively achieve this by pinpointing data samples that are essential for improving DNN performance. The method is particularly advantageous in large-scale industrial settings where labeling costs are exorbitant. The emergence of self-supervised pretraining highlights the capacity of models to leverage unlabeled data for significant enhancements. Integrating active learning with self-supervised pretraining allows the exploration of novel paradigms where the model can navigate through unlabeled data to identify optimal labeling targets. Despite the potential benefits, the current state of research is limited due to the absence of thorough investigations into active learning algorithms that can effectively exploit unlabeled data for finding high-value annotation targets. This paper provides an initial exploration into this unexplored area, encompassing both theoretical and practical aspects. We examine whether existing active learning algorithms can benefit from being combined with self-supervised pretraining and conduct an empirical study using popular AL algorithms on multiple SSO-SAL benchmark datasets. Our results reveal that employing current AL methods with self-supervised pretraining does not lead to anticipated improvements. This discovery prompts the development of novel criteria for evaluating SSO-SAL algorithms and inspires the creation of two new benchmark datasets that can facilitate future research in this area. Additionally, we introduce a unique AL algorithm known as AL-Encoder-Decoder, which is designed to exploit the structural information extracted by self-supervised encoder representations to identify valuable annotation targets. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method is capable of finding high-value annotation targets even when combined with diverse encoder models and outperforms existing AL algorithms even without the aid of self-supervised features. This research lays the groundwork for further exploration into the integration of active learning and self-supervised pretraining and encourages the development of innovative AL algorithms that can effectively exploit structural information for finding high-value annotation targets. All code and datasets developed as part of this research are available at https://github.com/zhengda Zhang/SSO-SAL.

Researchers who utilize silicon donor spin have reached a record for coherence time and one-qubit gate accuracy. To advance further, demonstrating the fidelity of two-qubit logic gates is now crucial. This advancement depends on the ability to control the exchange interaction between donor electrons by applying nearby metal electrodes to modify their environment through the coulomb force. To make progress in this area, it is essential to understand the intricate relationship between electron densities in two donors that are close to each other, particularly when they contain charged defects. To study this relationship, a comprehensive classical model of a silicon donor was developed that considers the influence of nearby charged defects, metal electrodes, and dopants. This model includes a parameter that represents the exchange interaction and shows that it can be utilized to develop a highly accurate numerical method for calculating electron densities in charged silicon donors. This method can be employed to devise a strategy to create a reliable and accurate two-qubit logic operation, such as the CNOT gate, that achieves a high degree of fidelity when the exchange interaction is turned on and off quickly. As an example, a layout for a CNOT gate was proposed where the exchange interaction between two donors can be initiated or terminated within a few microseconds by adjusting the electron densities in nearby metal electrodes. This suggests that researchers can build a reliable and accurate two-qubit logic gate based on silicon donors. This model can also be used to develop other two-qubit logic gates, such as the Toffoli and Jordan-Meier gates, and even multi-qubit logic gates like the Fredkin gate. Additionally, this model indicates that the fidelity of two-qubit logic gates can be significantly improved by employing a highly sensitive method to control the exchange interaction, known as "gate rectification," which involves using a reliable and accurate one-qubit logic gate to convert an inaccurate two-qubit logic gate into a correct outcome. As an example, a scheme was proposed to convert an inaccurate CNOT gate into a correct result using a nearby silicon spin qubit that can be controlled precisely. This indicates that researchers can build a reliable and accurate multi-qubit logic gate based on silicon donors. Wireless communication systems can make significant contributions to preventing road accidents through alert message transmission, particularly in high-risk areas like road intersections. Non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) has shown promise for 5G systems, and our proposed adaptive cooperative NOMA (ACN) protocol enhances VC's performance in this area. In a scenario where vehicles on intersecting roads generate interfering signals with a varying intensity, we develop a mathematical model to quantify this interference in a queueing theory framework. Numerical analysis confirms that the proposed ACN protocol significantly reduces waiting times for data to be transmitted, particularly in nomadic areas, by increasing the success probability of transmitting alert and safety messages by at least 90%. Furthermore, ACN outperforms other schemes like OMA and D2D systems by at least 75% in this regard. Moreover, ACN's performance is evaluated under dynamic conditions where vehicles' mobility is modeled as Markov process, and we investigate how the success probability of data transmission varies with different mobility patterns. Finally, we examine the impact of increasing nomadic activity on successful data transmission probability and find that ACN's advantages are more pronounced in busier environments. Overall, our study indicates that ACN is highly effective in facilitating safe communication on busy road intersections.

In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions. Additionally, increased independence in TDD scheduling decisions is shown to lead to diverse, optimal solutions. Furthermore, our results indicate that in some cases, dynamic TDD can provide better communication quality than static TDD solutions. Lastly, our method's performance is found to be robust in scenarios with moving cells and users.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes this metric to determine a confidence level and selectively seek human feedback to correct both types of errors. We applied this approach to two classification tasks and observed a significant decrease in both error rates and a more balanced performance distribution. Furthermore, we found that this method is computationally efficient and effectively leverages human resources. Additionally, we examined the benefits of incorporating three different types of human feedback into the system. To facilitate reproducibility, the code for our study is openly accessible on GitHub. By demonstrating the benefits and cost-effectiveness of this approach, we believe it has the potential to serve as a model for creating other machine learning scoring agents that can enhance both the accuracy and reliability of AI models.

In x-ray image analysis, identifying prohibited items contributes to maintaining public safety. However, the difficulty lies in detecting low-contrast, color-less objects which can result in unsatisfactory performance. Until now, there have been limited studies in this field due to the absence of high-quality specialized datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel dataset named High-quality X-ray (HiXray), which contains a comprehensive collection of 8 prohibited item categories and comprises 102,928 high-quality images. These images are extracted from real-world airport security inspections and annotated by experienced security personnel to ensure their practical relevance. To further enhance the detection of prohibited items, we introduce a simple yet effective module called Lateral Inhibition Module, which simulates the inhibition of adjacent objects by incorporating external object information into the self-attention mechanism. To facilitate future research, we also introduce a baseline model that utilizes HiXray features to achieve a mean average precision (mAP) of 0.416 on the HiXray validation set. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. Additionally, we establish a relationship between $J_n^T$ and a variant of the original colored Jones polynomial, leading to implications for its volume conjecture behavior.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in conjunction with structured knowledge for the purpose of solving WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both lexical and semantic data augmentation techniques are capable of enhancing the accuracy of WSD, with the latter proving particularly effective, especially when utilizing BERT.  A comparison of different fusion approaches for combining structured knowledge also reveals that the simple addition of knowledge vectors yields the best outcomes, which is particularly noteworthy given the straightforward nature of this approach.  Furthermore, an evaluation across multiple WSD tasks reveals that the proposed method is robust and effective. This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement. Moreover, a tool is provided for visualizing and evaluating the quality of generated SQL in relation to actual database contents. This tool is made publicly accessible for community review and is invite-only at https://tinyurl.com/44zcpksh; interested parties can request access by emailing the authors. With this tool, assessors can navigate the evaluation process presented in this paper and engage in discussions on future work in the field of cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing.

Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems and macroscopic quantum states, with quantum field hydrodynamics being a prominent approach for this simulation. Despite its utility, this method is typically restricted to systems near equilibrium due to the lack of a suitable nonequilibrium hydrodynamics framework. In this study, we extend the quantum field hydrodynamics to nonequilibrium situations by utilizing the positive-P phase-space formalism. This new description can be applied to any interacting Bose gases that exhibit quasiequilibrium behavior and allows for the simulation of phenomena like quantum shock waves and nonlinear sound waves. Furthermore, this framework enables the calculation of nonequilibrium phase transitions and quasiequilibrium phase diagrams for systems like superfluids in porous media or under magnetic fields. To validate this new hydrodynamical approach, it must be derived from a full quantum-field-theory description, which can be achieved through the development of nonequilibrium effective actions. This study proposes the use of inexact gradient methods for this purpose. By applying these methods to the quantum hydrodynamics of interacting Bose gases, we can derive the nonequilibrium hydrodynamics proposed in this study. This new hydrodynamical approach may also be relevant to other quantum systems, such as Fermi gases or systems described by the Helfrich theory. This research provides a framework for simulating nonequilibrium phase transitions in superfluids and may have implications for understanding shock wave behavior in these systems. This could be particularly important for interpreting experimental data obtained through high-intensity laser pulses on superfluid helium, where shock waves may be generated, leading to the creation of metastable states and defects.
