Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment. For proposal generation, we use Dual Context Aggregation (DCA) to consider global contexts and refine proposals by exploring the entire video duration. Our method has achieved exceptional performance on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14, achieving an average mean average precision (mAP) of 35.39% and 51.09% at a hard threshold of 100 proposals per video, respectively. Our code is openly accessible at https://github.com/zhengyangsui/DCAN.

The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic despite detailed documentation. A recently investigated explanation suggests that these structures form when magnetic field eddies caused by edge-localized modes trigger the development of a PTM seed island. However, this study instead seeks to provide an alternate explanation based on observations of edge plasma turbulence. A distinct feature of plasma turbulence is the existence of persistent structures known as blobs and holes in the scrape-off-layer. Measuring the currents within these coherent regions reveals that they follow the direction of the magnetic field. Hence, this study proposes that the active magnetic field within these turbulent structures could give rise to a PTM through a magnetic reconnection event occurring when a hole undergoes flux loss. This theory is further supported by a simulation demonstrating that the characteristic changes observed in a PTM can result from this reconnection process. Notably, this scenario may also explain the phenomenon of synchronized PTM occurrences in separate locations along the plasma border. It is suggested that this synchronization may be caused by a shared driving force, such as an edge-localized mode, acting on the turbulent edge plasma and leading to a coordinated transition between the 'on' state of a PTM and its 'off' state. It is also proposed that a PTM in the 'off' state could potentially be identified as a 'hole' state, providing valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms governing the edge plasma turbulence. Ultimately, this study advocates for a broader examination of the relationship between plasma turbulence and magnetic field activity in the edge regions of tokamaks. It is hoped that this investigation will contribute to a fresh perspective on the long-standing challenge of tokamak edge plasma confinement. It is also proposed that a global magnetic flux model, integrated with a turbulence solver, would be an effective tool in analyzing this phenomenon. This research focuses on resolving collision avoidance for non-holonomic robots moving at constant speeds in a two-dimensional space, leveraging dynamic vortex potential fields and their gradients to create cooperative behavior between the robots. A variable repulsive force field, sensitive to velocity and position of nearby robots, is introduced to prevent the emergence of local minima, and only activates when a robot approaches a potential collision with other mobile robots or stationary objects. It's demonstrated through kinematic analysis that a cooperating robot can escape by activating this field and by modulating the potential field's gradient to return to a safe path. The resulting control system is robust, simple, and free from local minima issues. Furthermore, we show that a group of identical, cooperative robots can maintain their individual avoidance strategies while moving towards common dynamic targets. The proposed method is verified through simulation and experimental tests on a mobile robot platform. These findings suggest that this type of potential field-based control could be an effective solution for cooperative collision avoidance in larger groups of non-holonomic robots moving at constant speeds. Given an independent and identically distributed sequence of letters cast into a random word, the annealed large deviation principle (LDP) for the empirical process is characterized by a rate function that equals the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution relative to the independent and identically distributed distribution. This characterization of the rate function is both necessary and sufficient for an independent and identically distributed sequence to exhibit an annealed LDP. Furthermore, this characterization of the rate function is also both necessary and sufficient for a sequence that is not necessarily independent and identically distributed to exhibit an annealed LDP under certain conditions of ergodicity and rate of mixing. Recent advancements in wireless communications research have led to increasing interest in the Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology. Comprised of passive reflective components that can modulate the characteristics of incoming waveforms, such as phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization, an IRS offers a means to actively control the characteristics of wireless channels. Given its promising properties, researchers are looking into the potential of incorporating IRS technology into radar systems to optimize target parameter estimation. This paper provides a theoretical basis for implementing IRS technology in radar systems, with a particular focus on scenarios where the line-of-sight (LOS) link between the radar and target is obstructed or weak. We investigate the potential of utilizing IRS technology to create a virtual non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link, enhancing radar performance and target parameter estimation. Through numerical simulations and comparative analyses under both optimized and non-optimized scenarios, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the virtual NLOS link in improving target parameter estimation when the LOS link strength is low. Additionally, our research indicates that when the LOS link is strong, the performance difference between the two scenarios becomes negligible. Furthermore, we examine the impact of different IRS capabilities on radar performance and target parameter estimation, highlighting the potential of customized IRS units to optimize system performance. Finally, our study suggests that deep learning techniques hold promise for further enhancing the effectiveness of the virtual NLOS link. Through this research, we establish a foundation for future studies on the incorporation of IRS technology in radar systems. Ultimately, this work has the potential to contribute to the development of next-generation radar systems capable of overcoming obstructions and achieving superior performance. Moreover, the concepts explored here may also be applicable to other sensing applications, enabling accurate identification and tracking of targets in complex, line-of-sight-constrained scenarios. Discovering vulnerabilities in programs through fuzzing is a crucial process, but measuring its effectiveness is still an unsolved issue despite the progress made. A widely accepted evaluation standard in software testing is mutation analysis, assessing the ability to detect artificial flaws, and it encompasses a variety of measures that evaluate the ability to trigger and detect faults of any difficulty. However, the traditional mutation analysis approach is impractically costly for fuzzing due to the need for independent evaluation of each mutation. This paper presents the application of modern mutation analysis methods, combining multiple mutations to assess the effectiveness of fuzzers for the first time. An evaluation framework for fuzzers has been introduced and utilized in conjunction with various popular fuzzers and testing subjects. The evaluation results indicate that contemporary fuzzers can detect mutations in only a small percentage, but this outcome serves as a motivation for future research to address the efficient detection of vulnerabilities in programs. To facilitate advancements in this area, the proposed evaluation framework is openly accessible online.

Following the success of pretraining techniques in learning representations, various methods utilizing pre-trained models in continual learning have been developed. Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal updates to the backbone. In this study, we challenge the necessity of complex designs by exploring a significantly simpler approach. We continuous learning is achieved by freezing a pre-trained model and leveraging its existing representations to facilitate accurate feature extraction across tasks. Our primary objective is to examine the relational coherence between tasks of varying difficulty in this context. To do this, we utilize a frozen pre-trained Vision Transformer as the base model for continual learning in image classification tasks. Our findings indicate that models can continually learn new classes with high accuracy even without parameter updates by combining easy and hard tasks in a balanced mini-batch optimization procedure. We demonstrate that this straightforward approach surpasses various complex continual learning methods using optimal neural networks and consistently yield high performance on three diverse datasets. Moreover, our technique demonstrates robustness to different pre-trained models and produces reasonable predictions for out-of-distribution data due to the use of pre-trained representations. To facilitate future research, we release the code and models employed in this analysis. Overall, our work highlights that contemporary pre-trained models possess an inherent capacity for continual learning in isolation. Additionally, our findings suggest that the primary challenge in continual learning lies in achieving optimal results through incremental changes rather than the fundamental difficulty of continual learning itself. To this end, our work offers the theoretical underpinnings for future research in optimal neural networks. Furthermore, our results in the appendices reveal a notable correlation between task difficulty and performance, with a notable plateau effect in the plot of performance against task difficulty. This indicates that the challenge of continual learning is likely a general problem applicable to various models and scenarios. Consequently, researchers should approach the subject with a more skeptical perspective, one that is supported by the notable improvements we observed in challenging scenarios, such as the sharp increase in accuracy when moving from the olla dataset to the olla+ dataset. We define a new concept of relative 1-homotopy type for mappings between a surface and a metric space that contains a specified set of Jordan curves, and investigate its properties. This enables us to prove the existence and local smoothness of the surfaces with minimal area within a particular relative 1-homotopy class in certain types of metric spaces. Furthermore, we establish that these surfaces have a specific level of smoothness, increasing to any desired degree under certain conditions of metric space smoothness. Additionally, we demonstrate that any two minimal surfaces with the same relative 1-homotopy class are smoothly homotopic relative to the boundary. These findings extend previous results of the first author and the authors' previous results concerning closed surfaces to non-closed surfaces. Moreover, we address maps between closed surfaces, demonstrating that the property of having minimal area is invariant under homotopy equivalence of target spaces. Lastly, we provide an example illustrating that the homotopy class of maps with minimal area is not invariant under homotopy equivalence of domain surfaces. The latter two conclusions stem from the investigation of abelian coverings of surfaces. In these investigations, previously utilized techniques from the study of closed surfaces prove unfeasible due to the fundamental differences governing the geometry of open surfaces. Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have yielded significant findings: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and for the first time, determine the spin and parity of the ground state. Additionally, this work builds upon previous findings placing the 0+1 state at 1.78 MeV, confirming it as a robust reference point for future studies of this nucleus. To achieve this research, scientists used the ATOMIC setup at the Barber-Driver Linear Accelerator in Los Alamos, New Mexico, where a high-current, relativistic 56Ni beam was incident on a thick 12C target, enabling the detection of neutron radiation through the (12C,16O) reaction and subsequent analysis of excitation energy spectra of 64Ni via the evaluation of neutron-electron angular correlations. By applying various methods to eliminate background and refine the results, the study pinpointed the energy of the 0+1 state at 1.78 MeV ± 0.02 MeV. Furthermore, this work demonstrated a new approach, demonstrating that by combining data from multiple experiments, extremely precise and robust results can be obtained for well-studied nuclei. However, for nuclei with only initial or limited experimental data, this model may not sufficiently capture their complex structure. Consequently, this work places the current precision for the 0+1 state at 0.02 MeV, a figure that is anticipated to drop to 0.01 MeV with the arrival of new, precision measurement facilities. Ultimately, this study provides a benchmark for future low-spin structure studies of the 64Ni nucleus. Furthermore, by placing the 2+1 state at 2.04 MeV, ± 0.05 MeV, and confirming that it exhibits a characteristic energy spacing of approximately 700 keV with the 0+1 state, this research validates theoretical models suggesting that 64Ni possesses a robust, spherical nuclear shape. Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. The evaluation reveals the j-k fold CV method yields substantial gains in model performance, amounting to a notable 5.3% improvement on the SST dataset. Furthermore, our study provides a framework for parameter tuning by means of variance optimization, introducing a novel technique to address the challenge of model reproducibility. The source code for the reduced variance j-k fold CV method is available online at https://github.com/zhengdf1234/var-j-k-fold-cv. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a material's impending failure, occurring when the force of repelling interactions surpasses that of attracting forces. To date, studies have focused mainly on shear thickening in mixtures with permanent attractions, with the current work instead investigating a dense non-Newtonian mixture featuring temporary repulsions within a nonequilibrium phase. This specific system, involving a dense solution of rod-like particles in a sheared viscoelastic surfactant solution, exhibits sudden and extreme thickening that can be precisely controlled through adjustments to the solution's elasticity. Notably, this shear thickening transition is found to occur before the onset of viscoelastic behavior in the solution and is influenced by the elasticity of its own rod-like particles. This work challenges the prevailing theory that friction is the primary driving force behind shear thickening and instead suggests the phenomenon's origin in the interplay between attractive and repulsive forces, with attractive forces being negligible in this particular system. Instead, the shear thickening transition in this rod-like solution is attributed to the failure of its own rigid rods to withstand high shear stresses, leading to a failure of repulsive forces to maintain stability and resulting in the sudden thickening transition. This work's innovative approach and novel insights offer a fresh perspective on the study of shear thickening in complex fluids. This research paper proposes a novel approach to developing safety-critical controllers for complex nonlinear control systems subject to input limitations. Specifically, it outlines the development of an Input Constrained Control Barrier Function, which pinpoints a secure subset of possible system states and designs a control mechanism to maintain those states. The devised controller can be optimized through an efficiently solvable quadratic program, enabling real-time application. Building upon earlier concepts of Higher Order Control Barrier Functions, ICCBFs demonstrate the ability to tackle a broader class of systems characterized by variable relative degrees. Finally, the paper showcases its efficacy through simulation examples in adaptive cruise control and spacecraft rendezvous.

The focus here is on domain representations via approximation spaces with CF-structures, which involve studying the category of CF-approximation spaces and their morphisms. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. In addition to improving computation speed, our exact algorithm also offers a reliable alternative to potentially biased Monte Carlo estimates. We've made our exact algorithm freely available for the benefit of the NLP community. To illustrate the value of this algorithm, we've used it to refutation prior research claims related to the evaluation of discourse coherence. This was only possible because our exact algorithm can quickly handle large numbers of samples. We believe that by utilizing this exact algorithm in the evaluation of NLP systems, we can enhance the rigor and the overall quality of this research. We've made our exact algorithm for computing paired-permutation tests available online at https://github.com/hahnfr8/ppexact. To access the code used in the experiments discussed in this paper, please visit https://github.com/hahnfr8/discourse-experiments. We've also included the results of the experiments conducted for this paper on GitHub. We'd be happy to share the results of the experiments conducted for this paper with researchers who are interested. We plan to expand on the findings presented in this paper in the future. We look forward to seeing how other researchers choose to use this exact algorithm in the NLP community. Furthermore, instructions on combining and verifying datasets are provided using the knowledge of shipping industry specialists and former top executives. A descriptive analysis of previously unstudied market phenomena known as the "container crisis" is conducted with this data. Structural changes in the data variables are then identified to demonstrate how the dissolution of shipping monopolies affected market behavior. A theoretical framework is introduced to illustrate how the shipping market can be seen as a multi-asset commodity market. We define loom spaces as a more general framework incorporating leaf spaces for pseudo-Anosov flows and link spaces for veering triangulations. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, it is demonstrated that there is a veering triangulation inherently linked to every loom space, with this triangulation's realization being topologically equivalent to 3D space. Furthermore, the realization of link spaces for veering triangulations can be viewed as subcomponents of the realizations of their associated loom spaces. Moreover, the volume calculations for these realizations can be optimized through the use of Thurston's point-counting technique. Moreover, for a given veering triangulation, its realizable 4-dimensional volume is equal to the volume of its associated loom space's realization. Consequently, to calculate the realizable 4-dimensional volume of a veering triangulation, it is sufficient to calculate the volume of its associated loom space's realization. Additionally, this approach enables the proof that the realizable 4-dimensional volume of a veering triangulation is equal to the minimum volume of all its non-degenerate resolutions. Lastly, this conceptual framework is coupled with geometrically-defined graphs called flight trees, allowing the derivation of volume bounds for link spaces and, by extension, veering triangulations through the consideration of flight trees' volume constraints. These bounds are expressed as nested cylinders within the graph's projection onto 4-dimensional space, leading to volume estimates that refine previous limit-set volume bounds. In particular, this approach yields a volume bound of at most 8 for link spaces and veering triangulations. Moreover, this method is demonstrated by calculating a non-trivial volume bound for a specific flight tree-linked veering triangulation with an infinite number of recurrences. This novel method for calculating volume bounds is anticipated to contribute meaningfully to research in the field. Lastly, this research is complemented by an unpublished investigation regarding the topological equivalence between the realizations of link spaces and loom spaces. In contrast, it is shown that there exist link spaces whose realizations are not topologically equivalent to the realizations of other link spaces. This distinction is demonstrated through the examination of a specific pair of link spaces, associated with the veering triangulations derived from the train track graphs of two pseudo-Anosov flows on the non-fillable surface S_g of genus 2. In this context, it is proven that these two link spaces' realizations are topologically equivalent, whereas the two veering triangulations themselves are not graph-isomorphic.

Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by leveraging relational data. These models combine node features with the graph structure, creating flexible and effective models, but they can be challenging to interpret due to their implicit representation of node interactions and graph connectivity. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Kedge, which involves explicitly modifying the graph connectivity to match reduced subgraphs, obtained through a minimum spanning tree algorithm, while maintaining model performance. By only modifying the graph edges, Kedge avoids the need for significant changes to node features. We demonstrate that Kedge graphs converge to the original graph, enabling the use of existing GNN training techniques, and showcase the method's effectiveness on three datasets by reducing the number of edges by a factor of at least five without a decline in model accuracy. Furthermore, Kedge facilitates transparent model interpretations by providing a clear visual representation of the underlying graph connectivity. The code for Kedge is openly accessible on GitHub. To facilitate fair comparison, we introduce the Kedge challenge, which includes preprocessed datasets and evaluation metrics.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch sketches. It's also interesting to note that this improved estimator still has practical value due to its ability to handle massive data sets with approximately 1.06 times the factor of k times the sketch size in terms of storage and computational resources. As for theoretical limitations, this increased safety comes at a cost of accuracy, with a reduced ability to recover the top elements by a factor of k. As a result, this study offers two general techniques that can be applied to various linear sketch algorithms employing randomized measurements. First, it highlights the challenge of maintaining safety in the face of changing inferences as a critical problem to be addressed in future linear sketch research. Second, it suggests that increased safety can be achieved through quadratically greater queries while maintaining practical applicability. Lastly, this study introduces an exhaustive method for analyzing the worst-case performance of linear sketch algorithms. To demonstrate this analysis method, a specific proposal is made to improve the top element estimator, only to be countered with a specific construction indicating that this proposal is, in fact, the optimal solution. Consequently, this study provides the optimal linear sketch algorithm for identifying the top elements of a given vector, demonstrating that this optimal solution can be achieved through the use of CountSketch sketches. As a result, this study concludes that the optimal linear sketch algorithm for identifying the top elements of a given vector is equivalent to the classic CountSketch estimator. As a byproduct of this analysis, an intriguing lower bound is derived, confirming that any linear sketch algorithm requiring fewer queries than the proposed estimator necessarily compromises safety. Furthermore, this study establishes an alternative formulation of the classic estimator and an intriguing new estimator. Interestingly, this new formulation yields an optimal solution to a related combinatorial problem by a factor of k. As a result, this study offers this new estimator as a component for a broader problem, essentially demonstrating its safety with an increased k factor

Building on previous findings, we observed in Part I that compact, singular areas within a manifold of positive scalar curvature can be conformally deformed to related minimal geometries sharing similar characteristics. This deformation preserves attributes like the number of connected components and the topological structure of the singular set. Focusing on Part II, we leverage this result to address two conjectures originally posed by G. Huisien. Firstly, we prove that the conformal deformation increases the number of components in $N$-fold symmetric products. Secondly, we demonstrate the same effect on the singular set's topological structure for manifolds with $N$-fold symmetry. To achieve this, we introduce a new variational approach that allows us to bypass the standard method of blow-up analysis. This new analysis not only confirms the conjectures but also reveals a key implication concerning the stability of certain minimal surfaces. Consequently, we establish that certain stable surfaces under $N$-fold symmetry correspond to those obtained through $n$-fold branched covering in a manifold of positive scalar curvature. This result extends a previous finding specific to $N=2$. Additionally, this new perspective enables us to formulate a conjecture regarding the minimality of certain $N$-fold branched covering surfaces within a manifold of positive scalar curvature. This conjecture is supported by numerical evidence. Lastly, we outline potential future directions by which this conjecture could be validated. These potential directions involve exploring related problems and investigating new approaches to studying minimal surfaces within manifolds of positive scalar curvature. These approaches may also provide insight into the original questions posed by G. Huisien. To conclude, we present an initial analysis aimed at understanding the topology of the singular set in a related setting discussed in Part III. This analysis raises new questions regarding the behavior of the singular set as well as the surface's topology in this alternative scenario. Consequently, this new question becomes a subject of investigation and may warrant further study in the future. Ultimately, this research introduces new perspectives and raises fresh questions in the ongoing exploration of the relationship between minimal surfaces and manifolds of positive scalar curvature. This relationship continues to hold significant importance within the broader context of geometric analysis. A model-based control approach known as model predictive control (MPC) has been widely adopted across various industries for optimizing future input values, with its effectiveness dependent on an accurate system model. However, real-world applications often involve significant model discrepancies due to unmodeled system dynamics, noisy observations, or aging system components. In such scenarios, the optimal future input values are often estimated using a limited and noisy observation window, leading to poor performance. To address this issue, we present a learning-based control approach called penalized predictive control (PPC), which incorporates a penalty term into the MPC cost function to favor inputs that minimize future prediction errors. This effectively enables the controller to utilize past prediction errors, even if the current observation is accurate, thereby improving robustness in the presence of model mismatches. The optimal PPC policy can be obtained through convex optimization with a user-specified prediction horizon, making it feasible for real-time implementation. We also establish the convergence properties of the resulting closed-loop system when the original system is stable. To facilitate real-time computation, we developed a fast algorithm for solving the PPC problem, achieving a average solution time of less than 1 ms on a personal computer for a system with 100 states. The effectiveness of the proposed PPC approach was validated through simulations and real-world experiments on an industrial robot, demonstrating its ability to compensate for significant model discrepancies due to motor aging, with an average improvement of 30% over traditional MPC methods. The fast algorithm and detailed instructions for implementing PPC in MATLAB on real-world robots are available for download at https://github.com/pscherrer/PPC-MPC. The code has been successfully tested on MATLAB R2019a and Simulink 2019a with Real-Time Windows Target and xPC Target. The recent interest in the stock market can be attributed to growing inflation rates prompting people to invest in equities, commodities, and other assets. Deep Learning's ability to accurately predict time series data has been consistently demonstrated. In the realm of technical analysis, using indicators is the most widely adopted approach among traders and investors. Another essential aspect is sentiment analysis, reflecting the emotional state of investors' willingness to invest, where various techniques such as Machine Learning and Neural Networks have been employed. From simple linear regression to advanced neural networks, researchers and investors have experimented with multiple methods to forecast the stock market. It is evident that the underlying factors influencing stock prices are interrelated and among them, the connection between news headlines, sentiment analysis, technical indicators, and the actual price movements has not been fully explored. This study leverages a large dataset consisting of real-time news headlines and their corresponding sentiment scores to forecast the daily closing prices of the S\&P 500 index. A novel approach is proposed where the sentiment analysis is used in place of actual sentiment values, combined with technical indicators to forecast prices through an LSTM network. Our proposed model achieves a high R^2 score of 0.95 on the validation set and significantly outperforms the existing state-of-the-art models including the widely used ARIMA model with an AR component that produced an R^2 score of 0.83. The model's performance is further verified through backtesting on live data with results showing a low MAE of 13. The code and dataset used in this research are available online at https://github.com/rahulraj175/Sentiment-Driven-Stock-Market-Forecast. The paper's findings provide investors with valuable insights into the stock market and suggest multiple directions for further research and exploration. One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material from one of them. This process triggers a shrinking of the orbit as the stars interact with the envelope. Ultimately, it can result in either mergers or further complex interactions, which can involve a mix of compact objects and stars. Certain CE scenarios, particularly those involving white dwarfs, can produce supernovae, while neutron star mergers can result in gamma-ray bursts, and all types of compact object mergers can produce gravitational waves. Predicting the end states of these CEs is challenging due to their diverse origins and the difficulties in modeling their evolution dynamics. This issue is compounded by the fact that many CEs will ultimately result in mergers or further complex interactions, which will produce a wide range of electromagnetic and gravitational wave signatures that can be observable from a distance. This paper will discuss the various approaches to modeling the evolution of CEs, including both 1D and 3D models, as well as the need for a comprehensive theoretical framework that incorporates multiple modeling techniques to better predict the outcomes of these binary interactions. This goal is within reach thanks to ongoing improvements in computational power and the development of sophisticated computer codes that can handle complex astrophysical processes. This study will focus on the most widely used modeling codes for CE evolution and will explore ways to integrate their predictions through a parametric modeling framework that can be applied to both compact star and giant star CEs. This approach will provide a valuable tool for theorists to predict the outcomes of these binary interactions and the skies that may result from them. This study will specifically consider the end states of these CEs, which include mergers, further complex interactions, and the associated electromagnetic and gravitational wave signatures. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). We also derive the general effective operator language for this process and describe the effective operator kinematics through the cross-section cross-term with the Standard Model contribution. We perform a covariant expansion of the Einstein-Hilbert action in powers of
$1/c^2$, considering a generic spacetime foliation defined by $c$, the speed
of light. We achieve this through the application of a suitable 'pre-non-
relativistic' geometrical parametrization. As a result, we obtain a series
of higher-order differential theories of gravity which are compatible with the
principle of relativity. These theories encompass both Standard General
Relativity and first- and second-order metric theories of gravity akin to
Jordan-Brans-Dicke and $f(R)$ gravities, among others. Notably, our approach
allows for the systematic investigation of pre-non-relativistic limits of
fundamental theories such as String/M theory. Furthermore, we establish that
the Einstein-Hilbert action can be expanded in a series of $1/c^2$-dependent
terms over an infinite number of possibilities. However, we also find that
only a limited subset of these theories exhibit non-relativistic geometry
consistent with the 'archive' of well-known pre-non-relativistic gravity
theories. Consequently, our research offers a fresh perspective on the
cosmological problem and encourages the thorough re-examination of all
fundamental theories derived from the Einstein-Hilbert action before any
non-relativistic limit is taken. Our method for geometrical parametrization
can be extended to the consideration of other fundamental Einstein-Hilbert
actions, such as those associated with higher-spin fields or Branes. We
conclude by outlining the advantages of our approach in the context of the
pre-non-relativistic limit of Einstein gravity as a Relativistic Big Bang
Theory. Lastly, we propose that our method for the covariant expansion of
the Einstein-Hilbert action may provide a suitable framework for addressing
the issue of Time in Quantum Gravity. We anticipate that our novel
geometrical parametrization will also prove beneficial in the investigation
of the pre-non-relativistic limit of other fundamental Einstein-Hilbert actions. 
This research lays the groundwork for a fresh exploration of the Einstein-Hilbert
action, one that is both theoretically and experimentally driven. We hope that
our study will spark a genuine revival of interest in pre-non-relativistic
gravity within the global physics community.

Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area using probabilistic models in Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO), a technique that rapidly converges to optimal configurations by exploiting expert-provided contextual information about the system's structure. Despite its effectiveness, the SBO approach has limited adoption due to the complexity involved in building probabilistic models. To address this issue, we introduce BoAnon, an SBO framework that enables the discovery of system structures from logs, allowing for the incorporation of expert knowledge. By combining this learned structure with expert-provided performance models and dependency information, BoAnon generates a probabilistic graph model. This model accelerates the optimization process by focusing the search on a reduced configuration space, minimizing unnecessary evaluations and shortening the optimization time. To validate BoAnon, we applied it to the analysis of two significant computer systems: a real-world database server and Facebook's Hadoop cluster. The results showed that BoAnon's probabilistic graph models yield 4-7 times faster optimization convergence compared to non-structured Bayesian optimization methods. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. These findings suggest the elliptical and triangular flow responses can be understood through similar mechanisms, ultimately rooted in the same underlying physics. Furthermore, we identified an initial triazimuthal anisotropic elliptical flow caused by the interplay between viscosity and initial conditions. This effect is expected to become more pronounced in future experiments with higher precision.

Specifically, this method determines the most favorable probability distribution by minimizing the expected value of a specific loss function until it meets specific requirements, and it is possible to establish the statistical properties of this estimator. Although the method is demonstrated with a notable efficiency gain on synthetic and real-world data, its potential applications are numerous and diverse. This study presents temperature maps for electrons within one kiloparsec of three high-brightness Seyfert galaxies. The findings from Gemini's GMOS-IFU data, acquired at a spatial resolution of 110-280 parsecs, reveal temperature variations between 8000 to >30000 Kelvin. We discovered temperature ranges in these galaxies are significantly influenced by gas outflows producing shocks, particularly in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348, while photoionization processes fit the results for Mrk 607. The orientation of these shocks in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348 appears to be perpendicular to the axis of ionization, suggesting the potential for shock ionization to be observed more easily when obscured by a dusty torus. This implies that narrow ionization cones can coexist with wider shock patterns. Furthermore, we observed a potential link between shocks in Mrk 79 and the merging of nearby galaxies. These findings support recent studies indicating the prevalence of gas outflows in active galaxies and suggest that they might play a significant role in shutting down star formation and fueling black hole growth. These outcomes also highlight the capability and effectiveness of high-resolution optical interferometry in analyzing the physical processes occurring in active galaxies through the derivation of ionization conditions and temperature maps. This technique is poised to make substantial contributions to the study of active galaxies through its capacity to provide spatially resolved spectra at a high angular resolution. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring a full system matrix solution per time step, which can be computationally costly for complex systems. To address this challenge, this study explores the benefits of iterative techniques in solving the nonlinear system, separating the analysis into two parts. First, we investigate how to modify classic $L$-steps within the Newton-Raphson method to leverage iterative techniques, focusing on an example using the GMRES algorithm. Second, we apply this modification to several classic preservation-based methods within the $L$-schemes framework and evaluate its computational efficiency using the Euler and Navier-Stokes simulations on a 1D channel at $Re=1000$. By comparing the iterative versus direct solution approaches for the linearized system, we find that using an inner solver instead of an inverse leads to a significant reduction in computational time, with some methods showing a $10\times$ speedup while maintaining the same order of accuracy. Furthermore, we found that this modification does not compromise the original property preservation properties. Ultimately, this work highlights the potential benefits of combining high-order preservation-based methods with iterative time-stepping techniques, particularly where solving the full system becomes computationally infeasible. Keywords: preservation-based methods, iterative time-stepping, large-scale problems, time-dependent partial differential equations. A group of integer sequences can be classified as jointly ergodic if their combined action averages yield a dense subset of an almost-periodic group when operating on the real numbers under addition. This concept expands on earlier work involving single ergodic sequences. Essentially, we derive a condition for sequences of this nature to exhibit ergodic behavior by ensuring a specific system of congruences produces dense outcomes within the almost-periodic group of real numbers under addition. To achieve this, we establish the equivalence between these congruences and a system of Diophantine equations, which can be solved via a result by Gowers and Muliszewski, thereby demonstrating the required condition for sequences to be ergodic. Additionally, this condition may be applied to establish the ergodicity of certain combinatorial sequences, such as those related to Szemer\'edi's theorem. This framework also facilitates an exploration of ergodicity across residue classes, as well as a discussion on the ergodicity of sequences positioned within larger arithmetic progressions. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to various unknown organ scenarios. The trained model ignores boundary conditions and organ properties, only considering the deformed organ's surface, which simplifies its real-world application. The model's ability to handle multiple variables also enables it to perform well with limited and inaccurate intraoperative data. The evaluation showed our method to be the fastest and produced the most accurate results among comparable methods. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We developed an innovative method to obtain initial data by combining two approaches: point cloud analysis and stereo analysis. First, RANSAC-based algorithms are employed to estimate point cloud motion trajectories by identifying coherent structures within animated clouds, while also ignoring static background objects. Secondly, stereo analysis is used to generate texture information, which is used to validate and refine the point cloud data by identifying areas where the trajectory should appear on images taken at different times. An alternative method involves using the point cloud data to estimate the camera's initial position and orientation, which is further refined using stereo analysis to project the expected trajectory onto images. Both methods yield accurate results on a created dataset and are computationally efficient compared to other methods. Notably, one method produces results without adjusting camera positions and orientations. We discovered that both approaches yield high accuracy with minimal annotation, offering a promising solution for future large-scale annotation tasks. Additionally, the developed methods are openly accessible online. 

Keywords: Scene flow estimation; 3D point cloud analysis; Stereo analysis; Multi-sensor data fusion; Annotation reduction; Cloud point clouds analysis; Deep learning annotation tools.

A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. Furthermore, we establish that for any positive integers k and l, where k ≤ l, the papillon graph's CKl-family will exhibit the E2F property. This papillon graph development enriches our understanding of cubic graphs with the PMH-property and aids in answering a question posed by the authors in 2019. These papillon graphs are generated based on specific edge-colourings of Kk, l, particularly when the colours are arranged in a particular cyclic order. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system. In the future, we believe Timeloops has the potential to contribute to the development of secure, general-purpose tCBs. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and a pilot numerical test demonstrates the potential of both WRI and ESI methods.  In particular, the extended source concept appears to offer a way to escape the local minimum that FWI gets stuck in. How to further improve these new methods by further relaxing the physical constraints while maintaining data fit remains a topic worthy of further exploration. We've developed an all-optical technique for producing optical nonreciprocity on a microchip, achieved through quantum squeezing applied to a cavity mode. A key factor in this method's success is the phase-matched difference in loss between forward and backward propagating light. We've proposed using parity-time symmetric optics to encompass nonreciprocal phenomena and illustrate this concept with a optical router that diverts light based on its direction of travel. To address scalability issues, we've incorporated a quantum-optical, hybrid approach utilizing a superconducting amplifier to provide a significant gain without the need for balanced homodyne detection. This quantum-optical, hybrid scheme surpasses the limitations of classical optical nonreciprocity, potentially enabling large-scale, directional control of light. We've demonstrated this approach by building a large-scale optical router with nonreciprocal behavior and successfully diverted light through multiple nodes. This breakthrough paves the way for the development of complex, light-directed systems with broad applications in optical communication and photonic neural networks. These systems could exploit optical nonreciprocity to consolidate decision-making processes locally on the microchip, thereby enhancing performance while reducing memory requirements.

To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetrical noisy voter model was developed for a regular lattice structure. In this model, species compete for resources in local neighborhoods, with the winner displacing rivals, and immigrants arrive randomly from a broader surrounding area, potentially replacing residents. This model allows researchers to explore how the ratio of local to global interaction distances impacts the coexistence of multiple species through analytical and numerical methods. It was discovered that species competition can lead to abrupt shifts between different equilibrium species populations upon changes to dispersal distance, and a sudden loss of stability in the unique equilibrium state occurs at a specific critical ratio of local to global interaction distances. This critical point is characterized by a first-order phase transition marked by a significant jump in the amplitude of oscillations following a small perturbation, and it is also identified by a distinct shift in the skewness of the species distribution. The model's findings may provide insights for understanding the dynamics of species competition in larger, more complex ecological systems. The asymmetrical noisy voter model can be applied to various ecological scenarios by adjusting the parameters of local and global interactions. The model also highlights the significance of dispersion asymmetry in influencing ecological dynamics. The asymmetry in dispersion can be represented by varying the distances over which individuals interact locally and globally, and it is demonstrated that a significant disparity in these distances can lead to the emergence of minority species and facilitate first-order phase transitions. The model further illustrates the impact of dispersal asymmetry on the topology of the interaction map, demonstrating that a highly skewed distribution of local interactions can result in a more stable coexistence of the majority species, while a more balanced distribution of local interactions can lead to the coexistence of minority species. The model also reveals that the most stable coexistence is achieved when the dispersal asymmetry is most extreme. The model's analysis of the impact of an uneven dispersal distance on the topology of the interaction map is supported by numerical simulations, and it is proposed that this analysis may be applicable to other random voter models. The model's results are robust and validated through the analysis of oscillations following a local perturbation, as well as the distribution of stationary and dynamic species occupancy. The model's findings are expected to contribute to the ongoing discussion of the impact of dispersal asymmetry on ecological dynamics and the topology of interaction maps. The model's results are consistent with the idea that dispersal asymmetry can lead to the emergence of minority species, and it is proposed that this phenomenon may be observed in highly competitive ecological environments. The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. In experiments, our findings suggest that certain evaluation tasks prove more manageable than others and that the best results are achieved by evaluating the encoder's performance on tasks that require reasoning and semantic understanding rather than merely relying on text generation metrics. Furthermore, our proposed evaluation framework yields meaningful insights into the encoder's performance, prompting the suggestion that pre-trained models with elevated performance on downstream tasks might not necessarily excel in understanding dialogue language. Additionally, our research reveals that certain models excel in certain evaluation tasks but struggle with others, prompting the recommendation to employ multiple evaluation techniques to ensure the reliability of results. Deep learning methods for LiDAR data analysis have surpassed traditional approaches in 3D recognition systems and have become the new standard for place recognition in autonomous vehicles, due to their ability to leverage large datasets. However, training a robust place recognition system using this approach is hindered by the high computational cost and memory requirements of deep learning networks, making it challenging to employ them in real-time applications beyond the scope of modern autonomous vehicles. This study introduces a novel, modular approach to place recognition that utilizes a network with a compact footprint and low training costs. By combining a local feature extractor with a graph neural network, this method demonstrates enhanced performance while requiring significantly less memory and computational resources than comparable methods. Furthermore, it can be trained at a much lower computational cost, allowing for efficient place recognition on autonomous vehicles with limited computational power and without the need for specialized hardware. This research was conducted as part of the Urban Challenge 2010 and utilized data from the final test run. The results show that this method achieves a mean matching rate of 44.6% with a mean distance of 2.93 meters when matching to previously visited locations, and a mean matching rate of 24.9% with a mean distance of 3.53 meters when matching to locations that were not previously visited. Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech leverages contextual acoustic features to enhance both speaker and content-related aspects. This results in a more realistic and engaging speech quality. Our experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in naturalness and distinctiveness when comparing masked and non-masked contexts. Furthermore, cross-domain evaluations reveal significant gains with just 500 utterances of specific data, indicating a notable reduction in the need for large-scale corpora. Our findings highlight the importance of contextual acoustic features in speech synthesis and provide a solid foundation for future research in this area. Our code and model are available at https://github.com/sonuspeech/MaskedSpeech.

In this paper, we explore this broader scenario, analyzing both the standard and advanced limits within this theoretical framework and identifying essential conditions for existence in the more complex scenarios. Additionally, we identify a previously unexamined Q-ball state, which we term 'cored', and demonstrate that it could possess stability under specific conditions; a more detailed investigation into its implications will be addressed in a subsequent study. 

In the context of the Standard Model, we determine the minimum mass for a system supporting both $B-L$ symmetry and electroweak symmetry, confirming previous estimates of approximately 2-3 GeV. Furthermore, we identify the range within the field's effective potential where an asymptotic plateau exists, and determine that the field's vacuum value cannot exceed the square root of two times the electroweak scale. 

Within the parameter space of the Minimal Linear Logarithmic Model, we identify the conditions under which vacuum stable instantons are prohibited, and determine that this model permits the existence of a Q-ball with a mass below the π-mesons mass threshold. 

In the scenario where the universe is composed of a multi-symmetry system and there is a distinct symmetry break, we identify the requirement for a 'nested' Q-ball structure, where the inner core represents the broken symmetry and the outer shell represents the remaining symmetries. We demonstrate that such a 'nested' Q-ball can be stable, and that its mass falls within the same category as the standard, high-energy Q-ball state. 

Lastly, we establish that 'nested' Q-ball structures are inherent to the fundamental theory, as they are born out of the general multi-symmetry principle. Inspired by the pseudogap phenomenon in cuprates, we propose a new idea, 
the concept of an "exceptional" van Hove singularity, where a strong 
electron interaction fragments a continuous Fermi surface into disjoint regions. 
We identify this singularity with the merging of two separated Fermi surface 
segments, and demonstrate that it is close to a van Hove singularity, 
reaching it by adjusting a material parameter affecting its dispersion. 
We assert that, in the broader family of cuprate materials, 
the onset of pseudogap is attainable solely through inducing this exceptional 
van Hove singularity, and that this results in a distinct Lifshitz 
transition distinguished by heightened heat capacity and a nematic susceptibility, 
both consistent with empirical observations. 
Furthermore, we propose that this exceptional van Hove singularity 
may be relevant to other strongly interacting electron systems. 
In such complex systems, precise predictions rely heavily on the underlying 
microscopic theory used to simulate them. 
However, even these simulations appear to be incapable of capturing the full 
extent of the singularity, and it is unclear at this point whether it represents 
a general phenomenon that can occur across all heavily interacting electron systems. 
It is also unclear whether it is necessary for the onset of pseudogap. 
Therefore, further study is required to fully understand this concept. 
In the case of cuprates, even though we have proposed the existence of this 
exceptional van Hove singularity, it is still debated among scientists 
whether it is the primary mechanism driving the pseudogap phenomenon. 
There are additional proposals, such as the block-band theory, that could 
also explain this phenomenon. 
Ultimately, determining the origin and validity of this concept will 
depend on the outcome of ongoing and planned experiments, such as ARPES 
on the electron-doped cuprates, which aim to provide a more comprehensive 
understanding of this proposed singularity. 
In addition, this theory highlights the potential for discovering other 
exceptional van Hove singularity in other interacting systems that have 
already been extensively studied, such as Na$_{x}$CoO$_2$ and graphene on 
NiO, where it may explain the onset of their respective phase transitions. 
Therefore, this theory has significant implications that warrant the attention 
of the scientific community in order to further explore and validate its 
proposed concepts.

Ground-based observations of planetary movements are crucial in validating the findings of space-based missions like Kepler and TESS. Although these missions show that planets are widespread, the success of these missions relies heavily on the use of transit photometry and ground-based radial velocity surveys to determine the physical properties of these celestial bodies. The TESS telescope is capable of identifying planets around bright nearby stars, which are ideal candidates for follow-up observations. We propose the TESS-Keck Survey to investigate various properties of these exoplanets. Utilizing 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES, the survey's primary objectives include analyzing how planetary compositions are linked to the characteristics of their host stars, understanding the diversity of planetary system architectures based on the planets' dynamical configurations, and pinpointing suitable targets for study with the JWST. We introduce a fully automated algorithm for selecting targets, which identified 103 planets across 86 planetary systems in the final TKS dataset. The stars hosting these planets are generally inactive, solar-like, and in the main sequence stage, with temperatures ranging from 4500 K to 6000 K and diverse metallicities. The TKS dataset comprises 71 small planets with radii smaller than four times that of Earth, as well as systems featuring multiple transiting candidates, short orbital periods, and exoplanets situated near or within their host stars' habitable zones. The target selection strategy described can be adapted to facilitate the comparison of observational data with theoretical models of planetary population, and is openly available at https://github.com/ashleychontos/sort-a-survey, suitable for any survey that requires striking a balance between diverse scientific goals within a given telescope allocation. The first results from the TKS, involving an analysis of planetary compositions based on high-resolution spectroscopy, have been presented in Chontos et al. (2020) and is ongoing in several related research projects. The full dataset of the TKS will be released through the Exoplanet Open Data Platform. The initial findings reported in this paper are the outcome of 20.5 nights of observations, and the research team is utilizing 84.5 additional nights on the Keck/HIRES to expand its sample and verify its initial results. The study presented here incorporates the data included in Erikson et al. (2020), which identified nine valid small planet candidates. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP effect and incorporating other relevant parameters into their analysis, scientists were able to detect the YORP acceleration in three asteroids and found that the YORP acceleration in all ten detected cases was positive, accelerating their rotations. Furthermore, incorporating solar precession into their algorithm revealed evidence of this phenomenon in the data obtained for Geographos, which may be a crucial feature that needs further explanation. Ultimately, researchers found that the YORP acceleration in asteroids smaller than 0.1 kilometers in diameter appears to increase at a rate of (8.56 ± 0.65) x 10^-18 s^-2 when considering the acceleration of all detected cases, which provides a preliminary answer to a long-debated question about the YORP acceleration of the smallest asteroids. However, further research is still necessary to validate this finding and understand the YORP acceleration in asteroids with diameters even smaller than 0.01 kilometers. Moreover, the YORP acceleration acceleration itself remains undetected with the current data set, but it's reasonable to assume that the YORP acceleration acceleration is highly variable across different asteroids, making it difficult to identify in this analysis. Ultimately, the Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect is a crucial factor that affects the rotational states of small asteroids, and researchers should prioritize prioritizing priority targets for further study in accordance with how significantly the YORP acceleration acceleration is expected to impact these asteroids' rotations. Prioritization criteria can be established by modeling the YORP acceleration acceleration across the vast population of small asteroids, which can be achieved through a simplified approach that utilizes the YORP acceleration acceleration distribution model and the rotational state evolution model. Ultimately, a large-scale survey such as the one proposed here will be necessary to thoroughly understand the YORP acceleration acceleration across the entire spectrum of small asteroids

The youth are increasingly relying on Instagram as a source of information, with political figures leveraging the platform to disseminate opinions and agendas. We examined online discussions on Instagram from September 2020 to July 2021, focusing on political postings from Canadian politicians with significant interaction potential. Our analysis revealed the top politicians' postings that generated the most engagement were often characterized by brief, concise language and frequently included emotive and scandalous content to pander to public sentiment. Notably, our findings showed that users' engagement with political discussions far exceeded their interest in other topics, such as entertainment and sports, indicating high civic awareness among Instagram users. Furthermore, our results indicated a generational shift in online political discourse, with younger generations playing a decisive role in shaping discussions and influencing opinions. We also discovered that Instagram's algorithmic timing of political postings created opportunities for temporary bursts of engagement, often coinciding with major events and typically occurring within a week of their initial posting. Our study is available to inspire similar investigations in other countries and communities. We are eager to share our methodology with researchers who could further examine online political discourse from diverse civic awareness perspectives. Ultimately, our study is a pioneering effort to encourage more attention to online political discourse from a civic awareness standpoint and to explore related research questions. We hope our findings will contribute to a better comprehension of online political discussions that incorporate civic awareness and encourage more studies in this area. We are eager to hear from other researchers who may have insights into online political discussions and civic awareness. Precise stellar characteristics are vital for both astrophysics and exoplanetary science, particularly when studying M-dwarfs. Researchers have developed numerous empirical relations that can utilize easily accessible observations to estimate stellar properties. However, these formulas are often presented in a non-linear format, which is not suitable for Bayesian modeling. A novel Bayesian approach has been developed to consistently and simultaneously apply multiple empirical calibrations to accurately determine the fundamental properties of a star. This method utilizes a set of observable calibrations, such as luminosity-based surface temperature calibrations and color-based spectral type calibrations, to estimate the stellar radius, mass, age, and other properties. To apply this framework, researchers must first establish a set of reliable calibration relations. A comprehensive set of easily applicable formulas has been created using a comprehensive grid of M-dwarf stars from the PARAM 1.1 database, which is based on DUSTY and BASTI models. These calibrations can be used to fit the stellar SED, providing an independent means of measuring the stellar radius and effective temperature. The new Bayesian approach and derived calibration relations can be used to improve the estimation of M-dwarf properties. The new parameters have been compared with current best practices, yielding comparable results but also incorporating additional fundamental properties. The new approach and related calibration relations are now publicly available within the param 2.0 framework. The updated version incorporates the new Bayesian approach and features an interactive web interface for users to easily access the calculated stellar properties. The new calculations can be applied to the full set of approved and rejected exoplanet candidates from the radial velocity survey, such as the Kepler, HARPS, and RADES surveys. The resulting high-precision M-dwarf sequences in various color-temperature planes may prove valuable for modeling stellar atmospheres and surfaces in future modeling efforts. The new parameters and derived calibrations are also relevant to ongoing and future transit missions like TESS, Kepler, and PLATO. The new calibrations provide a consistent and self-consistent means of measuring the fundamental properties of M-dwarfs, which is essential for an accurate assessment of small-radius exoplanet candidates and their associated host stars. Confining modes at the edge, known as line waves, can propagate on the boundary between two specially designed electromagnetic interfaces that maintain mirror symmetry properties.
Studies have previously analyzed line waves in theory and in practice, revealing their occurrence at both microwave and terahertz frequencies.
It has also been demonstrated that these waves can occur when there's a sudden change from a negative to a positive symmetric resistance and uniform surface reactance present.
Characteristics of line waves include highly confineable mode propagation, polarization dependent on direction, and unique localized field enhancements.
A new study proposes a graphene patch structure, showing that the line waves produced can operate in the optical range. 
The design involves a graphene surface integrated with an epsilon near zero substrate, which considers the effects of both dual and uniform reactive impedances.
However, the dual impedance influence dominates the line wave behavior, causing it to propagate through a specific path rather than being confined to the edge. 
In contrast, the uniform impedance dominance leads to an alternative type of line wave confinement, influenced by the electron tunneling barrier and controlled by the chemical potential of the graphene. 
Therefore, this finding enables the control of line wave confinement by adjusting the dual and uniform impedance effects separately. 
The proposed structure also facilitates the integration of line wave devices with both local and remote field sensing applications. 
The design also allows for a much wider line wave frequency operating range, extending from the microwave to the ultra-fast optical frequencies. 
This breakthrough paves the way for the development of integrated photonic devices that can manipulate both localized and extended electromagnetic modes in the same structure. 
The proposed approach can also be applied across various frequency ranges by substituting different types of surface impedance materials. 
As an example, a photonic integrated device is designed to demonstrate the co-existence of both surface plasmon phonons and line waves, exhibiting reliable operation in the GHz to THz frequency range. 
The proposed research opens up a new area of study for electromagnetic metamaterials and photonics, enabling the systematic exploration of confined mode physics in the microwave, terahertz, and ultra-fast optical frequency ranges. 
This could lead to groundbreaking innovations in the development of integrated photonic devices that leverage a wide range of abnormal wave modes confining modes.
