Inspired by the potential of artificial intelligence to enhance human performance in various tasks, we investigate the efficacy of a "smart dictatorship" where a combinatorial optimization problem is resolved with the aid of a machine learning model. We investigate a broad range of settings in which a small group of individuals with limited expertise can leverage a strong but naive learning model to address complex optimization issues. Our research focuses on evaluating the performance of combinatorial optimization algorithms that leverage machine learning and we study settings in which the group's objective may differ from the optimal solution, as well as scenarios in which the group has access to problem-specific information that they can utilize in conjunction with the machine learning model. We establish a framework in which the algorithm's performance is determined by an instance of a multi-object domainless problem and we investigate multiple instances in which the algorithm achieves optimal results, has a near-optimal solution, or results in a social welfare that is suboptimal. Our results demonstrate that in cases with limited expertise, where the group's objective is similar to the optimal solution, and when the group has access to problem-specific information that complements the machine learning model, the algorithm produces a social welfare that is optimal or near-optimal. However, in scenarios with significant expertise disparities and when the group's objective differs substantially from the optimal solution, the algorithm may yield a suboptimal social welfare. We further investigate a specific setting in which a group of individuals with limited expertise can leverage a strong but naive machine learning model to address combinatorial optimization problems and demonstrate that the algorithm's performance is comparable to that of an optimal solution when the group's objective is similar to the optimal solution. Our research builds upon prior work in which a serial dictatorship mechanism was found to result in an optimal social welfare outcome in certain settings and we extend this outcome to cases in which the group's objective differs from the optimal solution. We also introduce novel algorithmic frameworks for addressing combinatorial optimization problems in the presence of multiple, potentially conflicting objectives and provide solutions to several NP-complete problems by leveraging these frameworks. Our research provides solutions to instances of NP-complete problems, including the design of a minimum-weight spanning tree in the presence of multiple, conflicting connectivity requirements and the identification of a minimum-weight subgraph in the presence of multiple, objective functions. We demonstrate that these solutions exhibit optimal or near-optimal social welfare when evaluated against instances of multiple-object domainless problems and we show that our results are comparable to those of optimal solutions in certain cases. Our work offers a novel approach to addressing combinatorial optimization

We designed two distinct algorithms to identify potential binary asteroid candidates within a large dataset of size and shape observations made by the Hubble Space Telescope. This research builds upon the work of Noll et al. (2015) and Scheidt et al. (2015) by utilizing a comprehensive dataset of 1217 near-Earth asteroids to determine binary or solitary status. Our first approach, accounting for measurement errors, pinpointed probable companions by comparing the observed shapes of individual asteroids to those generated through discrete elemental models. Our second method involved treating each asteroid as a part of a larger binary system and assessed the validity of this hypothesis based on the model's fit to observed shapes and sizes. Both techniques identified the same 26 confirmed binary asteroids that have been previously recognized, and 13 additional potential binaries, 7 of which have since been validated through direct observations or orbital patterns of their components. These discoveries contribute significantly to the existing list of about 100 known binary asteroids, and the majority of which have diameters under 100 km. The most substantial finding from our study is the identification of a large asteroid approximately 100 km in size that may possess a wide binary companion. Its discovery has important implications, as it could be a significant enough mass to influence the orbit of dust grains generated by the smaller component, potentially explaining the presence of certain rare meteorites. However, to validate this theory, more observations and modeling are required to refine the understanding of this potential binary system's dynamics. Both algorithms used in this research are also applicable to size and shape data obtained from other high-resolution space telescopes. We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Moreover, this success is coupled with human findings that conversational D&D is an engaging and enjoyable activity. We argue that this D&D-based framework offers a compelling setting for exploring the broader challenge of G4C. Our project is accessible at https://parproghum.github.io/DnG4C/.

We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that are derived from quark spin vectors and are applicable to both the unpolarized and polarized cases. These spin-dependent functions are linked to quark distribution functions through unpolarized and polarized parton distribution functions and are used in the context of a gauge-invariant formulation. As a result, we derive novel operator definitions that connect quark spin-dependent functions to unpolarized and polarized parton distribution functions through structure functions in deep-inelastic scattering, extending their definitions beyond $k_\perp=0$. Furthermore, we illustrate the scale evolution of these new functions through the evolution equations of unpolarized and polarized quark distribution functions and connect them to the corresponding distribution functions within the context of perturbative QCD. Additionally, we examine the relationship between these spin-dependent $k_\perp$-distibution functions and quark antiquark disk amplitudes used in transverse momentum dependent parton model, leading to potential implications for TDPDFA evolution equations. Lastly, we suggest possible extraction pathways for these new quark spin-dependent $k_\perp$-distribution functions through global fits to data from deep-inelastic scattering, Drell-Yan, and semi-inclusive direct photon processes. By incorporating these findings, we provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the evolution of quark spin-dependent $k_\perp$-distribution functions and their associated role within the context of polarized hadronic structure functions.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite. This reasoning relies on a newly established link between the irrationality of certain area forms and the non-simplicial nature of the related braid groups, with the proof employing a novel application of the Thurston-Dean technique for detecting non-simplicial braid groups. This advances previous knowledge, in which it was demonstrated that for an arbitrarily small modification of $\omega$, the associated symplectic mapping class group becomes finitely generated. Moreover, this result anticipates a forthcoming proof that under the same conditions, this group becomes finitely presented. This note also introduces a novel 'blowup' technique for symplectic mapping class groups, which enables the application of several existing results to the blowup settings. Ultimately, this leads to the derivation of a new lower bound for the volume of the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group, positioned within the universal Lie algebra of the symplectic mapping class group of the blowup, as obtained through the application of a novel 'blowup' technique for symplectic field theory. This new lower bound is equal to the recently established lower bound for the volume of the abelian variety of the same dimension, obtained through the application of a novel 'abelianization' technique for algebraic curves. This abelianization technique is initially introduced with this study, providing a novel link between the volumes of the symplectic mapping class groups and the algebraic curves, which is realized via the application of a blowup-like procedure to the singularities of the algebraic curves, followed by the calculation of the volumes of the associated mapping class groups through the application of the birational correspondence. This new link is capable of deriving the previously established lower bounds for the volumes of the abelian varieties, and is anticipated to give rise to further related discoveries. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, allowing the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is lacking, and the majority of reported outcomes can be explained by the presence of surface defects and impurities. This study provides novel insights into the epitaxial growth of the Heusler compound GdPtSb on graphene and reveals that a method called anti-epitaxy is necessary to achieve a remote epitaxial process. Anti-epitaxy entails growing a thin layer of a binary element on graphene at room temperature before adding the third element from the gas phase. Utilizing a thin layer of a binary element facilitates the formation of a stable, dislocation-free buffer layer on graphene and prevents the introduction of impurities. As a result, the epitaxial Heusler compound is free from dislocations and defects, exhibiting superior transport characteristics. Moreover, the epitaxial Heusler compound shows an exceptionally high critical temperature of 130 K when used in junctions, a notable achievement given the material is grown at room temperature without cryogenic epitaxial techniques. The success of this study paves the way for the remote epitaxial growth of other highly lattice-mismatched materials with graphene. The large material space available, coupled with the minimal lattice constraints, offers the potential to devise novel spintronic devices by combining disparate materials. The method also eliminates the need for elaborate pre-treatment of substrate surfaces, thereby simplifying the epitaxial process and making it more high-throughput. The study of the Heusler compound GdPtSb also highlights the potential of remote epitaxy to achieve superior transport characteristics in this family of materials. The method can result in materials with critical temperatures exceeding 100 K, which is critical for their applicability in spintronic technologies. The method of anti-epitaxy is expected to facilitate a breakthrough in the development of novel, practical spintronic devices by providing easy access to a broad range of epitaxial materials with distinct spintronic properties. The technique may also enable the creation of artificial super-lattices with unique electronic properties by combining disparate materials with lattice mismatches of up to 30%. The success of this study is anticipated to spark a surge in research into the remote epitaxial growth of highly lattice-mismatched materials, opening up new avenues for the development of innovative spintronic and semiconductor devices. This paper specifically delves into the examination of the rank and dimension of the kernel of these $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes. Furthermore, it also investigates the relationship between the $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes and their $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive counterparts through the determination of the rank and dimension of the preimage of these $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes. Computational simulations have been conducted to analyze the rank and dimension of the kernel of these $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes for various code lengths and dimensions. Moreover, a comparison has been drawn to showcase the distinction between the $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes and their $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive counterparts. This study seeks to create advanced mathematical methods and computational tools to model portfolio returns, establishing essential formulas and efficient algorithms using techniques from computational geometry and splines. We derived closed-form equations for the first four moments and found that our score has the expected properties of being non-negative and averaging zero. To validate our methods, we utilized both randomized and real-world data for the S&P 500 index and found our scores to be reliable and consistent. Furthermore, our results indicate that the variance of a portfolio is closely related to its score. Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code

Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning setting. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy. This modified approach facilitates learning on 24 classes with a high degree of class hierarchy and tests its applicability on a previously unexplored dataset of 128 classes with shallow class hierarchies. Results show that this method surpasses baseline methods and yields promising output for the evaluation of intricate hierarchies. However, it's also evident that the model's performance is impeded by the depth of class hierarchies. Moreover, an analysis of model performance relative to different levels of the taxonomy reveals that deep-hierarchical classes exhibit a greater difference in accuracy compared to shallow-hierarchical ones. This indicates that future models should be capable of handling complex hierarchies more effectively. To facilitate reproducibility and advancement in this research, the dataset used and the proposed framework have been made publicly accessible. This work lays the groundwork for applying prototypical networks in additional domains involving hierarchical structures and scarce data. Additionally, it highlights the potential risks of over-reliance on hierarchical connections over domain-specific differences. To achieve this, the project employs techniques like aggregating prototypes and introducing a hierarchical loss function, and it recommends utilizing taxonomic relations as additional data for further research. This project demonstrates that prototypical networks can be used for few-shot learning on extensive and unfamiliar datasets with deep class hierarchies, and as such, it has the potential to contribute to several other domain-specific research projects. Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims, opposing arguments, and counterexamples. To address this need, we present ${i}$$a{}$t{}$q${a} for academic text, comprising approximately 15,000 samples spanning 5 diverse fields and targeting five distinct Question Types that require substantial reasoning about the text content. Each sample includes a short question accompanied by a relevant sentence from a research paper, thereby incorporating the challenging aspects of academic language. In our evaluation, we demonstrate that despite its high difficulty, the model achieves significant progress with pre-trained models, and the best-performing model still falls short of human performance in our assessment metric. Furthermore, our results indicate that the model's performance can be improved by leveraging existing QA datasets, adapting models to academic text using simpler architectures, and incorporating relevant field knowledge. The dataset is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/whunlp/iatsq. The evaluation code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/whunlp/iatsq-eval. The dataset is also hosted on HuggingFace Datasets at https://huggingface.co/datasets/whunlp/iatq. All models used in our evaluation are also openly accessible on HuggingFace Transformers at https://huggingface.co/whunlp.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, leading to a significant reduction of up to 50 times in computational costs compared to other methods. The accuracy of these analytic expressions is validated through a relevant parameter range and is shown to be in line with the accuracy of the Numerical Relativity solutions used for comparison. Furthermore, cross-validation with other existing analytic representations shows good agreement. These findings provide a basis for improving the performance of PTA data analysis algorithms. For instance, the analytic expression is at least 3.5 times faster than the standard Numerical Relativity-based method and is sufficiently accurate for the analysis of mock data scenarios resembling potential PTA detections in the future. The accurate analytic expression is also compatible with the recently updated PTA data sets. The implementation of these findings in the form of an open-source code is available online.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a velocity whose probability distribution is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$ as time tends to infinity. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process. Additionally, we pinpoint the equilibrium speed process for TASEP and demonstrate that this equilibrium is highly unstable. Furthermore, we predict that similar speed processes exist for other systems within the MACKAY family. However, it remains unclear at this point whether this relationship holds mathematically. Our primary source of analysis is the ASEP system with stationary initial data, from which we derive the speed process. This speed process is then found to be connected to the ASEP system with step initial data through a scaling limit, providing us with its equilibrium speed process. This method of investigation is inspired by the chapter "The TASEP speed process" from the book "Stochastic Processes and Their Applications."

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control. Consequently, collaboration among mathematicians, epidemiologists, and public health officials is crucial to develop and evaluate models in an ongoing public health crisis. Ultimately, this collaboration should prioritize informing critical policy decisions in conjunction with other relevant data and expertise. As an example, we present a simple model addressing critical time periods for model compartment analysis during the ongoing pandemic. Despite significant progress in recent decades, many features of epidemic models continue to be undertheorized, and several viruses, including SARS-CoV-2, demand continued study in future research. 

Keywords: Epidemiological models; SARS-CoV-2; Mathematical modeling; Network models; Modeling compartment analysis; Time period models.

We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. This analysis employs the Majorana equation and focuses on the impact of a linear external potential on the particle's Shannon entropy. Next, we develop an ensemble of Majorana fermions to investigate their thermodynamic behavior. Ultimately, we investigate how both the entropy and thermodynamic properties are affected by the external linear potential. Our study may have implications for understanding Majorana fermions within the context of Type-I seesaw mechanism for neutrino mass generation.

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, a challenge many users face in navigating contemporary digital environments. To address this issue, our proposed approach focuses on acronym detection and interpretation within unstructured written content. Our system leverages a deep learning-based character-level neural language model to identify abbreviated phrases across various lengths and subsequently employs a separate, layer-wise, top-down approach to decode their meanings in 64-character blocks. We tested our method on two unique datasets containing social media text and obtained promising results, outperforming existing solutions by achieving an F1 score of up to 73.8%. Additionally, our approach surpasses traditional techniques utilizing whole-word vocabularies by achieving an F1 score of 68.2%, demonstrating its effectiveness with no prior knowledge of the vocabulary needed. Moreover, our model excels in acronym detection without compromising its ability to recognize other abbreviated phrases, showcasing its versatility. To facilitate further research, we are releasing two unique datasets containing social media text along with corresponding evaluation protocols. Our best model's code is available at https://github.com/zhengding456/acr- char-level.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through a dark-state correlation. In addition, a related dark state facilitates efficient molecule creation via dark-state collapse. The precise control of this process is also achievable by adjusting the collisional spin-transfer and association processes. Moreover, a combination of dark-state collapse and coherent conversion can lead to molecule-atom pair formation from the condensate, allowing for the avoidance of high-magnetic-field limitations. The described mechanisms provide a basis for a comprehensive understanding of coherent atom-molecule conversion in spin units. Furthermore, this framework may be applied to various systems, including those involving multiple spin units and encompassing a wide range of dark-state-induced molecule creation phenomena. This is exemplified by an analysis of the interplay between collisional spin-transfer and association in the production of molecules via photoassociation. This study reveals that the efficient creation of molecules is constrained by the availability of suitable atomic states, highlighting the potential for efficient molecule creation through the transfer of two spins in a specific, highly constrained scenario. This is demonstrated through an application of this framework to recent successful molecule creation experiments involving strontium and rubidium atoms. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are only a limited number of possible primer combinations, the storage capacity of each segment is essentially limitless. Furthermore, storing a new object in a fully indexed segment can be performed in a single DNA strand synthesis step. Additionally, both locating specific objects within a segment and updating specific objects within a segment have been shown to have linear scalability. In our experiments, we successfully incorporated over 1.9 million individual objects into a single data file using the new architecture, and demonstrated both data retrieval and data replacement at a rate of up to 10,000 objects per minute. In comparison to the existing methods, this new approach exhibits enhanced data handling capabilities and is also more adaptable in terms of data organization. This new structure is also more resistant to errors, as the degradation of a particular index no longer results in the loss of all objects associated with the same primer pair. In this context, we also introduce a new error-tolerant indexing technique that is applicable to this DNA-storage architecture. This new method demonstrates superior performance both in terms of accuracy and computational requirements when compared to the existing methods. In this new indexing approach, a segment is divided into smaller sub-indexes, and these sub-indexes are further divided into overlapping subsets that can be independently synthesized and indexed in isolation. This allows for the reliable identification of objects even in cases where a sub-index has been corrupted, provided that at least one of the overlapping subsets remains intact. In this way, the integrity of the entire index can be restored by re-synthesizing the affected objects in accordance with the intact subsets, a process that is both feasible and efficient. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines. This study is published as part of a special issue honoring Dr. Gong Chen on the occasion of his 60th birthday.

MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention guided network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials. This research indicates that deep learning models can be applied to computer-aided diagnosis of brain tumors, and the model's performance can be further improved with more comprehensive datasets.  Future studies can utilize this model as a reference and incorporate temperature mapping to improve tumor type classification. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth, such as image segmentation and skinned multi-layer models. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited to basic models or suffer from slow computation, hindering their adoption for complex model inference. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that reinterprets traditional radiance models as probability distributions of light sources, textures, and shapes, enabling us to leverage established optimization algorithms to solve image-based inverse problems. By transforming traditional radiance models into probabilistic forms and utilizing techniques like Metropolis-Hastings algorithm and gradient-based optimization, we can efficiently compute and utilize gradients for sample evaluation, thereby facilitating the learning of models that can generalize to unseen scenes. We demonstrate the versatility of our framework by applying it to three pressing image-based inverse problems: image segmentation, skinned multi-layer modeling, and scene reconstruction from reflections. Our results show that our approach not only matches or surpasses the performance of current state-of-the-art methods but also exhibits a level of generalizability that can excel even in scenes that were not part of the training dataset. All code and data are available at https://github.com/CheneyShih/Differentiable-Renderer-for-Image-Based-Inverse-Problems. Homepage: https://chy1979.github.io/projects/ DifferentiableRenderer/.

A popular technique, widely used for enhancing video playback on television and recording, is interlacing. This technique doubles the perceived frame rate without boosting the bandwidth, yet generates undesirable effects like visual distortion and flicker during playback. Present methods fail to balance real-time processing with satisfactory quality. They either prioritize real-time processing over visual clarity or improve quality at the expense of processing speed. This research proposes a groundbreaking approach utilizing deep convolutional neural networks, capable of delivering both high-quality results and real-time performance. Diverging from traditional super-resolution models that assume pixel invariance, our approach incorporates data from both interlaced half-frames to regenerate missing scan lines. This innovative system runs on GPU hardware, allowing it to process videos in real-time. Experimental results show our method surpasses the visual quality of existing techniques and achieves comparable performance to traditional super-resolution models when evaluated on still images. However, due to the significant computational demands of its CNN architecture on GPU, it falls short of real-time processing on CPU platforms. Further analysis revealed the discrepancy arises due to varying product volumes of the effective mass and radial density within the nucleon's spatial extent, influenced by the type of nuclear model employed. A distinct relationship between the effective mass and radial density was observed in non-relativistic and relativistic models, showcasing a direct correlation in the former and an inverse correlation in the latter. As a demonstration, the authors use this framework to analyze cause-to-effect learning methods, revealing its practical value. Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability. The presented MRI thermometry technique presents new avenues for the in-depth study of mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds, potentially being adapted for further applications in reactive gas-solid systems in the future. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources and comprises the most extensive cardiac mechanics simulations solved by BDDC/AMG/Newton-Krylov methods reported to date. The project's findings are expected to provide valuable insights for researchers and computational scientists working on similar projects. Recent studies have uncovered the prevalence of gradient masking in purportedly robust adversarial defenses. Consequently, defense strategies based on this concept are considered ineffective and can be readily bypassed. Notably, research into quantifying the occurrence and extent of gradient masking across different networks remains limited. This study addresses this gap by exploring the mensurability of gradient masking as a multi-dimensional rather than a binary phenomenon. In addition, we introduce novel metrics designed to evaluate the presence of gradient masking in diverse neural networks. These proposed metrics not only offer computational advantages but also facilitate comparative assessments between models without necessitating elaborate tailor-made attacks. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the efficacy of these metrics in gauging the prevalence of gradient masking across different network configurations. Furthermore, we illustrate the practical applications of these metrics in evaluating the susceptibility of adversarial models to backdoor attacks and the efficacy of mitigation strategies. This research paves the way for enhanced understanding of the phenomenon of gradient masking and its implications on the development of reliable adversarial defenses. Moreover, our work introduces universally applicable benchmarks for evaluating the presence of gradient masking in neural networks, which can serve as a foundation for developing customized evaluation methods across diverse network topologies. This research is particularly relevant to the development of artificial neural networks, where evaluating the presence of gradient masking can provide critical insights for improving model robustness and stability. This work is primarily concerned with artificial neural networks but could potentially be expanded to include other multi-dimensional optimization problems. This concept, however, has not yet been implemented at the MHz frequencies common in ultrasound imaging due to difficulties in fabricating complex microstructures. Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish a relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to an intermediate scale, demonstrating its utility in distinguishing between similar diffusion processes through their distinct spatial signatures. Furthermore, we illustrate the potential of this method by analyzing empirical data sets comprising the dispersal of a frog species and the movement of a marine species within a sediment layer. Our analyses reveal that the population's spatial distribution is governed by a similar diffusion process characterized by fractional exponent in the range between 0.5 and 1.5. We also find that the population's ability to explore and navigate its environment is constrained by a characteristic length scale that represents a balance between local movement and larger-scale diffusion. This research provides a framework for analyzing the spread of populations that exhibit time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics and may contribute to a deeper understanding of biological systems that diffuse through their environments. We also identify a critical distinction between subdiffusion and the intermediate behavior often observed in biological systems, which may be useful for inferring the time-dependent diffusion characteristics of a process from spatial data. However, confirming these inferences would require a separate analysis that leverages time and spatial information simultaneously. We suggest that a multi-scale fractional relaxation process may be an appropriate next step in this analysis but acknowledge that developing and applying such models is a subject for future research. We also present a theoretical argument for the possibility that the characteristic length scale that constrains a population's ability to explore and navigate its environment may be an expression of the population's optimal search strategy, which balances local movement and larger-scale diffusion. Although this idea is purely speculative at this point, it may have implications for our understanding of biological systems that exhibit intermediate diffusion behavior. A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically applied to a waveguide with a microresonator in close proximity, enabling the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms. Furthermore, a dimensionless equation is derived to describe the dynamics of two identical counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator and, under the condition of mode identity, it is proven that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation. The disproportionate impact of cross-phase modulation is experimentally verified in a silicon photonic loop system. The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based models have a common issue with overconfidence, stemming from the limited relationship between their predicted confidence and actual accuracy. To address this, we took a holistic approach that simultaneously enhanced both performance and calibration of the model. Initially, we used an ensemble of decision functions to produce a more reliable confidence assessment. Furthermore, we employed an expectation-maximization based method to adjust the decision boundaries, thereby improving accuracy and correcting the model's confidence bias. The proposed method demonstrated superior results when tested with three diverse datasets, surpassing the baseline models in both performance and calibration. The model's improved accuracy and calibrated confidence made it more suitable for high-stakes applications where reliability is paramount. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning in controlled environments, its potential is significantly limited due to its typical requirement for access to an accurate model and numerous high-quality training examples. In contrast, most real-world problems involve constantly changing conditions and scarce high-quality training data. To address this, the field requires a paradigm shift to effectively handle the uncertainties inherent in reinforcement learning. This study introduces a new framework for online decision-making that enables learning from scarce, high-quality training examples and moderate amounts of cheap data in dynamic environments. This framework is mathematically defined and demonstrated through a practical application in online dialogue management, yielding a system capable of learning user models from limited interactions and promoting engaging conversations. Experimental results validate the benefits of this approach. The software and data are freely accessible online.

However, the data volume from Liger is exceptionally large, which poses computational challenges for on-demand science data processing. To address this issue, we are developing an artificial neural network-based approach to quickly identify candidate sources and prioritize observations for further processing. Prioritization is critical because Liger cannot process all data simultaneously and needs to focus on the most significant discoveries first. To train this neural network, we used vast amounts of simulated data coupled with traditional astrophysical source extraction methods and Liger's data processing algorithms. The neural network demonstrated superior performance compared to existing methods and could prioritize sources with an accuracy rate of over 90%. This model can significantly reduce processing time from several days to just a few hours. Furthermore, this technique can be adapted for other complex survey data sets. Prior source lists can also be integrated into this system, making it suitable for observing modes with specific targets and prior knowledge. Ultimately, this artificial neural network-based approach will play a key role in maximizing the scientific value of Liger's data. Optical systems that measure intensity in the far field are constrained by the Rayleigh criterion, a resolution limitation imposed by the system's aperture. Research has shown that using spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) allows for maximum collection of field information, thereby surpassing the Rayleigh criterion in certain cases. While previous SPADE approaches have relied on resolving the lateral splitting of a Gaussian wavefunction, our work investigates a novel scenario in which one of two photons from a bi-photon source, generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, undergoes a horizontal separation. Through coincidence measurements following the projection of both photons onto Hermite-Gauss modes, we demonstrate the ability to super-resolve this separation, a capability thought to be constrained by the Rayleigh criterion if traditional measurement approaches were applied. Our findings therefore illustrate the ability to overcome this limitation with SPADE. Furthermore, our work utilizes a quantum optical setup, offering an analytically tractable model that enables a comprehensive understanding of the proposed method. We also establish the conditions under which SPADE is preferable to conventional approaches and discuss these findings in the context of optimal SPADE performance. Our research provides theoretical foundations for the evaluation of SPADE schemes in any bi-photon measurement application. This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties. Although algebraic geometry benefits from the Kirchhoff rule in studying abelian varieties, research in this field is still in its initial stages. To illustrate this, consider the work of Mumford, Kirwan, and others on compactifying moduli spaces of curves and abelian varieties. Their studies employed a combination of geometric and representation-theoretic methods to apply Hodge-theoretic principles. This is demonstrated through a simplified analysis of the compactification of moduli spaces of curves by B. H. Gross. This overview is part of a broader discussion on the related topics presented in his lecture series. It is an excerpt from his written notes, which are available under the title "Some Aspects of Hodge Theory". These notes are now made accessible in this revised format.

In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is highly beneficial. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey in an infinite habitat, engage in Lotka-Volterra dynamics. To this existing framework, a delay is introduced in the prey population's response to the impact of the predators, mirroring a typical example from ecology where consumer feedback often exhibits significant lag times. The model is analyzed in a neighborhood of a stable equilibrium where the system exhibits a unique, irregular behavior - chaotic mixed-mode oscillations (MMOs). This phenomenon, rare in biological models, arises when the delay exceeds a certain critical period and induces chaotic patterns in the prey population's recovery phase. As a result, the model transitions from a stable, coexisting equilibrium to an environmentally sensitive state prone to sudden fluctuations. The discovered mechanisms may provide insight into detecting early warning signs of population collapse in ecological systems and the role of delay in ecological instability. Furthermore, this study highlights the challenges and difficulties in modeling real-world ecosystems using dynamical systems and suggests that the interplay between continuous and discrete dynamics can give rise to complex and unpredictable behaviors in ecological models. To explore this possibility, we need to understand the star formation patterns within bulges and disks at various redshifts. I study the NII-based star formation rates in the central regions of both bulges and disks up to $z=5.5$. By selecting galaxies with low dust content and using NII-based star formation rates, I find the star formation rates in bulges and disks are similar from $z=4.5$ to $z=2.5$. However, a notable increase in the Sersic index $n$ in low-mass galaxies at $z=4$ to $z=3$ indicates the presence of small, highly dense bulges. These observations suggest the growth of bulges is primarily driven by in-situ star formation, with the mass of massive bulges being shaped by massive star clusters at $z=4$ to $z=2.5$. Furthermore, I observe a correlation between the Sersic index of low-mass galaxies at $z=2.5$ and a given line of sight's local density, indicating an effect of environmental density on the structure of bulges and a potential indicator of gravitational influence. The structure of bulges is therefore shaped by a combination of local density and massive star clusters, with a potential for bulges to act as cosmological probes. The proportion of bulge-dominated galaxies remains relatively stable across the redshift range $z=4.5$ to $z=2.5$, with approximately $0.75^{+0.15}_{-0.12}$ of massive star-forming galaxies at this range having a significant bulge component. Consequently, the growth of bulges is likely the primary driver of the observed slowdown in star formation at $z=6$. The proportion of bulge-dominated galaxies may have begun to influence the mass-density function of galaxies, potentially contributing to the slowdown in the galaxy mass-density function at $z=5.5$. The potential for this effect to continue driving the slowdown in the galaxy mass-density function at lower redshifts requires further investigation. This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array. Although content-addressable memories have been successfully implemented on FPGAs, our design uniquely captures Caxton C. Foster's pioneering ideas on parallel processing, incorporating the concepts of simultaneous parallel writes and the merging of output values – features commonly omitted in typical CAM applications like network routing. The resulting system allows a host computer to interface with the CAPP over USB/UART using a simple serial communication protocol, which has been effectively demonstrated with a Python-based driver. The integration of an external memory and the parallel processor's core have been successfully validated using a combination of Python and Verilog scripts, while the entire system has been shown to function correctly using a Python-based test program. The report also presents the results of a performance assessment, where the CAPP was able to locate and update specific addresses at varying speeds, showcasing its capability to support a wide range of application scenarios. The completed CAPP board has also been operational with the host computer, successfully executing several test programs that leveraged the content-addressable nature of the processor. The developed system and its associated software are now available for download, marking the completion of this project. We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, utilizing high-resolution near-infrared spectroscopy. This allowed us to measure the star formation rates, obtain spectral energy distributions, and estimate the stellar and black hole masses for each galaxy. Observations reveal a notable suppression of star formation in galaxies with irregularly shaped disks, as well as a significant relationship between their mass and radius. This relationship is consistent with the idea that massive galaxies with lopsided disks are experiencing suppressed star formation due to an encounter with a massive object, such as a galaxy with a dense, compact core. An observational indication of this object's impact is seen in one of the galaxy cores, where we observe an anomalous increase in the star formation rate at $\rm 0.12R_{180}$ with associated outflows and gas consumption. We re-examine and revise the predictions of the Universal Texture Zero (UTZ) flavour model as initially presented in the study arXiv:1710.01741. The revision is made with reference to more accurate experimental restrictions and refined numerical analysis methods. Specifically, our team developed an in-house Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to extensively evaluate the viable parameter range of the UTZ model, encompassing primary and secondary contributions in its effective operator expansion. Furthermore, we obtained for the first time precise UTZ predictions for previously underdetermined CP-violating phases of lepton interactions and neutrino mass hierarchies within the θ_{13}-inverted and normal mass ordering scenarios. Our findings validate the UTZ model's viability and support its potential to predict unique signatures for lepton-flavour violation processes accessible to ongoing and future experiments. The revised UTZ scenario also offers a more robust and detailed flavour explanation within a slightly refined effective operator framework. The revised UTZ flavour model may provide a coherent framework for combining lepton and quark flavour properties if its principles can be extended to the quark sector. Current cutting-edge neural code models excel at generating individual code segments but often struggle with complex tasks, like entire function code production. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages static code analysis for weak supervision. Our neuro-symbolic method allows a deep generative model to leverage a static-analysis tool to identify code connections generated, and trains on this data to generate code based on this analysis during training. When tested on the task of creating full Java functions within existing classes, our results reveal our approach surpasses state-of-the-art neural models while also enabling straightforward integration with pre-trained models through transfer learning. Our findings demonstrate the potential for this neuro-symbolic approach to facilitate significant advancements in code synthesis beyond the current neural code generation milestones. Furthermore, code samples are available at https://github.com/ghnaouel/code-synthesis and model weights can be accessed at https://huggingface.co/ghnaouel/code-synthesis. We have determined the dispersion relations for relativistic fluid modes in various configurations - scalar, vector, and tensor - and found the differences between their behavior in divergence-based and relaxation-time-approximation models. Our comparison also shows correspondence with first-order causal theories and highlights how a specific divergence-based model can predict a damped tensor mode, in contrast to earlier viscous tensor mode studies. Furthermore, we found that a hydrodynamically-corrected causal theory can reproduce the divergence-based model's results. This theoretical framework can be applied to study the properties of particles emitted in relativistic fluid systems.

Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced methods due to shifting concepts and ongoing learning requirements. Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or nearest neighbors with fixed memory, can struggle to accommodate frequent fluctuations, remove smooth outliers, and adapt to deep neural network architectures. We introduce a new technique for continuous real-time anomaly detection based on quantum measurements, which can process infinite data streams at constant $O(1)$ update complexity and effectively estimate changing densities through random Fourier features and an exponential moving average. This approach was thoroughly evaluated by comparing it to 12 prominent algorithms for real-time anomaly detection on 12 diverse data streams. The results show our quantum-inspired method surpasses classic algorithms and often outperforms memory-augmented neural network baselines while requiring essentially no computational updates. The code is openly accessible on the Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS) website.

This study presents a novel, high-order numerical method for solving the linear Fokker-Planck equation under a constant diffusion term. The devised method integrates elements from the Lagrange-Galerkin and semi-Lagrangian techniques to capture the equation's transport and diffusion properties. The Lagrange-Galerkin approach is used to derive a continuous mesh-free formulation, which is then approximated by a discrete scheme based on the method of lines. The resulting system is solved through a direct algorithm due to its symmetric positive-definite nature. To demonstrate the method's validity and efficiency, several test cases are analyzed in terms of convergence and compared against a respected benchmark method. All test cases demonstrate the method's high-order accuracy and its ability to achieve comparable results with superior performance. Furthermore, the method is capable of solving large-scale problems with substantial spatial domains due to its efficient direct solver. To illustrate this, the study concludes by presenting a large-scale problem with a domain of $[0,1]^5$ and a step size of $10^{-4$ for the time discretization. The resulting system is solved in approximately 320 seconds for a quadratic interpolation scheme, which is a notable achievement given the method's computational complexity. All code and data are openly accessible on a reputable repository platform.}

Advancements in machine learning and signal processing have generated substantial interest in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), which excel at solving complex, engineering-driven problems. Nonetheless, employing such networks for critical life-altering decisions demands a deeper understanding of their decision-making processes. Unfortunately, most artificial neural networks, including DNNs, function as opaque systems, hindering insight into their internal workings. Although some research has initiated the quest to illuminate their behavior, the field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) remains underdeveloped. This study aims to offer a thorough exploration into comprehending, visualizing, and explicating the inner workings and global behavior of DNNs. A diverse range of techniques, including computational neuroscience-inspired methods and global analysis techniques, is examined to achieve this goal. Furthermore, innovative graphical representations are proposed to provide enthusiasts and experts with a unified visual understanding of the networks. The proposed concepts are further demonstrated through the development of user-friendly tools that facilitate effortless exploration of the networks. The unique features of these solutions include open-source code, freely accessible datasets, and preprocessed data available for download. All source code, along with the accompanying data, has been openly contributed to an associated GitHub repository to empower further development and facilitate collaboration among researchers in this domain. The collaborative approach is seen as pivotal to propelling the field of XAI forward and initiating significant advancements in this area. The techniques and tools showcased in this work have far-reaching implications, given the widespread adoption of DNNs in various life-altering applications, including healthcare, finance, and transportation. The field of XAI holds immense potential to address pressing concerns related to trust, safety, and the societal implications of such systems. The future of this domain is expected to be shaped by a combination of advances in computational neuroscience, global analysis, and robust collaboration among researchers, fueled by open-source contributions and accessible methodologies. Our study uncovered evidence for the occurrence of a specific behavior in low-mass stars that have expanded into giant planets, characterized by the distinct rotation rates of their core and outer layers. This particular observation emerged during the analysis of a group of 15 low-mass giant stars, all of which had been subjected to spectroscopic measurements that allowed for the assessment of their stellar parameters, including temperatures, metallicities, and several other properties. Furthermore, by conducting a detailed assessment of chemical abundance patterns, we were able to identify and eliminate any stars displaying anomalies resulting from contamination by planetary material. To further our research, we employed stellar oscillations to collect information about the stars' internal structures. By analyzing the frequencies of these oscillations, we were able to create 3D maps of how different elements are distributed inside the stars. Our analysis revealed a notable discrepancy in the rotation rates of the outer and core regions in four out of the 15 studied stars. This distinct rotation pattern in low-mass giant stars has no previously documented instance. We propose that the observed rotation differential could result from angular momentum conservation during the expansion of the star, similar to the phenomenon we have previously described in higher-mass giant stars. Our research expands our understanding of this process, suggesting it may begin before the stars have fully enveloped their planetary systems. Additionally, we discovered an inverse relationship between the rotation rates of the core and the outer layers, with a possible timescale of about 1 billion years for this process. This finding may have implications for the behavior of giant planets within these stars' gravitational influence. Our study highlights the value of studying giant stars through spectroscopy and seismology, providing a window into how these stars evolve and their internal structures, which in turn can shed light on the history of their planetary surroundings. This research is a part of a larger study aimed at identifying signs of planetary interaction with giant stars through oscillations and their potential impact on these stars' internal structures. This work is also relevant to ongoing and upcoming missions such as Ganymede, TESS, and PLATO, which will be capable of detecting a wide range of stellar vibrations, which could reveal details about the stars' internal structures and their interactions with surrounding planetary systems. This research will be continued with an expanded dataset of 1000 low-mass giant stars that have been or will be subjected to spectroscopic and seismic analysis as part of the Ganymede survey. This study will provide a comprehensive understanding of how the behavior of these stars' cores and outer layers contribute to their internal structure

This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. It is demonstrated that when $\kappa$ equals zero and the initial data is smooth and odd, the solution will eventually become singular over a finite period of time. Additionally, we find that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ also leads to the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time. This indicates that this specific model shares a similar feature with the Euler equation, where a singularity will inevitably form in a finite amount of time. This paper investigates the age of information (AoI) in a discrete-time status updating system that employs the Ber/G/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that utilizing a two-dimensional state vector which simultaneously monitors AoI and packet age enables derivation of the stationary AoI distribution via analysis of a constituted stochastic process. We present the general formula for the AoI distribution and derive an explicit expression for geometrically distributed service times. We also examine the relationship between AoI and packet age through the mean AoI, and compare it to a priority queue that only considers packet age. We establish that the mean AoI in the discrete-time system is equal to the sum of the mean service time and one, and derive the mean AoI for geometrically distributed service times as $2-\frac{1}{\rho}$, where $\rho$ represents the service rate. We further investigate the efficacy of two discrete-time scheduling policies that minimize AoI, and provide numerical examples to illustrate their performance. Additionally, we investigate the fundamental limits of AoI in this system and its connection to time diversity. We conclude that time diversity enables reduction of the mean AoI to the mean service time. We also establish that the AoI distribution in the discrete-time system has an upper bound that asymptotically approaches $2e/\rho$ as $\rho$ increases. We anticipate that this bound asymptotically approaches the mean AoI, and present a related open problem. We contribute the novel idea of utilizing a two-dimensional state vector to analyze AoI in closed-form, and introduce an innovative approach to analyze AoI through the constitution of stochastic processes. These methods are particularly applicable to queueing systems with single-server and minimal capacity, where the arrival process has a low rate or is Poisson. We hope that these novel concepts and analytical methods will be useful in analyzing AoI in various communication systems. We also highlight the significance of considering both packet age and AoI in the analysis and design of status updating systems. We believe that our results pave the way for further research on the statistical distribution of AoI in queueing systems. We propose that future studies consider systems with multiple servers, non-normally distributed service times, and age-based scheduling algorithms. We anticipate that these extensions will significantly contribute to a deeper understanding of AoI in complex communication systems. We are confident that our results and open problems will stimulate research on the age of information in queueing theory. We hope that this research will ultimately lead to the development of more efficient scheduling algorithms in dynamic status updating systems. We

This work delves into various quantum algebras that arise from a special type of set-theoretic solution to equations representing bialgebras, with a focus on those that satisfy the property of being quasi-triangular or bialgebraic. Building on previous findings, we establish that set-theoretic solutions to complex equations representing bialgebras yield collection of elements that form a set, rather than a traditional vector space. Consequently, many established techniques from linear and differential algebra are not directly applicable to this context. Nevertheless, we demonstrate the potential of our approach by deriving key relationships for the quantum algebras $U_q(\mathfrak{g})$, $F_q(\mathfr{g})$ and $O_q(\mathfr{g})$, based on established set-theoretic solutions. Moreover, we show that by defining a specific set of coefficients, many of these quantum algebras exhibit the desirable characteristic of quasi-triangular quasi-bialgebras. As a result, we can establish the ground field for these algebras, determined by the minimal closure of a set containing 1, in accordance with its definition as a quasi-bialgebra. Notably, this understanding leads to an accurate description of the algebra structure for $U_q(\mathfrak{g})$, $F_q(\mathfr{g})$ and $O_q(\mathfr{g})$, offering a fresh perspective that differs from common matrix realizations. Lastly, we identify the relationship between the generic quantum group $U_q(\mathfr{g})$ and its non-degenerate representations, establishing that every non-degenerate representation of $U_q(\mathfr{g})$ is isomorphic to an quotient of $U_q(\math{g})$ by a quasi-triangular coideal. This connection serves as a departure point for an exploration of the generic quantum supergroup $U_q(\mathfr{g})$, particularly in relation to its fundamental non-degenerate representation, often denoted as $\hat{U}_q(\mathfr{g})$. This study sets the stage for expanding our analysis to various other quantum algebras and their set-theoretic solutions. Lastly, we outline the potential application of our approach to set-theoretic solutions of quantum algebras that do not correspond to bialgebras, such as the Faddeev-Altschuler-Takita quantum Yang-Baxter equation. Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can be leveraged by silicon quantum processors through valley quantum tunneling of phosphorus dopants.  However, the valley quantum tunneling of phosphorus dopants in silicon is hindered due to the large energy difference required for a valley transition and the lack of valley degeneracy caused by an external magnetic field.  This limitation can be addressed by developing precise control over the position of single-electron spins in silicon, a concept known as "valley-sky."  This paper outlines a new method for determining the valley position of electrons by combining a new valley contrast agent and a previously established technique for precisely measuring the spatial extent of single-electron states.  This new approach enables the development of valley-entangled states and facilitates the direct observation of valley tunneling, thus providing a means to study the unique properties of valley quantum mechanics.  This study demonstrates the capability to accurately measure the unique characteristics of valley quantum mechanics, making it possible to control the position of single-electron spins based on their valley and enabling the direct exploration of valley tunneling. Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behavior. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By demonstrating that neural network functions can equivalently represent system parameters and dynamics, we were able to generalize this approach to analogous exponential algorithms. However, our method also reveals that the inherent linearization of these algorithms hinders their accurate modeling. Consequently, we propose a novel direction for universal function approximation using neural networks on graphs, which can serve as a starting point for exploring other exponential algorithms and a deeper understanding of the neural network representation itself. Our source code is available at https://github.com/strawman-hub/graph_bello_prop.

We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria across all possible totals, thereby covering every natural number interval from $n$ to $MN$, where $M$ and $N$ are any two given natural numbers. These formulas have a hierarchical structure and can be understood through the lens of recursive combinatorial construction, encompassing the union over all possible prior configurations of sets that meet certain divisibility criteria, thereby linking them to the counts for smaller natural number intervals. As a result, this hierarchical framework allows for efficient calculation of the counts for any given interval through a mere calculation of the counts for all preceding intervals with smaller totals. In addition, we establish a notable connection between these counts and a well-known sequence of numbers with Fibonacci-like properties. 

Furthermore, we derive an intriguing formula that expresses the counts of non-negative integer solutions to systems of linear Diophantine equations with specified coefficients and upper bounds, demonstrating a profound connection to the concept of recursive combinatorial construction and showcasing the profound implications this has for the underlying binary integer partition counts. 

Last but not least, we introduce an intriguing conjecture that remains unproven at this point, yet offers a compelling framework for further exploration within the realm of combinatorial construction and recursive calculation. 

In the second part of this paper, we delve into a distinct yet related topic, where we explore a specific game-like scenario that involves an infinite sequence of nested choices, ultimately giving rise to a binary decision tree with an astonishing $2^{\aleph_0}$ possible paths. Strong nonlocality, a phenomenon where systems demonstrate nonlocality without entanglement, can be seen in multipartite states with certain properties. Unextendible product bases (UPBs) have shown nonlocality without entanglement in previous research, and their quantum metrology potential has been theoretically demonstrated, suggesting they could have strong measurement uncertainty advantages. However, a large UPB in higher-dimensional spaces made of high-dimensional systems was missing until this work, where we created a maximum-sized UPB in a 3-party, 4-dimensional space (3D$@{\times}3D@{\times}3D$) using two photons from a spontaneous parametric down-conversion process. We further showed that this UPB has strong measurement uncertainty by outperforming entangled states in a particular quantum metrology scenario, indicating that this UPB can exhibit improved precision under certain conditions of application. A proposed method for a quantum nonlocality test involving UPBs could also enable the detection of nonlocality in a multi-partite system without requiring the ability to measure entanglement. This discovery of a large UPB in high-dimensional spaces, along with its proposed measurement uncertainty demonstration and nonlocality test, can contribute to the understanding and potential applications of nonlocality in high-dimensional systems. This work is also a source material for the related research on a high-dimensional local conversion test proposed in a separate work. GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a unique, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods. The source code for this study is openly accessible on GitHub at the specified URL.

We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs. This new collection supplements existing examples, including Cayley graphs for finite groups and extended generalised wreath graphs. Furthermore, we outline a method to classify quasiprimitive twisted wreath structures by identifying key automorphism group properties that define these structures within the broader star normal quotient twisted wreath framework. This approach enables the detection of potential locally arc-transitivity in these structures. As a demonstration, we serendipitously identify a previously unrecognized locally arc-transitive graph, dubbed $\textrm{GS}(9,8,3)$, featuring a 2728-vertex arc-orbit. This discovery places it among the smallest known examples of locally arc-transitive graphs with a quasiprimitive automorphism group. Additionally, we describe a higher-order twisted wreath structure, $\textrm{WΣ}(9,8,3,5)$, and conjecture that it embodies a locally arc-transitive graph with an exceptionally large arc-orbit. To support this conjecture, we present a 14348256-vertex locally arc-transitive graph, $\textrm{WΣ}(9,8,3,7)$, among whose automorphism group orbits contain a massive 52622544 vertex set. This paper's findings respond to questions posed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger and address a longstanding question regarding the existence of locally arc-transitive graphs with quasiprimitive automorphism groups within the twisted wreath structures category. Our approach builds upon recent developments in the study of locally arc-transitive graphs.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size. Furthermore, the algorithm exhibits practical applicability when compared with a recent high-dimensional estimation method for grouped variables. Additionally, the implementation of the proposed method is made accessible through an R function included in the package 'RAGene'. The package's installation instructions and a brief overview of the algorithm's R implementation are also provided.
