To understand the model's behavior at large p, it was simplified and demonstrated that this spin model shares the same phase structure as the 3d QCD at large N. As a result, its phase diagram includes both a low-temperature symmetrical phase and a high-temperature phase with O(3) symmetry. To study the high-energy phase, researchers applied the 1/N expansion, which transforms the SU(3) spin model into a triplet of interacting Dirac fermions on a triangular lattice. To determine the triplet's interactions, researchers used two main approaches: the first relied on matching coefficients from the SU(3) expansion, while the second employed a weak coupling analysis. Both methods yielded consistent results for the interactions, which were then utilized to analyze the phase diagram. Although the interactions were not sufficient to yield an exact solution, they allowed for a numerical study that indicated the O(3) symmetric phase persisted up to an extremely high critical temperature. Notably, this temperature was significantly higher when compared to self-dual fixed point found in the Z_N crossover model. Moreover, an exploration of the model's ground state revealed that both the large p and N limits yielded similar results when compared to exact SU(3) calculations. As a result, the large p limit could be regarded as an extension of the large N limit. A new implementation of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method has been developed to efficiently achieve robust convergence for well-behaved central potentials. The method converts HF equations into a generalized eigenvalue problem by using a B-spline basis in a finite-size box and incrementally increases the strength of electron-electron interactions. The developed approach offers a strong foundation for large-scale, converged HF calculations in the large-size limit. We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it has a desired property of slow convergence; (2) in the medium-distance region, it exhibits local convexity; and (3) far from the target, it possesses a property called Poincar\'e-like convexity. Our analysis can be performed under a geometry that is native to the factorized domain, and it provides a more detailed analysis of the original problem for positive semidefinite matrices. To our knowledge, this is the first time a matrix optimization problem with a semidefinite constraint has been analyzed in a way that is intrinsic to the underlying geometry. We also derive a local linearized convergence analysis, which can be viewed as an extension to matrix-valued functions under a specific geometry. To demonstrate the applicability of our analysis, we examine its connection to nonnegative least-squares and phase recovery problems. Furthermore, we demonstrate the feasibility of our analysis by conducting a numerical study on its own computational efficiency. Lastly, this efficiency suggests that our analysis may be used to design computationally efficient optimization algorithms. 

This research is motivated by the challenge of developing globally convergent optimization algorithms for large-scale positive semidefinite cones. To this end, we conduct an exploratory global landscape analysis of the Burer-Monteiro factorization of a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we identify distinct local landscape regions: (1) a neighborhood of the target parameter with local curvature, (2) a medium-distance region with local convexity, and (3) a far-field region with a convex structure analogous to that of the Poincar\'e ball. Our analysis can be performed under a geometry native to the factorized domain and includes a local linearized convergence analysis, extending a matrix-valued convergence theorem to an alternative geometry. To demonstrate computational efficiency, we examine the computational cost of this analysis. Although this analysis is an exploratory study, it suggests that an understanding of the local structure of optimization problems with nontrivial constraints may inform the development of computationally efficient algorithms.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. The focus of this paper is on a different conjecture related to edge coloring, specifically looking to determine the minimum number of colors required to color a complete graph of odd size, when constraints are placed on the colors used for specific edge sets. It is first shown that for certain even numbers of vertices, this number can be as low as 2 times the logarithm of the number of vertices, but it is also demonstrated that for larger, sufficiently high numbers of vertices, this number must be at least almost as large as the logarithm of the number of vertices. The main component of this proof involves another graph theory concept, that of an arc-coloring, but first it is necessary to establish a relationship between arc-coloring and edge coloring. This could be possible if these particles once controlled the universe's energy density and led to a transition to a matter-dominated period before decaying in time for Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis to occur. We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to replicate players' learning behavior and assess their capacity for convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. Utilizing simulation outcomes with a particular approach as well as general statistical analysis, our results showed that "social" learning outperformed "individual" learning across all specifications, with the exception of one scenario where they performed equally. Furthermore, we found that allowing the sharing of past outcomes among players enabled faster convergence to the Nash Equilibrium, ultimately reaching it within a smaller number of iterations. Conversely, shared past outcomes failing to lead to convergence to the Nash Equilibrium within the set number of iterations led to failure to converge in at least one additional simulation. Additionally, "social learning" was found to outperform "individual learning" even when the algorithms were compared under restricted knowledge settings, resulting in successful attainment of the Nash Equilibrium within the set number of iterations in one additional simulation where "individual learning" failed to converge. 

Our research provides empirical evidence validating the theoretical concept that social learning algorithms can facilitate convergence to the Nash Equilibrium, in line with recent experimental research. Moreover, our findings highlight the capacity of genetic algorithm variants to replicate complex strategic behavior in oligopolistic settings. We also suggest that the success of these social learning algorithms may stem from evolutionary principles, where the sharing of past experiences among co-evolving species enhances collective learning and drives the convergence to optimal equilibrium through a process of cultural evolution. Conversely, individual learning, characterized by shared experiences leading to distinct personal discoveries, may result in divergent outcomes and failure to reach the Nash Equilibrium. 

Our research also explores the effect of knowledge restrictions in shared knowledge settings, demonstrating a superior outcome for social learning algorithms even when the algorithms are compared under restricted knowledge settings. This finding indicates that the capacity of social learning to attain the Nash Equilibrium is robust and unaffected by the availability of all past outcomes among players. Lastly, the research reveals that genetic algorithm social learning variants exhibit a capacity for cultural evolution, converging to the optimal equilibrium more efficiently when allowed to share past outcomes among players. 

In conclusion, our research validates the concept of social learning algorithms achieving the Nash Equilibrium through additional, theoretical analysis, as well as providing empirical evidence for the success of these algorithms in a range of oligopolistic models. The Ising model falls within the domain of equilibrium statistical mechanics, in contrast, the voter model represents a system out of equilibrium. Our analysis focuses on an opinion formation model, a hybrid of Ising and voter agents, with concentrations of $p$ and $1-p$. Notably, even though detailed balance is violated for $p<1$, it has been shown that on a fully connected graph the stationary state average magnetization for any $p>0$ follows the same equation as for the pure Ising model ($p=1$). This behavior is further confirmed by numerical simulations; however, the observed equivalence with the pure Ising model is limited to magnetization. While susceptibility diverges at the same temperature as magnetization, its values vary according to the concentration of Ising agents $p$. Simulations conducted on a random graph also reveal that even a minimal proportion of Ising agents can trigger ferromagnetic ordering. Moreover, this indicates that a small minority of dedicated individuals can significantly influence the opinions of a larger majority in a connected population. Further analysis on this phenomenon is proposed. Lastly, the dynamic behavior of the hybrid model is compared to that of the pure Ising and voter models. The introduced model offers a framework for exploring opinion formation dynamics and has implications for the study of complex systems where cooperative behavior may emerge as a result of the interaction between adaptive and non-adaptive elements. The proposed model can be applied to any system where interactive decisions are based on local, pairwise interactions and where the distribution of interaction weights is given and unmodifiable. The hybrid model specifically models a scenario where there is a coexistence of two different cognitive architectures, one being a dedicated and adaptive agent and the other a conformist who simply follows local influences. The latter may be viewed as representing background social norms which can be perceived as having a life of their own. The background social norms can then be seen as the social equivalent of the system's thermal bath in statistical mechanics. The introduced model also offers an opportunity to reassess the concept of temperature as it may not always be an intrinsic property of the system but rather a characteristic of the interplay between adaptive and non-adaptive elements. The proposed model also raises questions about the applicability of the Boltzmann principle of maximum entropy, particularly when the distribution of weights is highly uneven. The hybrid model may also be seen as a system of interacting spins where some spins are independent of the external magnetic field. The COVID19 virus is spread through contaminated droplets expelled by infected individuals when they cough, sneeze, speak or breathe. Understanding how these virus-carrying droplets behave under changing environmental conditions is essential to tracking the infection's spread. To investigate this, we examine the movement of evaporating droplets influenced by gravity and varying weather, observing how they change in size until either settling on the ground or breaking down into small particles that can linger in the air. Our analysis reveals significant impacts of humidity and temperature on evaporation, with large droplets falling due to gravity's dominance despite evaporative losses and smaller droplets suspended in the air due to evaporative cooling. The size of intermediate droplets is highly dependent on weather conditions and is critical to infection spread, underscoring the need for physical distancing and highlighting potential risks associated with breathing or speaking in confined, humid spaces. Ultimately, our study highlights the complexity of virus spread through droplets and emphasizes the importance of multidisciplinary research in understanding this phenomenon. It also suggests that numerical models of virus spread may be improved by incorporating interactions between viruses, temperature, humidity, and air particles. Lastly, its implications encourage researchers to explore other complex phenomena involving multiple interacting forces and substances in motion. Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data constraints, model choices, connectivity, and computational constraints. Despite the importance of understanding uncertainty in NN-based predictions, there is a noticeable absence of a comprehensive framework that systematically addresses uncertainty in NNs. This article fills this gap by presenting a unified theoretical framework that categorizes uncertainty associated with NN-based predictions into three primary dimensions: data-related uncertainty, model uncertainty, and algorithm-related uncertainty. Furthermore, the paper explores the inherent connections between these uncertainties and their manifestations in various forms such as noise, parallax, model complexity, optimization, saturation, and computational limitations. The framework is then applied to analyze the impact of these uncertainties on NN-based prediction techniques including supervised learning, unsupervised learning, neural operators, and neural-neural closures. The discussion on this framework is supported by numerical examples that demonstrate its applicability. The proposed framework is poised to elevate the understanding of uncertainty in NNs and its interactions with data, models, algorithms, and physical laws, paving the way for more informed decisions in NN-based problem-solving. This forward-thinking approach is anticipated to shape the direction of future research in NNs. This work is intended to spark lively discussions and propel research in this direction. Using an exact partition function, we analyze a unitary matrix model based on a single plaquette configuration at a finite $N$ for both the SU($N$) and U($N$) symmetries. This allows us to investigate the eigenvalue distributions in detail. For the SU($N$) symmetry, we derive an explicit formula for the joint density of eigenvalues, revealing a relationship with a Schur process derived from a one-row Young diagram. For the U($N$) symmetry, we find that the joint density of eigenvalues corresponds to a last row Schur process and obtain explicit formulas for various correlation functions. Furthermore, we establish a connection between these U($N$) Schur processes and Plaquette CA in the Ising model, demonstrating that the U($N$) Schur process can be viewed as a representation of Plaquette CA. This connection enables us to determine the spectral statistics for models related to U($N$), including a symmetric version of Fyodorov-Shepp's matrix model. For large $N$, we identify the eigenvalue density spectra for both SU($N$) and U($N$) symmetries, including a symmetric Tracy-Widom distribution. Additionally, we find that the diagonal U($N$) spectral density at the Plaquette CA ground state corresponds to a generalised step statistic, which is a known distribution in probability theory known as Weyl's volume formula. This relationship between U($N$) spectral density and last row Schur process provides an alternative solution to a long-standing conjecture posed by Borodin and Olshanski. Our analysis extends beyond Plaquette CA, encompassing a broader class of local Hamiltonians. This study offers an innovative blend of mathematical physics, random matrix theory, and representation theory through its exploration of one-plaquette unitary matrix models. This work is an outgrowth of the authors' prior research on plaid Schur processes and quantum plaid systems. Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, screening for hardware malfunctions that could cause inaccuracies in vision capabilities. Presently, detecting hardware errors in neural networks poses a complex problem. This study introduces a technique to identify hardware errors in convolutional neural networks by comparing their output against predetermined safe limits, thereby preventing accuracy degradation due to hardware issues. By comparing the proposed method with alternative error detection techniques, this research demonstrates the effectiveness of clipping activation functions to prevent precision problems. The proposed method demonstrates substantial error detection accuracy improvements (up to 95.5%) over conventional techniques when evaluating a CNN with various hardware setups. The reliability of this method is further validated through a rigorous evaluation of 150 distinct CNN modules, showcasing its broad applicability to a wide range of computer vision applications. Additionally, this research highlights the error propagation patterns that influence the accuracy of the network, in addition to illustrating the precise error types that the clipping activation function technique addresses. Ultimately, this study emphasizes the value of combining reliable hardware with robust neural networks to ensure the overall dependability of computer vision systems. The error detection technique developed as part of this research has been made publicly accessible to facilitate its use by other vision system developers. The code is available online at https://github.com/axelconti/CNN-error-detection. The research detailed in this paper has been submitted to IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems. Essentially, netting represents a different method for companies to make payments to each other, involving an agreement in which each party deducts debts owed from debts owed to it. By combining the debts between parties, the usual payment process can be substituted with a direct settlement. In this research, we present a suite of graph algorithms capable of generating optimal netting solutions suitable for a national economy's scale, yielding efficient results in a timely manner. Our analysis utilizing Romanian Ministry of Economy invoice data demonstrates that conventional graph algorithms can still tackle highly significant contemporary challenges effectively. This research is an expansion of previous work where we established the necessity for balanced bipartite graphs and identified the minimum size of such graphs that can exemplify optimal netting solutions. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. All code and data are openly accessible at https://github.com/zhunghui/mmespaces.

The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains considerable annotation errors that significantly impede the robust training of models. The recent releases of refined datasets, MultiWOZ 2.1 to 2.4, are not entirely noise-free, especially in the training subset, rectifying them proves costly. Instead of addressing the issues of annotation quality in the current datasets, we develop a versatile framework named ASSIST, aiming to train dialogue state tracking models with high reliability even from inaccurate labels. The proposed framework first uses an auxiliary model trained on a smaller clean dataset to generate accurate labels for each data sample, then utilizes both the generated pseudo labels and existing flawed labels for the training of the primary model. The framework is mathematically justified and is experimentally verified to boost the dialogue state tracking joint goal accuracy by up to 28.16% on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset and 8.41% on the MultiWOZ 2.4 dataset compared to training from just flawed labels alone. The developed framework is accessible at https://github.com/leelexin/ASSIST. The code has been successfully integrated into the popular dialogue state tracking framework DialogBPTT, downloadable at https://github.com/leelexin/DialogBPTT-ASSIST. Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization to navigate effectively, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals, although they have difficulty training and efficiency limitations. This paper proposes an external memory attention learning-based VIO framework, capable of efficiently combining the data from both the camera and inertial sensors for state estimation, and we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this model by accurately estimating the pose in various challenging scenarios, surpassing even the traditional and current state-of-the-art VIO baselines in various scenes. Moreover, this model exhibits better performance and lower training/processing time when compared to the widely-used torchio tool's default settings. The source code of this paper is available at: https://github.com/zhengzhengalex/attentionMemoryVIO.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. Furthermore, we predict that SHOWS can host both zero-energy surface states and hinge states. To separate and distinguish the contributions of different hinge points to the surface states is also proposed. Additionally, we propose that SHOWS can be used to design a hinge current amplifier and a zero-energy surface state interferometer, which can amplify and accurately measure the topological properties of materials. These innovative proposals have the potential to advance the field of topological electronics.

This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cannot freely share their results. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, which leverages the strong performance of pre-trained models by tapping into their existing capabilities rather than necessitating access to the training data itself. To illustrate the feasibility of FedSA, we created a framework where multiple teachers contribute their pre-trained language models for a student model to benefit from through a federated learning process. To demonstrate the effectiveness of FedSA, we designed an experiment in which a student model was trained to recognize hate speech by utilizing multiple teachers who had trained their models for entirely different projects. The FedSA approach outperformed both the baseline models and a model that integrated the data of all teachers, indicating that our method successfully capitalizes on the strengths of multiple pre-trained language models with minimal need for large hate-speech data. The results show FedSA to be superior to both FedML (deep learning) and Annealed Model Averaging (annealed Bayesian) approaches, achieving a notable 6% improvement in accuracy. Moreover, the FedSA approach proved computationally efficient, requiring significantly less calculation than both FedML and annealed Bayesian. To facilitate further research, we are releasing the code and data utilized in this research project. The data comprises 10 diverse datasets containing a total of 43,000 samples with corresponding labels, covering multiple categories of abusive language. The outstanding performance of the FedSA approach suggests that this novel technique has vast potential applications, especially when collaborating with organizations that operate disconnected datasets. Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases.  Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law.  Once middle-aged, its rotational velocity plateaus, except for the star's outer layers.  Older stars exhibit slower and nearly uniform rotational velocities at all radial distances, along with slower differential rotations.  The plateaus' onset is linked to the activation of the solar tachocline, a stable region with distinct differential rotation.  A simplified model of convective flux reversals predicts that the Rossby number, a ratio of rotational to laminar flux timescales, triggers this transition.  However, this model requires adjustment to accommodate the stars' polynomial potential energy diagrams.  By refining the model and incorporating the activation of the tachocline, we can predict its onset for individual stars based on their mass, radius, and age.  This, in turn, enables the derivation of age-dependent rotational velocity profiles for these stars.  As a result, we can distinguish between primordial and secular slowdown in solar-type stars.  Our findings demonstrate that the stars' rotational velocity distributions reflect their primordial origins, with the secular component only emerging after the Sun-like transition to the plateau phase.  This research offers a fresh perspective on the stars' rotational evolution, incorporating the tachocline's dynamics and convective flux patterns.  It also highlights the significance of the Rossby number in driving the differential rotation's transition.  By applying this model to exoplanets, we can anticipate a similar transition in these planets' evolution, given their composition and size.  This study is a starting point for a comprehensive theory that explains the relationships between convective flux patterns, the stars' internal structures, and their rotational evolution.  As such, it positions us to explore the connections between these processes and other stellar phenomena, such as magnetic field generation and stellar activity levels.  Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for a deeper understanding of the interplay between convective flux, stellar internal structures, and rotational evolution, with implications for both solar-type stars and the broader universe of convective stars.  This work is complemented by a Python package that enables users to compute the stars' rotational velocity profiles based on their mass, radius, age, and metal content.  This code is available online at an specified repository.  In the future, we plan to expand this model by incorporating the activation of the tachocline

Consider a unit cube, $Q_n$, in $n$-dimensional space and a function space, $C(Q_n)$, consisting of continuous functions from $Q_n$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Define the norm of a function as its maximum absolute value over $Q_n$. Let $\Pi_1\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)$ be the set of polynomials of degree at most one, i.e., linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. An interpolation projector $P$ is introduced that maps functions from $C(Q_n)$ to linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$, using nodes within $Q_n$. When the number of nodes is an Hadamard number, a non-degenerate simplex can be formed with vertices at $Q_n$. Various methods will be discussed for establishing upper bounds for the norm of $P$ in the form $\|P\|_{Q_n} \leq c \sqrt{n}$ for the corresponding interpolation projector $P$. Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. Furthermore, we investigated the dielectric properties of amorphous aluminum films with thicknesses ranging from 5 nm to 60 nm, discovering a linear relationship between film thickness and carrier concentration. We also demonstrate the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating methods to reduce carrier concentrations, a crucial step in optimizing quantum device performance. Additionally, we investigate the dielectric properties of amorphous aluminum films with linear carrier concentration relationships, demonstrating the importance of crystal amorphization and film thickness on carrier concentrations and providing insights essential for optimizing aluminum film deposition. This research highlights the significance of terahertz near-field optical microscopy in gaining a deeper understanding of quantum device functionality and suggests its potential as a diagnostic tool for resolving decoherence issues.

The atmosphere of Venus, with its thick and unbreathable gases, has long intrigued scientists. Despite significant research, much of Venus' atmospheric history remains unclear. Recent discoveries made during orbiting spacecraft missions have revealed new insights, particularly the presence of carbon dioxide molecules rotating in a peculiar manner and phosphorus chemical compounds found in volcanic plumes. To better understand these findings, a new theoretical approach is proposed, which utilizes a general circulation model to study the interactions between the atmosphere's chemical composition and circulatory systems. By incorporating chemical reaction processes and external influences such as volcanic outgassing, this model simulates the evolution of Venus' atmospheric chemistry over thousands of years and offers a new perspective on the planet's atmospheric history. The model also highlights the potential for the Earth to influence Venus' atmosphere through tidal interactions and a possible escape of atmospheric gases during the Earth's massive impacts. Theoretical simulations also suggest that volcanic plumes could provide a source of primitive materials that could be studied to gain insights into the composition of Venus' core and the early history of the planet. The model further suggests that the current state of Venus' atmosphere may result from a gradual increase in volcanic activity over billions of years. The model is the first of its kind to study the complex chemistry and circulation systems of Venus' atmosphere and could serve as a foundation for future research and more comprehensive models. The approach proposed here could also be applied to other planets and moons with substantial internal heat and active chemistry, such as Jupiter's moon Ganymede. The model has the potential to shed light on the early history of these bodies and provide a framework for understanding the fundamental processes that govern their atmospheric evolution. Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have reached optimal performance in medical image segmentation, the process is hindered by a large number of required annotations for training. Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) techniques have potential in decreasing this burden, but they are hindered when datasets are small and have few labeled images. One method to enhance performance involves leveraging existing annotated datasets of similar anatomical structures for training. Nevertheless, a challenge arises when adapting the model to cross-anatomy domains due to differences in image modalities and target structures' appearance. To overcome this, we propose Contrastive Semi-Supervised Domain Adaptation (CSDA) for medical image segmentation, utilizing unlabeled target images and annotated source images of similar structures. We employ Domain-Specific Disentanglement Masks to separate domain-specific differences, then employ a contrastive learning approach to find similar structures across domains. By combining these methods, we enhance the model's ability to adapt to target domains with minimal unlabeled target data and few labeled target images. Experimental evaluations on two datasets demonstrate CSDA's superiority over baseline methods. Code is available at https://github.com/zwangmed/CSDA.

Depending on $\tau$-beam polarization, final state $\tau$-lepton decay modes that involve hadrons or leptons can be used to determine the expected signature and sensitivity. For unpolarized $\tau$-beams and a 4 GeV, 80 ${\rm fb}^{-1}$ dataset, the expected signature for a zero form factor hypothesis is $5.5$ standard deviations for semihadronic decays and $4.5$ for semileptonic decays. These expected signatures can be achieved in $d_\tau(s)$ with a magnitude of $10^{-20}\mathrm{e}^{-i\phi}$ or an on-shell value of $\Delta g_1^{\tau}(Q^2=s) = 1.3\times 10^{-5}\mathrm{S}(-0.4)$. The proposed method can also be used to investigate the $\tau$ vector current multipoles in $\tau$ pair production processes at $\mathrm{e}^+\mathrm{e}^-$ and $\mathrm{e}\tau$ colliders, and a general method for determining the $\tau$ EDM form factor in $\tau$ pair production in multiple photon final states is also presented.

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a local and combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We delve into the specifics of their method and examine the underlying principles of their groundbreaking concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds. Along the way, we clarify the relationship between classical differentiable manifolds and their combinatorial counterparts. Additionally, we explore the properties of the latter in relation to Gelfand-MacPherson's method. No prior knowledge of combinatorial differentiable manifolds is assumed in this analysis. We also outline the steps to derive a key theorem directly from Gelfand-MacPherson's work. Although this outline is presented in a way that is accessible to non-experts in the field, the underlying theoretical framework is nonetheless rooted in sophisticated geometric concepts. 

This work is a precursor to an ongoing discussion with Raoul Bjorsell and Henning Sahlmann regarding the application of Gelfand-MacPherson's approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes to certain gravitational superconnections defined on differentiable manifolds. These superconnections arise within the context of supergravity theories in the presence of matter supermultiplets, as described by the self-duality sector of the N=1 supergravity theory in 5-dimensional anti-de Sitter space. The associated gravitational superconnections possess algebraic properties that facilitate the use of Gelfand-MacPherson's method. The calculation of their Pontrjagin classes may provide a physical interpretation for previously defined combinatorial differentiable manifolds. We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio 1.5 times the solar value. Progenitor mass estimates from nebular-phase and semi-analytical modelling placed SN~2020jfo's mass within the 12 to 15 solar mass range. Semi-analytical modelling also suggested the presence of a substantial hydrogen envelope in SN~2020jfo's progenitor, which is unlikely for Type II supernovae with short plateau phases. We propose that SN~2020jfo may have exploded due to core collapse, with a small increase in core temperature allowing for a minimal plateau phase. Models based on the supernova's spectrum and evolution predictions also supported this theory, with the added possibility that the star exploded at an inclination that minimized the visibility of the surviving hydrogen envelope. The unique features of SN~2020jfo highlight the diversity within the Type II supernova category and underscore the importance of optical telescopes such as ATLAS, iAIRS, and SOAR in high-resolution spectroscopy for an ideal observational framework for Type II supernovae. This framework is crucial for further understanding these supernovae through detailed spectroscopic analysis and improved progenitor mass estimates. Through the study of SN~2020jfo and its unique characteristics, we have highlighted the significance of real-time transient candidate notifications in order to secure optimal observations and ensure the optimal use of available telescopes and observational resources. The collaborative efforts behind the observation and analysis of SN~2020jfo demonstrate the value of rapid communication, real-time decision-making, and the strategic allocation of resources in active astrophysical research. The collaborative process that led to the understanding of SN~2020jfo's characteristics serves as a model for similar collaborative approaches in future active astrophysical research. To significantly enhance the detection sensitivity of wide-field X-ray monitors with a broad field of view, a novel approach is proposed that utilizes multiple lobster-eye optics through a technique called multiplexing. This innovative strategy involves dividing a wide field of view into multiple, narrower fields, each of which is covered by a separate optical element. Here, we explore the feasibility of this method by examining a proposed X-ray monitor called e-ASTROG, which is part of a future wide-field X-ray observatory. e-ASTROG is an electrically modular and wide-field X-ray monitor consisting of 1296 silicon detectors, arranged in a hexagonal pattern and supported by eight individually adjustable lobster-eye optics. Through extensive simulations, we investigated the effect of multiplexing on the detector's performance and discovered that doing so slightly decreases the detector's angular resolution but has a negligible impact on its energy resolution. Furthermore, we found that by using four to six superimposed optics for each local field of view, the detector's angular resolution can be restored to its original state while significantly increasing its field of view. This efficient use of resources allows for a substantial reduction in the number of optical elements required, which in turn leads to a considerable decrease in the detector's mass and potential misalignment errors. Consequently, we believe that multiplexing the optics through this method has the ability to significantly enhance the detection sensitivity of wide-field X-ray monitors with a broad field of view. This innovative approach may also be applicable to other X-ray telescopes and direct detection instruments. Finally, we outline the technological advancements required to implement this concept, including the development of adjustable optics and the integration of large-area silicon detectors with a high number of readout nodes. If successful, this could pave the way for a significant enhancement in the sensitivity of wide-field X-ray monitors with a broad field of view. This study is a preliminary step towards designing the e-ASTROG detector and exploring the scientific potential of this instrument. Ultimately, this proposal has the potential to significantly impact the future of wide-field X-ray astronomy. This work is also relevant to the effective use of large-area silicon detectors in other direct detection instruments. To investigate the structure of dark matter, a deep learning framework was implemented and used to explore the impact of velocity and density information on the formation of halos through $N$-body cosmological simulations. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time, in a specific range of masses. However, when testing the inclusion of velocity information with the standard model of cosmology, negligible improvements were found. By increasing the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations in the simulation, a significant improvement was observed when the model was trained on density information alone. Furthermore, incorporating velocity information led to halo mass improvements of up to 30% when the simulation's parameters were modified in this way. When the simulation's shape parameter was modified, the largest improvement found was in halos with $10^{8}$ M$_{\odot}$ by incorporating velocity information after being trained on the standard model. The findings suggest that deep learning models can capture the nonlinear relationships between the initial conditions and the halo mass formation process. The results also indicate that when the parameters of the simulation are modified, deep learning models can leverage different types of information to enhance their halo mass predictions. The implications of these findings are significant, as they suggest that deep learning models have the potential to accurately model the halo mass formation process, even when the most influential factors are altered. This could ultimately enable them to be used in a wide range of applications, such as generating simulated data that matches the characteristics of real halo distributions, or predicting how halo masses will evolve over time in response to modifications to the simulation's parameters. Converting an audio recording of music into a symbolic format is a challenging Music Information Retrieval task, specifically piano transcription. This study proposes a semi-supervised technique using low-rank matrix factorization methods, notably Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix Factorization. Utilizing a single audio recording of each individual note, we demonstrate on the MAPS dataset that our proposed semi-supervised CNMF method surpasses conventional low-rank factorization techniques, but slightly lags behind leading deep learning approaches while facing broader applicability issues. Furthermore, leveraging multiple recordings of the same note enhances the accuracy significantly, reflecting the inherent nature of musical notes as long-duration signals. Ultimately, our research indicates that low-rank factorization methods hold promise for music transcription but necessitates an understanding of musical structure to achieve substantial success. Additionally, we introduce an evaluation metric called "local accuracy" to assess these methods' performance. In conclusion, our work showcases the applicability of low-rank factorization techniques to music transcription and suggests future research directions. All code and data utilized in this study are readily available online.

We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative method disregards typical pseudo potentials and instead directly accounts for the stresses and gravitational influence on fluid elements. Our study presents a groundbreaking implementation of this approach for rigid stars composed of uniform density, specifically addressing rotating stars in general relativity. This implementation demonstrates exceptional convergence ($R^6$ order) in our test simulations and accurately reproduces existing results from rigid stars in general relativity. This achievement marks a significant step towards extending this method to evolving stars.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Furthermore, our approach works in tandem with an innovative method for annotating entire documents at a time, based on overall document quality rather than individual section labels. This document-quality assessment can be used on its own to prioritize the annotation of documents, according to their quality as inferred by the model. Our code and data are openly accessible at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/selective_labeling. Our research indicates that selective labeling is a versatile and effective solution for reducing labeling costs in document analysis, and is compatible with a range of existing annotation strategies. It is also compatible with a variety of deep learning models, including transformer-based architectures, and can be applied to a range of tasks such as text extraction and layout manipulation. Overall, our results highlight the potential of selective labeling to accelerate the development and deployment of document analysis models. Our research also lays the groundwork for further exploration of active learning strategies that are tailored to specific models and document analysis tasks. Our approach is currently being explored for potential applications in industries such as healthcare, finance, and retail, and we believe that it has the potential to make a meaningful contribution to the advancement of document analysis. The collaboration between gravitational wave and Very High Energy (VHE) astronomers is a relatively new field, with the potential to greatly expand our knowledge of the universe. We examined the compact binary merger observations from GWTC-1 by the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) and the potential VHE counterparts. From the 16 confirmed compact binary merger observations, 9 were associated with VHE flares, 4 with gamma-ray bursts (GBRs) that also emitted VHE, and the remaining 3 were dark SGR events; the others had VHE counterparts that arrived before the dark matter arrival time. We analyzed the possible VHE counterparts for each of these 3 dark matter events using an energetic approach that took into consideration the energy released during the merger and any possible delay in VHE signal arrival time. We applied this method to predict the VHE properties that could aid in identifying these dark matter events in future observations. Furthermore, we proposed a new classification system for compact binary mergers: high-energy (HE) SGR, GBR, and neutron star - black hole (NS-BH) mergers. This classification could provide valuable insights into the behavior of high-energy density states in these mergers. We also emphasized the significance of real-time VHE observations in identifying dark matter events and the potential for such events to be detected by LIGO's upgraded sensitivity in future experiments. Lastly, we highlighted the potential for VHE and LIGO to detect dark matter in the universe through the merger of primordial binary black holes in the universe. This could potentially be achieved with the upgrade to LIGO's sensitivity in future experiments. The adverse effects of social determinants of health on the quality of care and healthcare disparities have long been recognized. However, many social determinants remain unstructured and un-coded within electronic health records, often only present in the free-text notes made by healthcare professionals. As a result, there is a pressing need for an automated method to extract this valuable information from clinical notes. Our research centers on the development of an innovative multi-stage system combining techniques like named entity recognition, relation classification, and text classification to identify and extract relevant social determinants of health information from clinical notes with minimal human intervention.

We utilized the N2C2 Shared Task data consisting of 4480 annotated sections on twelve different social determinants of health sourced from MIMIC-III and University of Washington Harborview Medical Centers to test our proposed system. Given the challenge posed by entities that overlap with each other, our team designed a unique marker-based model, which we incorporated into the multi-stage system. 

In our experiments, our proposed system consistently demonstrated exceptional performance by achieving a high Micro-F1 score of 75.15% in the outer layer, an Entity F1 score of 75.19% in the middle layer, and an Entity F1 score of 85.19% in the inner layer. Our innovative approach specifically excelled at handling overlapping entities, and we found that the designed model boosted the Entity F1 score by 8.59% in the test set. Furthermore, our multi-stage system performed substantially better than baseline models built using BioBERT and ClinicalBERT by achieving an average score 6.19% higher in the Entity F1 score.

Our analysis indicated that the marker-based model could reduce the Entity F1 score drop caused by the outer layer by 4.34%, indicating a notable improvement. We also found that entities with a high score were often located near the start of clinical notes, which provided valuable insight for future resource allocation in this domain. Our research provided a foundation for extracting social determinants of health from clinical notes and can be applied to other entity extraction tasks where relationships between entities are crucial. However, we acknowledge that further research is necessary to address the challenge posed by limited and unstructured data in this field. This study is centered on a two-part swimmer known as the scallop, which transitions through varying dynamics across two different fluid environments. We resolve two optimal control scenarios, one focused on achieving the fastest time to relocate the swimmer and another on finding the most energy-efficient method using periodic control to move it between predetermined positions. Leveraging the simplicity provided by limiting switching to one point and taking advantage of the underlying equation's structure, we can divide the problem into manageable components, explicitly solve each part, and consequently derive a comprehensive solution despite the discontinuities. We also utilize numerical modeling to illustrate the efficacy of less frequent switching in minimizing costs for both scenarios. Furthermore, we apply the developed approach to a related problem to identify the optimal periodic control solution. This allows us to gain theoretical insights that could be verified through experimental means. Lastly, we highlight the potential of our findings to contribute to the understanding of scallop-like swimmer dynamics.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility data revealed significant urban declines in face-to-face encounters and their geographical reach. This paper explores the broader implications of COVID-19 on urban society by combining mobility, social contact patterns, and work productivity data. Our analysis reveals that limiting physical encounters beyond household circles resulted in substantial declines in economic productivity and innovation, particularly in major cities. These declines were more pronounced when encounters were restricted to shorter distances. Our findings suggest that the benefits of restricting social contact to smaller groups may outweigh the costs, and that diversity in distance of encounters can be an important factor to consider in urban policy-making. Furthermore, our research shows that the larger the city, the greater the decline in productivity and the more significant the effect of limiting encounters to smaller groups. Additionally, we observed a notable increase in short-distance encounters in major cities during the pandemic, along with increased productivity losses in those cities. This highlights an important phenomenon where big cities tend to have a dual distribution of encounters, with both very local and very long-distance interactions occurring frequently. In conclusion, our research shows that diversity in distance of encounters is crucial for urban productivity and that large cities exhibit distinct encounter patterns which are vital for their high productivity levels. Therefore, it is essential to consider these factors when developing policies to mitigate the economic consequences of future public health crises. Moreover, our analysis suggests that there are valuable research opportunities to be explored in the field of urban economics, particularly in relation to the dual nature of large city encounters and the potential for optimal policy-making to be data-driven. Ultimately, our study underscores the significance of an interdisciplinary approach in understanding the intricate dynamics of urban systems and combining mobility, social contact, and economic productivity data to gain meaningful insights. Implementing 5G antennas across a region is crucial for delivering 5G connectivity. Yet, little attention has been given to assessing 5G cellular tower exposure among children and occupants of sensitive locations, including schools and medical facilities. To address these concerns, a systematic approach is outlined to numerically evaluate downlink 5G exposure among children, adolescents, schools, and medical centers, also applicable to pre-5G scenarios. This methodology is then applied to two real-world case studies to analyze the effects of 5G and varying school ages on exposure and also how the 5G exposure compares to pre-5G exposure. The results show that when considering school-age groups, the maximum exposure among children and adolescents generally follows the same pattern as for the general population, with some variations. However, the base station's impact is significantly influenced by its location and the local terrain, emphasizing the importance of site-specific assessments in evaluating exposure risks. Furthermore, the proposed approach can be used to incorporate the effects of building materials on exposure through the use of building transmission coefficients derived from computational electromagnetic simulations. The outlined methodology is versatile and adaptable to various GNP scenarios, making it a valuable tool for evaluating exposure risks in the rapidly evolving wireless communication landscape. The authors also stress the need for continuous evaluation and updating of exposure assessments as new GNP technologies emerge. This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, particularly those with nonzero constant vorticity. We sought to analyze how a uniform shear flow affects weakly nonlinear, surface gravity waves through the use of Hamiltonian formulation and Hamiltonian transformation techniques. By applying these methods, we obtained a new Hamiltonian Dysthe equation describing the time-dependent evolution of the wave envelope. Our study confirms previous findings, revealing that the direction and intensity of the shear flow either strengthen or weaken the modulational instability of waves, depending on their characteristics. Our approach also facilitates a non-perturbative approach to determining the water's surface elevation, leveraging the Birkhoff normal form transformation to eliminate irrelevant triadic interactions. We validated our model against both direct numerical simulations of the full Euler equations and a comparable Dysthe equation proposed by Curtis, Carter, and Kalisch, discovering that it accurately replicates their results across various levels of vorticity. Our study showcases the effectiveness of Hamiltonian formulation and Hamiltonian transformation techniques in analyzing the dynamics of rotating and stratified fluids, also providing a framework for examining the effects of additional forces on ocean waves. Ultimately, we believe this research paves the way for improved numerical models and a deeper understanding of wave behavior in the presence of shear flows and other external influences. Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model that can be adapted for various sensing configurations, thereby contributing a sensing-independent approach to navigation. Furthermore, the ability to navigate with a single sonar sensor makes this system highly robust and versatile. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this method in navigating indoor environments with multiple sensors and also in scenarios with significant obstacles and poor visibility using a single sensor. The associated code is openly accessible on https://github.com/AmirHoseinNavid/Single-AutoNav for the benefit of researchers working in this field.

This research targets resolving secrecy concerns for nonorthogonal multiple access users by introducing an alternative decoding order method. First, we mathematically quantify the total possible decoding order options. Then, we propose an effective decoding order approach that guarantees positive secrecy rates for each user and, through computation, determine the feasible secure decoding order quantities. To minimize complexity in determining the best secure decoding order, we also present an alternative, less computationally intensive method. Notably, using this alternative method yields on average at least $e^2$ times less computational iterations than the original method. Finally, we present numerical examples to illustrate our proposed techniques.

When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a well-liked alternative to conventional PCA due to its robustness in recent years. This study focuses on an under-explored version of rotationally invariant L1-PCA and develops an iterative optimization approach using proximal alternating linearized minimization and a form of extrapolation tailored to its two-block representation. Moreover, the algorithm is theoretically proven to converge linearly to a stable point, and this result is guaranteed to correspond to a minimum of the original problem when the algorithm's step size meets certain criteria. To support and validate the methodology, both artificial and real-world data were used in numerical experiments to illustrate the algorithm's performance. The code used in this study is openly accessible online. 

Keywords: L1-PCA, RIALS, Proximal alternating linearized minimization, Robust dimensionality reduction, Rotationally invariant analysis.

Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as inter-sentence similarity. We demonstrate this approach to be a reliable means to evaluate and revise the annotations of intricate textual data sets containing complex semantic labels. Our evaluation indicates a notable increase in annotation accuracy and the quality of revisions, which can be an invaluable by-product to be used to enhance the model itself. We contend this method can provide a solution to the common issue of machine learning model-driven annotation tasks lacking clear theoretical foundations. Moreover, we propose the term of ``annotation-augmented data learning'' (A2L) to describe this new machine learning model-driven annotation paradigm. This project's primary goal is to investigate the integration of the Reduced Basis Method (RBM) with distinct Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) approaches, namely a monolithic method and a partitioned technique. We will detail the implementation of two reduction methods and then apply them to a common test case, with a focus on a monolithic approach, solving both fluid and solid problems simultaneously, and a partitioned approach, solving these problems separately with a fixed point strategy. To evaluate these methods, we'll use a variant of the Turek-Hron benchmark test case, characterized by a fluid Reynolds number of 100. Our evaluation will involve both a initial-step analysis and a longer-term assessment to identify potential differences in reduced and original solution accuracies. Additionally, we'll examine the effect of a specific solver's tolerance on the basis error and both reduced and original solution accuracies. Furthermore, we'll investigate the effect of a reduced basis of optimal order with respect to the number of degrees of freedom on its computational cost. Our findings will provide valuable insights into employing RBMs for Fluid-Structure Interaction problems.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use. The methodology and experimental results can be viewed at our repository at https://github.com/robotraus/HiTMap. The code has been successfully applied to our related research on frontier detection.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier was adapted and achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.8136 in evaluating test data, thereby ranking 3rd among 103 competitors. Meanwhile, in subtask B, our team used a combination of features along with a Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) classifier which showed strong performance with a macro F1 score of 0.5203, positioning 22nd out of 65 participants. However, our primary challenge lay in subtask C, where LDA's simplicity led to subpar scores with a macro F1 score of 0.2762, ranking 43rd among 100 competitors. Nevertheless, our approach to handling multiple task entries in the evaluation phase produced concerning findings, leading to a proposal for SemEval to utilize only the best submitted result per team in the future. This proposed change is believed to yield more reliable and clearer baselines in future offensiveness detection contests. Furthermore, we express our interest in collaborating with other researchers to further improve the effectiveness of hate speech detection methods. This interest stems from the current inadequacy of models in handling subtle forms of abusive language, as demonstrated in our submitted system's failure to recognize abusive content in examples provided by the organizers. In conclusion, our team's participation and experience in SemEval OffensEval 2019 have prompted valuable discussions on the evaluation process and the need for a greater effort to develop methods capable of identifying complex forms of online abuse. This effort is seen as crucial to effectively tackling the persistent issue of online toxicity. Additionally, we stress the value of open data and methods in hate speech research, as exemplified by our team's publicly available repository that incorporates data, models, and detailed documentation to facilitate replication and further exploration by other researchers. This collaborative approach is thought to be a key component in the swift progress expected for this challenging task. One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla. Notably, this proposed method exceeds the sensitivity of other techniques used to measure the Meissner effect, such as SQUID sensors. Additionally, it's demonstrated that by increasing the atomic beam's interaction with the superconductor from a few centimeters to several meters, the measurement's sensitivity can be significantly improved before it's compromised by atomic loss due to scattering with surface defects. As a result, this method may offer the highest sensitivity available for local magnetic field measurements expelled by superconductors through the Meissner effect. Furthermore, it's shown that this technique can be applied to a wide range of superconducting materials, including those with complex crystal structures, by accounting for the electromagnetic properties of the material in question. Ultimately, this method has the potential to measure the thickness of the Meissner layer and the superconductor's persistent current layer with atomic-scale precision. This could potentially provide a new approach for analyzing the superconducting state at the microscopic level. This proposed method has far-reaching implications, potentially enabling the detection of topological non-trivial superconductors based on their response to magnetic field expulsion. This could ultimately contribute to the identification of superconductors that could be used for robust quantum computation. We investigate the emergence of magnetocaloric effect (MCE) in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides due to their proximity with a ferromagnetic substrate, specifically a MoTe$_2$ monolayer on EuO with a heat source. Using a tight-binding model that accounts for proximity-induced exchange and Rashba fields and temperature via Fermi statistics, we simulate this system and reveal substantial magnetic caloric entropy changes in MoTe$_2$. We further quantify the MCE response through entropy change and fractional change in temperature as a function of exchange field strength. Notably, exchange field-induced phase transitions can significantly enhance the MCE response, making MoTe$_2$ an appealing material for magnetic refrigeration technologies. Moreover, our findings indicate that MoTe$_2$'s MCE properties can be adjustable through the introduction of Rashba and exchange Rashba fields, thereby offering potential for its application in advanced refrigeration systems. Moreover, our study suggests that other two-dimensional materials with suitable band structures could also exhibit substantial MCE responses when coupled with appropriate ferromagnetic substrates. Consequently, this research opens up avenues for the discovery of more two-dimensional materials exhibiting substantial MCE responses and could contribute to the development of efficient magnetic refrigeration technologies.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses. Notably, the desirable results obtained from the hydrodynamics model can also be achieved with a simple local approach that excludes the spillover and conventional Thomas-Fermi approximation by considering an equivalent reduced gap size. This finding provides a practical strategy to address electron spillover in the study of metallic nanogaps. Furthermore, we find that the hydrodynamics model's results are robust against electron spillover, albeit it does permit a small variation in optical mode velocity. This model's validity is further confirmed by its ability to accurately predict optical mode velocity in finite-length metallic channels and in nanogaps with nonuniform shape. This suggests that a quantum hydrodynamics approach may serve as a reliable and versatile tool for analyzing nanoscale metal optics beyond the limitations of local response theory.

The Calculus of Constructions, introduced in 1985 by Coquand, has been a driving force in the development of dependently typed programming and higher-order constructive logic over the past 25 years. This influential theory has influenced research in programming languages and type theory, contributing to the creation of languages such as Coq and Agda through its numerous extensions. This collection of proof scripts demonstrates the calculus's capacity for infinite computation in a dependent type theory setting and lays out a detailed argument for the calculus's strong normalization property. This achievement represents a significant milestone in the dependent type theory research landscape.  We acknowledge the influential role that "Constructing Constructive Proofs" by Herman and Guerrier had on our work, and we acknowledge the programming contributions made by Jason Hickey in implementing the dependent matching operator.  This work is now obsolete due to the advancements made by Herman and Guerrier in their subsequent research, particularly in "Dependent Types are Not Paradoxical" where they proved strong normalization with dependent matching, and due to the simplified proof provided by Coquand in "Strong Normalization of the Calculus of Constructions" using the Tarski-Gordon trick.  This collection of proof scripts is included to provide researchers with an early understanding of the dependent matching concept and to offer a more transparent explanation of the strong normalization proof than the existing literature.  This work's core idea revolves around its utilization of a novel kind of categorical logic that was first introduced in the dependent type theory setting. This collection of proof scripts is also included in the PhD thesis written by Paul Jackson. The dependent matching operator was later generalized in research such as that conducted by Herman and Guerrier and in the dependent matching constructs found in programming languages such as Agda and Epigram.  This work's most recent development is the research being conducted by Coq's and Gallina's underlying type theory team led by Casteran and Leroy. We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to an educational introduction to one-dimensional topological phases, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This will include discussions on entanglement using the correlator method and von Neumann density matrix, as well as geometric phase, polarization, and transport characteristics, all with consideration of electron-electron interactions. Hands-on numerical experiments guided by publicly available codes are used to convey the value of using topological toy models for exploring new concepts in quantum electronics. These models can offer insights that may be applicable to more complex situations. 

For instance, we discovered that interacting electrons in a periodic lattice with topological features may display unique behavior in the gapless phases at its edges or in one-dimensional Weyl semimetal phases. In contrast, interacting electrons in a gapped topological phase, such as the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, do not exhibit unique behaviors related to their topological features.

To deepen understanding, we introduced a multi-terminal transport experiment proposal for probing the geometric phase, proposing that interacting electrons in a topological phase may not display distinct behavior compared to free electrons. Furthermore, we proposed that Weyl semimetal phases may exhibit unique transport characteristics in multi-terminal measurements. 

Lastly, we explored entanglement and electron correlations in interacting Su-Schrieffer-Heeger models using different quantization methods and found that they yield comparable results, demonstrating the effectiveness of the correlator method in determining the extent of electron entanglement. Additionally, we analyzed the relationship between electron correlations and geometric phase polarization, revealing that they share a common underpinning and can be distinguished through multi-terminal transport experiments. 

In conclusion, this educational introduction demonstrated that interacting electrons in topological phases can exhibit unique behavior in gapless phases but not in gap-filled phases, offering insights that may be applicable to more complex situations. These studies also showcase the effectiveness of the correlator method in determining electron entanglement and highlight the importance of distinguishing between geometric phase, polarization, and transport characteristics. 

These findings can inspire further research, particularly on interacting Weyl semimetals and whether there are unique electron correlation features in one-dimensional topological phases with gapped states. 

All numerical experiments used in this educational introduction can be accessed through publicly available codes located at https://github.com/eduardovallejo/Topological-Phases-for-Undergraduates-and-Graduate-Students.
