We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for four graviton supermultiplets in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using a preamplitude construction, confirming the findings of Huang and Yuan. The method involves the use of a Casimir operator that determines the amplitude up to certain ambiguities. A specific set of four-dimensional 'zigzag' integrals is found to accurately capture the leading logarithmic discontinuities at any order. Furthermore, an analysis reveals a previously overlooked crossing symmetry in the preamplitude, which can be utilized to create a symmetric function exhibiting the desired logarithmic behavior in various channels. Through this approach, an explicit expression is obtained for the two-loop correction to anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators with generic spin. The formula incorporates terms related to harmonic sums, specifically alternating nested ones up to weight three. In addition, an extension of the bulk-point limit for AdS amplitudes is proposed, demonstrating that this limit accurately retrieves the entire flat-space amplitude. With this modified understanding of the bulk-point limit, the model can accurately reproduce scale-dependent logarithmic threshold terms observed in type IIB string theory in flat space. As a key outcome, the proposed approach yields an explicit expression for the two-loop anomalous dimension of the symmetric operator $\Delta_{J}$ in $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM, confirming results derived by various hypergeometric series methods. The study also uncovers an intriguing connection between AdS amplitudes and harmonic sums, highlighting the role of zigzag integrals in determining the scale-dependent logarithmic threshold terms in type IIB string theory in flat space. The proposed method for calculating anomalous dimensions is anticipated to be applicable to other twist-two operators. For an example, the proposed method is applied to calculate the two-loop anomalous dimension associated with the operator $F^4$ in $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM, leading to the derivation of a comprehensive expression for the related harmonic sums up to two loops. The accuracy of the derived two-loop correction to the anomalous dimension of generic twist-four operators with spin $J$ is verified through a direct AdS/CFT correspondence in an AdS$_5$ background. The associated harmonic sums exhibit alternating nested ones up to weight three. The study demonstrates that the AdS/CFT correspondence can effectively capture scale-dependent logarithmic threshold terms observed in type IIB string theory in flat space. The proposed method is expected to be applicable to a broader range of twist-two operators, extending beyond the specifically considered symmetric operators.

This approach leverages the separable nature of the Fourier spectrum for efficient feature extraction. By circumventing the need for convolutional operations, FourierMask achieves instance segmentation performance on par with Mask R-CNN (a state-of-the-art approach) using half the number of mask-specific convolutional operations. Additionally, our work showcases the versatility of FourierMask by applying it to other tasks like semantic segmentation and object detection. Our explicit implementation of the Fourier transformation facilitates the adaptation of the method to any task that requires explicit feature manipulation. We have released our code and models on MMEditing and scale.ai GitHub repositories.

Our investigation focused on a laser pulse with frequency variations, which results in a critical density threshold dependent on time. The model we applied goes beyond the initial assumption of linear relationships. Our analysis reveals that a laser pulse with decreasing frequency requires a lower initial peak intensity to break down, while a increasing frequency peak intensity must be higher to cause the same effect. Notably, a negatively chirped laser achieves the same goal with lower than needed peak intensity, outperforming unchirped or positively chirped counterparts. As a result, a thicker layer of the target can be exploited for particle acceleration, leading to enhanced performance. In this scenario, electrons with up to 50 MeV and ions with up to 26 MeV/u can be accelerated, and the ability to achieve higher energies is limited only by the available computational power. Nevertheless, our model also highlights the critical importance of further experiment-theory integration to validate and advance these findings. Ultimately, the potential for a significant impact on the understanding and advancement of laser-aided particle acceleration is evident.

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  Additionally, our research highlights the significance of accurately accounting for all atoms within a supercell, as well as utilizing sufficient spatial separation, to minimize unwanted interactions that can influence the results.  We also emphasize that relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions is essential to obtain reliable results.  Finally, our study underscores the value of cross-validation through multiple theoretical approaches, as the results we obtained were initially obtained using the GGA+U method but were re-calculated and verified via the PAW method.  We believe that making these results available will contribute to a deeper understanding of TiO2 and its various defects.

This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$, significantly surpassing current top-quark decay sensitivity limits. Additionally, I showcase that forward proton tags can impose constraints on certain rare top-quark interactions with a spin and a photon with a rare Compton scattering rate on the order of $10^{-5}$. Observations of the intra-cluster medium with X-rays offer a rich understanding of galaxy clusters' dynamics. Maintaining equilibrium within the ICM is thought to result from a combination of thermal and non-thermal pressures. X-ray observations can also reveal the ICM's temperature, allowing for inferences about its magnetic field strength. While observations of the ICM are extensive, modeling its dynamics is often simplified by assuming the ICM's equilibrium is known. This study aims to reconcile this understanding by accounting for the ICM's equilibrium and free magnetic field variations. Dynamic processes such as the movement of radio sources through the ICM highlight the need for a more comprehensive approach that considers the cluster's dynamics in the context of its magnetic field network. The model developed here uses observed properties of the ICM and magnetic fields to predict the cluster's radio source dynamics. The model is applied to observational data for the radio source Centaurus A, located in the galaxy cluster Cen A GRS, to analyze its interaction with the surrounding ICM. The results show that the cluster's dynamics play a significant role in its equilibrium, with its magnetic field playing a crucial part in the cluster's dynamics. The findings also indicate that the cluster's dynamics are supported by non-thermal pressure to a greater extent than previously thought, with a significant contribution from the magnetic field's dissipation of energy. The study estimates the cluster's magnetic field strength at approximately 10-20 $\mu$G, consistent with observations of the ICM's magnetic field in other galaxy clusters. However, the study also highlights the cluster's magnetic field's complex nature, with localized fields deviating significantly from this average. Therefore, the study suggests that the cluster's magnetic field's reversals are related to the cluster's dynamic processes, with the potential for further investigation into their cause and effect. The model developed here has the potential to be applied to other galaxy clusters with radio sources, providing a deeper understanding of the ICM's dynamics and the cluster's magnetic field network. Ultimately, this approach could contribute to a greater understanding of the cluster's magnetic field's role in its dynamic processes and its impact on radio source interactions. The model is available online for further use and can be modified to accommodate additional processes within the cluster. The study's approach can be employed across multiple frequency bands, offering a comprehensive approach to modeling cluster dynamics and magnetic field networks. The model's potential to be applied across multiple frequency bands could reveal a more unified understanding of the cluster's magnetic field's nature and its impact on radio source interactions.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5. Our findings are achieved through the application of a randomized approach and the probability-pumping method. Moreover, our method yields new, significantly tighter upper bounds for upper density problems within finite graphs in some instances. For example, in graphs consisting of four vertices, we prove the existence of an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling a triangle with an upper density of at least $2-\sqrt{7}$, surpassing the previous record of 4/3. We also establish a generalization to structures resembling cliques of any size. Additionally, we derive a lower bound of $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{67}}$ for upper density problems within cycles of odd sizes and demonstrate the applicability of our method to various Ramsey theory problems. To our knowledge, this is the first time a randomized approach has been utilized to investigate upper density problems within Ramsey theory. Our work is also accompanied by non-hierarchical lower bounds for specific cases, obtained through alternative methods. Lastly, we pose new questions in the realm of upper density problems within graphs, particularly focusing on structures comprising cliques and cycles within odd sizes. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between upper density problems and Diagonal Ramsey theory, an area that has thus far been largely uninvestigated. Consequently, our research significantly expands the scope of upper density problems within Ramsey theory and suggests that the application of probability-pumping methods may yield groundbreaking insights in other areas. Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that this characteristic is equivalent to the group containing a large abelian subgroup. As a result, groups with this characteristic are a broader class than those characterized by Kazdansu groups or their extensions. Additionally, this research establishes that polynomially-sized generating sets are sufficient to achieve a polynomial diameter in groups with this characteristic. This implies a group G has a polynomial diameter when its Kazdansu group has a polynomial diameter. This finding is further supported by the discovery that many families of finite groups with this characteristic have polynomial-sized diameters. This research is complemented by the identification of groups with both large abelian subgroups and polynomial diameters, such as Burnside groups, nilpotent groups, and certain families of Coxeter groups. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ. To enhance the system's reliability, the design incorporates a fault-tolerant algorithm, ensuring accurate temperature readings in the presence of a faulty analog backend. The design's innovative frequency-based temperature conversion method and modular architecture provide a versatile solution for adaptive voltage and frequency scaling systems. Long-lasting stability in the magnetic fields of Ap-stars, white dwarfs, and neutron stars has been observed but the exact stellar interior conditions responsible are still the focus of ongoing research. Studies have revealed that magnetic fields purely in the toroidal or poloidal configurations inevitably succumb to instability. In contrast, numerical simulations have consistently shown stability in the axisymmetric configurations of the magnetic fields found within non-turbulent stellar interiors. These stable configurations consist of intertwined toroidal and poloidal components resembling a twisted torus. Prior studies have established that the equilibrium conditions meeting these stable configurations must conform to the frozen flux theorem while also being topologically consistent. Furthermore, 3D simulations have validated that these stable configurations can withstand small perturbations within their volumes. Additionally, it has been found that magnetic fields adhering to these criteria resist decay, reaffirming the fundamental premise established in the 1970s by Woltjer. Moreover, both local and global stellar stability studies rely on the frozen flux theorem. In the context of the frozen flux theorem, the motion of stellar fluids is described by incompressible and turbulent MHD equations. A stable equilibrium state where magnetic energy significantly surpasses both thermal and turbulent energies can be classified as turbulent. This study extends the realm of stable equilibrium states to include magnetic energies comparable to turbulent energies, thus broadening the framework's applicability. To achieve this, the equilibrium state is represented by a twisted torus with uniform internal magnetic field patterns in both the toroidal and poloidal directions, facilitating its comparison with the stable configurations observed within stellar interiors. The implications of this research are further underscored by the formation of the Sun's magnetic field patterns revealed through solar magnetogram images. The discovery that the Sun's poloidal and toroidal magnetic field components are comparable in strength challenges the traditional assumption held since the 1970s that the Sun's poloidal component is an order of magnitude more substantial. The findings of this study suggest that solar magnetograms may have a more intricate structure and that both components should be reevaluated in the context of the frozen flux theorem. This involves setting up flow equations for the model's parameters and establishing an equation for the renormalized two-point functions. This process is complicated by the presence of non-abelian symmetries, which require separating the spectrum according to irreducible representations. Setting up the renormalized two-point functions in this way allows us to investigate the model's evolution from a fundamental level, which is particularly important when dealing with the challenging issue of symmetry breaking. This research builds upon previous studies, expanding the range of possible symmetry breaking scenarios by considering an additional set of non-abelian symmetries and generalizing the renormalized two-point functions in this context. As a result, more comprehensive insights are gained into the mechanisms governing the renormalization group flow in this class of Higgs models. Furthermore, this work provides a framework for tackling more intricate problems, such as the renormalization group flow in systems comprising multiple Higgs fields competing for symmetry breaking, which is anticipated to have significant implications for the study of fundamental physics. This research anticipates its will contribute to the development of the 'physics from all scales' approach, which aspires to incorporate the fundamental principles underlying the renormalization group flow in a unified and self-consistent manner. Our innovative proposal is for a music-centric search engine called Pied Piper, which will serve as a comprehensive meta-search tool, enabling users to find relevant music information by searching for lyrics, song metadata, audio, video, or a blend of any of these options. Unlike existing music search solutions that are often tied to specific services, Pied Piper will act as a unified interface for music search across multiple platforms. In this paper, we outline our approach to developing a relevant music retrieval system, which leverages machine learning to rank search outcomes and deliver accurate results when users reissue the same query. We also highlight the benefits of a music-centric search engine like Pied Piper, which includes the ability to recommend new music to users. To achieve this, we propose integrating a collaborative filtering-based playlist recommendation feature that will enable the engine to suggest music based on the user's search history and preferences. Our primary objective in developing Pied Piper is two-fold: to create a user-friendly music search engine that can effectively recommend new music and facilitate music discovery. To demonstrate the feasibility of our proposal, we conducted a user-centered assessment to gather feedback from music enthusiasts and validate our design, which we plan to evolve through iterative testing to ensure it aligns with users' evolving needs. Ultimately, our vision for Pied Piper is to establish a benchmark for music search engines and contribute to the advancement of music information retrieval technology. To this end, we are releasing the code for our prototype, which is currently hosted on GitHub to facilitate further development and improvement. In the future, we intend to enhance Pied Piper by integrating more music data sources, upgrading the recommendation system, and exploring new features to enhance its search and recommendation capabilities. To this end, we invite music technology experts to collaborate with us and contribute to the ongoing enhancement of this comprehensive music search engine. Additionally, we are open to collaborating with music industry stakeholders to leverage Pied Piper as a platform for promoting artist work, detecting music trends, and preventing music piracy. This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric constructs over Lie groupoids and differential stacks. Building on the foundations laid out in [arXiv:2103.04560, arXiv:2012.08447, arXiv:2012.08442, arXiv:1907.00375], the study establishes connections between key concepts within the field. Notably, a significant correlation between gerbes over stacks has been established in [arXiv:1907.00375], the development of the Chern-Weil map for principal bundles over Lie groupoids equipped with a connection has been introduced in [arXiv:2012.08447], the relationship between connections on principal bundles over Deligne Mumford stacks has been examined through the Atiyah sequence in [arXiv:2012.08442], and topological groupoid extensions were defined along with their correspondence to gerbes over topological stacks in [arXiv:2103.04560]. The research also discusses the process of obtaining gerbes over topological stacks as pull-backs of topological groupoid extensions in the context of reduced, compact, and orientable topological groupoids. Additionally, the study leverages this relationship to translate invariants of gerbes over stacks into invariants of topological groupoid extensions, offering a new framework to study gerbes over stacks through the physics of topological field theories. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  In addition, we discovered that infrared dark clouds, which are born in massive star-forming regions, do not follow the core mass function observed in small molecular clouds.  Instead, they follow a power law with an index of 2.0, in contrast to the cumulative core mass function found in small molecular clouds, which follows a power law with an index of 2.1.  Therefore, we propose that infrared dark clouds, which are formed in large star-forming regions and give rise to the most massive stars, should be treated as inherently distinct from smaller, more localized core formations.  Therefore, I suggest that the name 'irregular dark cloud core' would be a more descriptive and accurate term for these notable objects.  In conclusion, our analysis of the Dragon infrared dark cloud, combined with previous findings from the Spider and the G11V1 infrared dark clouds, indicates that a significant proportion of massive protostellar cores, specifically those with masses greater than 100 solar masses, are already evident before the onset of outflows, indicating that massive star formation can and does occur through the rapid growth of lower-mass cores.  Therefore, I recommend that future observations of infrared dark clouds be configured to detect these massive protostellar cores in real-time, allowing for a better understanding of the massive star formation process.  In addition, I propose that future statistical analyses of infrared dark clouds be conducted with a core radius of 0.1 parsecs to provide a more accurate representation of these objects' core mass functions.  In doing so, we may uncover additional key features of the core mass function within infrared dark clouds, potentially revealing further important insights into the underlying physics governing massive star formation. LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, allowing for updates to digital elevation models and applications such as glacial monitoring, detecting structural changes, forest assessment, tracking shoreline and beach alterations, landslide risk analysis, habitat mapping, and urban planning. One crucial step in these processes is the classification of 3D point clouds into basic categories. For example, the classification can distinguish between plant life, man-made features, and bodies of water. Our research aims to present an initial evaluation of various classification techniques for 3D LiDAR data, including diverse feature engineering methods. Specifically, we show that supplying contextual information about neighboring points to each LiDAR data point enhances the performance of subsequent machine learning algorithms. We also examine multiple dimension reduction techniques, spanning PCA to neural network-based encoders, to illustrate their influence on classification outcomes. Our results reveal that combining feature engineering with a method like PCA leads to better classification accuracy when compared to straightforward classification of raw data. Furthermore, our research indicates that feeding 3D coordinates directly into neural networks can yield superior performance when compared to methods requiring dimension reduction. We made our experiments publicly accessible to facilitate replication and comparison with other evaluation approaches. By contributing our findings to the discussion on LiDAR classification, we hope to stimulate further research and improvement in this vital step in LiDAR data processing. The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for many years. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos as they offer a direct and magnetically unbiased glimpse into hadronic interactions of cosmic rays. This paper introduces three new strategies to link neutrino and UHECR arrival directions. With upgraded data sets from IceCube Neutrino Observatory and ANTARES for neutrinos, as well as from Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array for UHECRs, statistical significance and accuracy are significantly enhanced compared to the results from 2015. The analyses comprise looking for UHECR-UHECR excess around neutrino sources, searching for the largest UHECR excess across all neutrino paths, and finding the shortest distance between UHECR arrival directions and high-energy neutrino trajectories. The studies reveal neutrino-UHECR excess at $4.9\sigma$ confidence with an UHECR density 1.4 times the total density, further supporting the cosmic ray-neutrino connection and hinting at the UHECR neutrino source distribution having a real anisotropic component. The findings also support the Spure-Diffuse scenario proposed in 2015. The anisotropy in the UHECR distribution along high-energy neutrino paths, as observed in previous studies, is confirmed and its anisotropy density now becomes apparent at the $3.1\sigma$ confidence level with an anisotropy density 0.84 times the total anisotropy density. The studies provide fresh insights that can be utilized in developing theoretical models that can be tested with the upgraded data sets from IceCube, ANTARES, Pierre Auger Observatory, and the Telescope Array. Furthermore, the findings pave the way for a deeper analysis that can incorporate further data sets and UHECR masses higher than 102 kilograms. The research also highlights the significance of maintaining low lateral and scattering UHECR contamination rates in future UHECR experiments. The strategies introduced in this paper can be modified to investigate other cosmic ray components such as galactic UHECRs, UHECRs in magnetic fields, and the UHECR distribution within galaxy clusters. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, our study reveals that the interaction between a solid surface and a liquid film made of non-Newtonian fluids occurs in three different ways, depending on the surface's roughness: when it's smooth, there's a stickier area in the middle; if it's moderately rough, there's a less sticky area in the middle; and if it's very rough, stress is evenly distributed and doesn't change much with changes to the surface's shape. This balance of forces along the interface determines how the liquid flows and whether it forms long connections or short paths. By controlling the surface's roughness, it's possible to manage these interactions and guide the liquid's flow. This understanding and control could make a difference in various industrial processes that involve dealing with non-Newtonian fluids. This research focuses on liquid polymers but may also have implications for other complex liquids. Furthermore, we investigated the challenge of predicting lesion types from text-based features extracted using recurrent neural networks. Our approach demonstrated robust performance on outlier detection and demonstrated potential for predicting lesion types from image descriptions. Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible processes. We present an innovative solution to overcome this limitation, using a system that undergoes free expansion without an external influence, and demonstrate that the proposed method aligns with thermodynamic principles. Our solution identifies the dissipated energy as a thermodynamic average of work performed by each individual microstate and confirms its nonnegative value during free expansion, which holds surprising implications. We demonstrate that the proposed method aligns with established theories for thermodynamic equilibrium and nonequilibrium processes with changing phase space volumes. Furthermore, we illustrate the utility of this approach by analyzing the dynamics of systems experiencing expansion or contraction in both thermodynamic equilibrium and nonequilibrium conditions. Lastly, our solution reveals the relationship between work, heat, and macroscopic currents, offering a comprehensive understanding of the underlying thermodynamics. We validate our solution by applying it to three distinct scenarios: (1) the expansion of an isolated system in nonequilibrium, (2) the contraction of a system in thermodynamic equilibrium, with the pressure and temperature being different, and (3) the contraction of a system in thermodynamic equilibrium, with the pressure and temperature being the same. We believe that this success will enable the development of microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics into a powerful tool for analyzing and predicting the dynamics of complex systems. This achievement is complemented by a publically accessible numerical implementation that can be utilized for various applications. This code allows users to calculate the time-evolution of temperature, entropy, and potential energy and further enables the numerical determination of microwork, heat, and dissipated energy for distinct expansion or contraction scenarios. This code is also compatible with Monte Carlo simulations, enabling the exploration of the proposed theory's implications in systems comprising interacting particles. This research marks a significant step in the development of microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, making it feasible to directly link the irreversible thermodynamic changes observed in complex systems to the underlying irreversible changes in their individual microstates. Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities indicating they are approximately ten times less abundant than cyclopentadiene. A possible detection of ethynyl benzene (C6H5CCH) at a column density roughly ten times greater than the cyclopentadiene derivative is also reported. The inferred abundances of these molecules are directly linked to their parent interstellar molecules and follow a linear correlation with cyclopentadiene and benzene, respectively. The observed frequencies for the cyclopentadiene isomers fall within a range consistent with the rotational constants of the ethynyl benzene molecule. A theoretical analysis of ethynyl benzene's hyperfine structure resulting from the spin of individual nuclei also confirms the earlier reported values of its rotational constants. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. Notwithstanding its own development, the field of translational medicine requires improvement. A more effective approach would break it down into manageable segments, learning from established models like the software industry's V-model. This approach, which extracts knowledge from experience-based development, emphasizes the importance of joint planning across stages. It also highlights the need for a continuous, adaptive cycle of learning and refinement. We propose refining this cycle to accelerate knowledge exchange, focusing on the identification of common goals and mutual understanding across disciplines. This, in turn, can be achieved through collaborative planning and knowledge management. Ultimately, this approach has the potential to enhance the self-improving nature of translational medicine. We illustrate this by analyzing the development of type 2 diabetes treatment from research to application. This approach can be applied to any medical condition and may serve as a framework for other complex development processes. We suggest that this approach be tested in real-world settings through methods like action research. We also believe that a data-driven refinement of this approach could further amplify its benefits. Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for estimating unknown functions while incorporating prior knowledge about their behavior.  While multiple Gaussian process models are accessible in the context of Euclidean space, their selection is significantly limited when working within the context of undirected graphs. This research adapts the stochastic partial differential equation formulation for Mat\'ern Gaussian processes - commonly employed in the Euclidean space - to analyze and extend its applications to undirected graphs of any connectivity. We also establish the equivalence between its applications and the widely-used spectral matrix Gaussian processes, and then demonstrate the adaptability of this model to handle real-valued functions by leveraging the Hilbert space framework. This allows us to utilize established operational tools such as point-wise prediction, marginal distributions, and posterior evaluation. Moreover, our method enables the efficient computation of quantities of interest through the efficient manipulation of the underlying spectral representation. This is further illustrated by means of a linear operator Gaussian process in a bounded domain. This work provides a comprehensive foundation for incorporating prior spatial dependencies into Gaussian processes across various domains, including, as an example, the analysis of medical imaging scans. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. To find the theoretical framework, we employ the Earth as a laboratory to look for signs of these phenomena through J/ψ and D^0 meson studies. Specifically, we analyze current experimental data from the BESIII collaboration to determine the upper limit for J/ψ invisible decay and the direct production of J/ψ and D^0 mesons. Our study demonstrates that stricter J/ψ invisible decay limits yield more stringent constraints on light sterile neutrinos, while more precise D^0 meson production data constrain certain dark matter scenarios. Furthermore, we establish the upper limit for the J/ψ invisible decay mode to be less than 4.04%, and set the constraint 5.56 × 10^-10 < σ·L(total) < 1.04 × 10^-9 for the J/ψ total cross-section, both at 95% confidence. We also establish the upper limit for the D^0 meson production cross-section in the 1.4 GeV < E_CM < 3.8 GeV range to be 2.6 × 10^-6 μb (10^-5 μb) for the J/ψ (D^0) signal enhancement scenario. These constraints lead to the upper limit on the J/ψ total hadronic decay width to be less than 0.558 KeV, thereby improving the current world record, and yield the model parameter constraint 1.13 × 10^-3 < |g_N|^2 / (4 π)^2 < 8.44 × 10^-4 (9.56 × 10^-5) for the invisible decay (visible decay) mode of the J/ψ particle. This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, making critical decisions in the process. Yet, surprisingly, little research has focused on comprehending the complex workings of these algorithms, particularly those that operate behind closed doors. Previous studies revealed the ease with which these scoring models can be manipulated. This paper aims to investigate the underlying causes of this unexpected sensitivity and instability. We examine the interplay between model sensitivity and stability using the example of a sophisticated deep learning-based automated essay scoring system developed by Pearson. The results showed that a surprisingly minor modification - in this case, altering the name of a prominent historical figure - was enough to significantly impact the model's score, both in terms of its ability to accurately assess the content and its propensity to produce erratic results. Furthermore, we found that incorporating more data with noise improved the model's robustness, but intriguingly, the relationship between model stability and accuracy appears non-monotonic. Additionally, we discovered that the model's sensitivity and stability were influenced by the presence of redundant features, such as word order, which can be removed to some extent using the data compression technique known as autoencoders. The findings of this study highlight the limitations of contemporary deep learning models when applied to complex tasks like automated essay scoring and suggest potential avenues for improving the reliability of such models. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods to automatically isolate nuclei from these complications. In this study, we present a novel technique called Automatic Nucleus Cleaning, which utilizes a generative adversarial network to split merged nuclei into individual cells. Our approach utilizes a custom-designed discriminator that focuses on distinguishing real cell masks from generated mask candidates, which has shown significant improvement over conventional methods such as link-based splitting algorithms. Moreover, this technique has a key benefit of being neutral to the underlying nucleus segmentation model, allowing it to be integrated with diverse segmentation algorithms. Experimental results on publicly available datasets demonstrate that this technique can accurately split complex nuclei with high precision and recall rates of 83% and 73%, respectively. Furthermore, this method demonstrated a notable advantage over alternative techniques such as LinkNet, U-Net, Link-Net with atrous block, and U-Net with atrous block in our experiments. In addition to its application in cancer diagnosis, this technique may also be useful for other cell analysis tasks. The code is available at: https://github.com/ChenChen312/Nucleus-Cleaning. Xiong and Liu previously provided a definition for graphs G that have hamiltonian n-th iterated line graphs, L^n(G), where n is 2 or greater. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate how GCNNs, particularly those employing convolutional layers with fixed filters, can be viewed as normal neural networks that apply learned input transformations to fit a particular invariant pattern. By doing so, we uncover the connection between GCNNs and traditional neural networks utilizing transfer functions that apply specific transformations to achieve rotational and relational invariant representations. We further explore the implications of this finding on learning representations in GCNNs. Our analysis suggests that high-level neural network invariants may be considered as specific rotational and relational invariants, potentially enabling more efficient learning algorithms that take advantage of system symmetries. We demonstrate the concept with a simplified example involving a symmetric data set. Our research provides a clearer understanding of GCNNs as a type of neural network that leverages invariance to capture complex data patterns and facilitates the exploration of novel, efficient learning methods. We also propose a method for identifying symmetry groups in data sets, which can be used to devise customized learning algorithms. Our approach is supported by theoretical analysis and a practical example involving a symmetric data set. We believe that our analysis and suggested methods for symmetry detection and learning algorithm design can contribute to the development of more effective learning algorithms. In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our algorithm's clustering output is close to optimal, with a distance of at most $O(\sqrt{d}\sigma)$, where $\sigma$ represents the optimal clustering's radius. The novelty of our approach builds upon an novel low-rank approximation technique that leverages a storage-efficient variant of the Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform. The underlying idea for this method, derived from affine subspace embeddings, enables us to maintain an accurate representation of the data's intrinsic dimension in the presence of noise. By combining these methods, we solve the $k$-means problem with optimal storage efficiency in the dynamic streaming model. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games centered on individual grid cells, and a comprehensive 'grand game' that encompasses the overall state structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We utilize multi-agent reinforcement learning to train agents for the grass game and the grand game, while employing linear programming to analyze and refine expected payoffs within the macro-state framework. Our method demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements for substantial grid worlds beyond current PEG solving capabilities. Moreover, our method allows us to seamlessly integrate random grid dynamics into playable environments. Experimental results show that our hierarchical approach yields comparable or superior performance when compared to flat Nash equilibrium policies across a range of grid sizes. Additionally, we find that our method effectively captures intricate state structures and anticipates unexpected grid dynamics. Lastly, we explore the integration of dynamic grid updates into the learning process. To facilitate replication, all code and data are openly accessible online. Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_i$ for $i$ ranging from 1 to n-1, and the likelihood of $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ is $x_n$. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We demonstrate that any nontransitive cyclic triple may be represented as $\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}, \frac{1}{\phi}, \frac{\phi}{1}\right)$ where $\phi$ is the golden ratio. We further show that the probability distribution associated with a random selection from such a nontransitive cyclic triple is strictly bi-modal. 

We also establish a key property for cyclic n-tuples of length greater than 3: if there exists a solution that satisfies the original condition, there will also exist a solution in which no two consecutive elements are equal. 

In addition, we explore the relationship between the likelihood of specific orders arising in a random selection of elements from a cyclic n-tuple, and the corresponding probabilities in an analogous scenario involving uniform distributions over intervals. 

Our analysis is conducted with a focus on nontransitive cyclic triples, and substantial generalization to higher-order instances is anticipated. 

A central aspect of our investigation is the identification of distinct 'phases' that arise based on the size of the interval [0,1] relative to the specific characteristics of the cyclic n-tuple at hand. 

For cyclic triples, we are able to thoroughly examine all possible scenarios, whereas for cyclic n-tuples with n greater than 3, our analysis is confined to establishing the existence of the aforementioned property. 

In the context of cyclic triples, our findings are corroborated by numerical simulation. 

Our study is an initial step in exploring the counterintuitive properties arising from the conditions defining cyclic n-tuples. 

It is our contention that the unique phenomena observed in instances of cyclic triples provide a compelling framework for further mathematical investigation

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory demands. In response to these issues, we have introduced a new cycleGAN framework based on a single, adaptable generator. By incorporating a noise pattern and a transformation function derived from the latent code and input noise, our model successfully replicates the original input image. With a modified adversarial objective function that includes a total variation regularization constraint, the network is trained in an unsupervised manner using two reconstruction cycles. Our results show that the proposed method not only outperforms the original cycleGAN but also other state-of-the-art unsupervised methods in terms of both PSNR and SSIM scores, achieved on the public LIDC database for low-dose CT images. Moreover, our model demonstrates comparable performance to supervised methods while avoiding the need for labeled training data. Additionally, the technique successfully mitigates noise and enhances the contrast of images, without over-smoothing structures, as evident from the accompanying video. The proposed method's simplicity and effectiveness make it a suitable starting point for future research aimed at improving unsupervised CT image denoising. Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this limitation, this study introduces a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. The model's structure allows related dialog nodes to share latent representations while preserving uniqueness for unrelated dialogs. To pre-train the model, a novel multi-level contrastive learning approach is proposed where similar dialog topics are brought closer while unrelated dialogs are kept apart. This method leverages both batch and group information to enhance the model's performance. Evaluations on various dialog understanding tasks demonstrate that the proposed model excels over strong baselines, also showcasing consistent improvements in model extensibility and supporting the method's effectiveness. The model's structure also facilitates interpretability, highlighting dialog topic representation's significant influence. This study's innovations offer design guidelines for future pre-training methods dealing with similar multi-instance classification problems. The code has been made openly accessible.

To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halos, we utilized the angular momentum projection method on wave functions derived from the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory. Our self-consistent approach effectively accounts for interactions between ground and rotational states and does not rely on adiabatic assumptions. By applying this method to isotopes of $^{42}$Mg and $^{44}$Mg, we observed that deformed halo states possess specific patterns of orbital occupation and characterized distribution shapes. These findings demonstrate rotational vibration modes within these exotic nuclei and pinpoint potential anomalies in charge distribution when spun at medium to high speeds. Furthermore, our research highlights the importance of using relativistic mean-field forces that include non-point-like contact interactions to accurately capture the properties of distorted halo nuclei.  For $^{42}$Mg, our calculations confirm experimental observations of low-energy monopole oscilli and predict analogous phenomena in $^{44}$Mg. Additionally, we identify possible shifts in binding energy caused by medium to high angular momenta due to centrifugal forces and these shifts are observable in both calculated and experimental data. These studies provide a thorough understanding of the interplay between rotational and ground states and centrifugal potential effects on binding energies in distorted halo nuclei. Lastly, our research suggests that the unique characteristics of these exotic systems make them suitable for testing relativistic nuclear physics theories that have been successfully applied to study more conventional nuclear phenomena.

representation-driven. We argue that using latent state variables can help
capture the task structure and facilitate transfer learning. To test this,
we introduce a new algorithm called Latent Multi-Task Policy Iteration (LMTPI)
that learns a shared representation and associated latent state variables
incrementally, allowing for efficient transfer learning. To evaluate LMTPI, we
create a multi-task gridworld environment with variable obstacle configurations
which requires adapting to new state spaces while retaining previous learning
capabilities. Results demonstrate that LMTPI achieves significant performance
gains through rapid adaptation in novel states and can successfully apply
previous knowledge to overcome obstacles. To validate the efficacy of the
learned latent state representation, we employ both dimensionality reduction
techniques and a semantic similarity test. The code for the algorithm and the
evaluation environment is openly accessible on GitHub. Overall, our study
demonstrates that learning a shared representation and associated latent state
variables in multi-task reinforcement learning settings can facilitate efficient
transfer learning and adaptability in complex and dynamic environments. The
algorithm and methodology devised in this research can be applied to a
broader range of applications requiring efficient transfer learning. The code for

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. Building upon these theorems, we formally establish the Fundamental Theorem of Formal Systems claiming that any formal system rich enough to capture basic mathematical reasoning and proof principles necessarily operates within an inherently incomplete framework. This conclusion can be viewed as the foundational rationale underlying the development of the Limits of Formal Methods movement within the philosophy of mathematics. Moreover, our formal framework allows for a more precise definition of what it means for a formal system to be computationally powerful and capable of embodying fundamental mathematical reasoning. This, in turn, prompts a renewed examination of the relationship between mathematical truth and the computational processes underlying formal systems. Ultimately, our work provides a clear, self-contained framework for understanding the core implications of the Limit of Formal Methods within the philosophy of mathematics. This will be demonstrated through a revised analysis of Paul Benacerraf's classic argument regarding the limitations of deductive reasoning. Lastly, our work is positioned within the broader context of contemporary debates surrounding the nature of mathematical truth and the foundations of computational processes.

In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting the camera's positioning directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent PnP calculations, and a third method using estimated depth and segmentation maps to calculate the camera's position through iterative closest point alignment. When evaluating the methods against each other and established traditional approaches, we found an unexpected result in which direct prediction outperformed other strategies. Further analysis into these findings involved assessing the methods' performance under various noise levels. Our study demonstrated that employing an eye-in-hand camera and artificial intelligence to predict the camera's position from an image is a viable approach, surpassing other methods that we tested while also exhibiting robustness to image noise. Additionally, direct prediction proved to be the most effective approach, yielding superior results even when compared to methods that have been theoretically optimized for better performance. Consequently, we suggest considering artificial intelligence-based direct prediction as a reliable alternative to other methods for this specific problem. Furthermore, our findings also indicate that the methods' robustness to noise could be further improved by employing real, rather than solely simulated, training data. Nonetheless, our research was conducted exclusively with simulated data due to processing efficiency and consistency. Ultimately, this research provides a foundation for exploring other computer vision tasks in robotics from a deep learning perspective.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. Additionally, our technique improved processing efficiency by using a GAN discriminator that also serves as an operator for the 1-layer proximal operator, which facilitated solving an inverse problem inverse problem while maintaining the diversity of samples. We demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach on various inverse problems and compared it to current methods on public datasets. The code is available online for public access.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore invariant curves in polynomial maps, polynomial flows, and rational maps through a combination of theoretical and computational approaches. Following this, we provide a detailed analysis of the relationship between invariant curves and the topology of phase spaces in polynomial maps and rational maps. Additionally, we discuss the connection between invariant curves and Lyapunov exponents in polynomial maps and rational maps. Furthermore, we discuss the concepts of hyperbolicity and chaotic dynamics in the context of polynomial maps and rational maps. We also present a discussion on the limitations and potential extensions of the presented ideas. Lastly, we highlight the significance of this work in relation to ongoing research.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. A statistical analysis of these patterns using flux and shape metrics shows that they follow simple Gaussian distributions in real and frequency domains respectively. This is unexpected because similar analyses of other pulsars' scintillation patterns have not been as comprehensive. Furthermore, determining the physical dimensions and velocities of the screens requires assumptions about the screen's shape and velocity distribution. Under the assumption that screens are spherical, velocities are found to be consistent with the expectations of the interstellar medium's velocity distribution. However, screens appear larger than predicted by the interstellar medium's scale, potentially indicating that additional factors are influencing the scintillation patterns. Additionally, the analysis identifies potential variations in screen velocities and sizes along different lines of sight to the pulsar. The findings of this analysis provide a more nuanced understanding of the screens responsible for scintillation in this particular line of sight. The methods employed here could also be applied to studies of screens around other pulsars. Ultimately, this research highlights the benefits of using time-series data to study these complex astrophysical phenomena. This paper introduces a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the reliance on convolutional structures in WaveNet. Our proposal leverages pitch-dependent dilated convolutional neural networks to maintain model efficiency while significantly expanding its production capacity. We demonstrate that both spectral and temporal objectives can be achieved with an area-efficient architecture. Furthermore, our method showcases superior performance in both subjective and objective evaluations when compared to the baseline WaveNet model. The proposed QPNet architecture also facilitates the development of cross-domain audio waveform generation models. To further facilitate progress in this area, we have released our code and model weights on GitHub.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, but most such studies have been confined to spherical geometry. This paper introduces a novel hyperbolic graph convolutional network (HGCN) that leverages the unique properties of hyperbolic geometry to represent complex graph structures. By employing the Lorentzian distance as a loss function, HGCN is capable of learning precise representations of node similarities that extend beyond local neighborhoods. Experimental evaluations on numerous datasets have demonstrated substantial improvements over state-of-the-art Euclidean and spherical GCNs in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, the proposed method's ability to learn hierarchical representations is explicitly illustrated through a case study. This paper's code is openly accessible at https://github.com/zhunghong/hgcnp.

Additionally, it may also enable the amplification of squeezed phonons, enabling the transfer of squeezed states into stable environments. This advancement could significantly contribute to various sensing and communication applications.

The proposed system can be applied to a wide range of optomechanical systems, including optico-optical, optico-mechanical, and optico-electromechanical systems. Finally, this method paves the way for the development of novel optomechanical sensing and communication technologies, such as sensitive optical and electromechanical measurements, phonon amplification, and squeezed state-based optical communication.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context. Furthermore, our model's data fitting process is more efficient
than the popular Hyperbolic model, according to a simulation study, and we
include a Python implementation of our model for easy replication of its
results. Additionally, we include a numerical example illustrating how our
impulsivity measurements can be utilized in reward optimization problems. We
conclude by discussing potential applications and areas for extending our model
in future research. Our model and associated code are available at

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  This specific harmonic gauge is obtained by perturbing a non-dynamical "stiff" Einstein gravity, resulting in the harmonic gauge being equivalent to the transverse traceless gauge for quadratic action terms.  Nonetheless, unlike the case of linearized gravity, where the harmonic and transverse traceless gauges are equivalent at quadratic order, this specific harmonic gauge is not the same as the conventional Bardeen-Zucker gauge derived from linearized Einstein gravity, despite both arising as solutions to the same first-order differential equation.  Instead, the distinction lies in their dynamical harmonic gauge being defined by the equations $g^{\mu\nu}\tilde{\Delta}_\mu = 0$ and $\tilde{\Delta}_\mu = K_{\mu} - \frac{1}{d-2(D-1)}K^\mu$, where $K_\mu$ represents the conformally flat part of the connection associated with the symmetric tensor field, leading to the harmonic gauge being associated with the mass propagator.  Consequently, this model exhibits a normalizable massive mode in flat spacetime, thereby supporting Lin's conjecture.  Notably, this conjecture also implies that the de Sitter-like solution of the standard Fierz-Pauli theory corresponds to an unstable overton.  Furthermore, this specific harmonic gauge can be employed to analyze the linearized massive gravity model with an arbitrary potential for the scalar field. The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature. In addition, we propose a novel, intuitive explanation focusing on the distribution of energy within a two-level system to enhance students' comprehension. This novel explanation is designed to provide undergraduates with a cohesive, two-level model that can help them visualize and grasp the concept of negative absolute temperature. Furthermore, we suggest that this approach may facilitate similar comprehension in more complex, multi-level systems. Ultimately, we believe that this method has the potential to promote a more in-depth understanding of the statistical mechanics and thermodynamics behind negative absolute temperature within such systems. 

For simplicity, consider a system composed of three level states: two that are equally spaced and separated from a third, higher energy level. If a system is placed in contact with a heat bath at negative absolute temperature, it will release energy, occupying the two lower levels. If we then monitor the distribution of energy within this system over time, we will observe the gradual transfer of energy back into the higher level due to its higher average energy compared to the other two. This phenomenon directly illustrates negative absolute temperature through the increasing occupation of the highest energy level. Although this concept of negative absolute temperature may seem abstract, its implementation is made accessible by utilizing a two-level model, which can be applied to a broader range of multi-level systems. 

As an illustrative application, we apply this approach to a system of atomic resonators, demonstrating the occupation of the highest energy level due to its higher average energy when in contact with a system at negative absolute temperature. This finding is confirmed through both mathematical and graphical means, as shown in the accompanying figures. 

In conclusion, we believe that this two-level model provides an accessible understanding of negative absolute temperature for students, which can be extended to a broader range of multi-level systems. Additionally, we propose that this approach may facilitate a more in-depth comprehension of the statistical mechanics and thermodynamics behind negative absolute temperature within such systems.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization. It can be utilized in isolation or in conjunction with other publicly available datasets to train and validate models, as evidenced by our UniToPatho baseline network's ability to achieve promising results on the task. A novel numerical approach has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues, primarily centered around analyzing the impact of smoothly varying material inhomogeneities on plane waves. This method's efficiency is optimal for high-frequency scenarios and is adaptable across any given frequency $\omega$. The approach operates within a time-domain framework, consisting of three main components: generating a suitable incoming plane wave with compact propagation direction, solving the time-domain scattering problem, and ultimately deriving the time-harmonic solution via Fourier transformation. Crucial to this approach is a dynamic front-tracking mesh adaptation technique which minimizes the required computational degrees of freedom, thereby enhancing overall performance by reducing the size of support for the incoming wave and its reflections within the desired time of $O(1)$ hours. This strategy is complemented by an enhanced version of the Enquist-Majda preconditioner tailored to the time-domain problem, offering further improvements in convergence rates. Successful applications and results are showcased using the PDE system defined within a time-dependent front-tracking code, demonstrating the method's efficacy and performance, particularly with large-scale front scenarios. Furthermore, this method can also be applied to tackle other wave propagation problems, such as identifying unknown obstacles, by reformulating these problems as equivalent acoustic scattering problems. This approach has the advantage of utilizing existing front-tracking technology while also enabling the development of innovative numerical solutions. As an example, a variant of this method is used to solve an inverse problem involving the identification of a small, sharp obstacle within a medium with significant scattering properties, achieved by adapting the front-tracking mesh to better align with the identified shape. This novel solution was conceived as part of a broader research effort to explore innovative numerical solutions for complex PDE systems, driven by the advancement of modern computational technology. As an additional outcome, this work has led to an interest in studying the performance of these solutions within the context of optimal control problems.
