We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water content in pyroxene minerals from recent chondrite falls in Benenitra (2018) and Chelyabinsk (2013), as well as three older chondrite finds in Antarctica. In contrast to the water-rich Antarctic samples with terrestrial contamination, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals showed lower levels of water (around 0.018-0.087 weight percent H2O) and D-poor isotopic signatures, ranging from -444 to -44. These more D-poor hydrogen isotopic values are consistent with the D-poor values found in chondrites and suggest that the water in the pyroxene minerals originated from the alteration of chondritic materials. Water content and hydrogen isotopic values in the Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals exhibited a positive correlation, supporting the idea of water formation from the reduction of oxygen by organic carbon and the release of hydrogen gas, as previously observed in the Antarctic chondrites. This supports a chondritic source for the water delivered to the Earth in the form of volatile-poor aqueously altered materials during the planetary accretion stage. Furthermore, this indicates that the Earth's water origin is a result of the accretion of chondritic materials and does not support a need for the addition of volatile-rich materials from a different planetary body during the giant impact hypothesis. This study provides new insights into the delivery of water to the Earth based on the analysis of fresh and intact chondrite falls that have not been affected by terrestrial contamination. This is made possible by the recovery of the Benenitra and Chelyabinsk meteorites in their intact form shortly after their entry into the Earth's atmosphere. This is significant because it sets the stage for further analysis of the Earth's pre-accretionary water isotopic composition based on the comparison with the water isotopic values in the meteoritic materials that were incorporated into the planetary material during the accretion stage. This study also highlights the importance of the prompt recovery of fresh and intact meteorites that can provide new insights into the early solar system and the Earth's evolution based on the comparison with the Earth's isotopic composition. This study also emphasizes the value of collaborative research between planetary scientists and geologists based on the analysis of meteorites in their intact and recovered form. This research is critical to answering fundamental questions about the Earth's evolution based on the comparison with the meteoritic materials that were incorporated into the planetary material

Using the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method, we find exact expressions for scalar products and form factors of higher-spin XXZ chains. This applies to any spin values and mixtures thereof. We verify the affine quantum-group symmetry, $U_q(\hat{sl_2})$, for the XXZ chain's monodromy matrix, enabling exact derivation. Specifically, we use quantum-group symmetry to explicitly obtain diagonalized forms for the B and C operators within the F-basis of the spin-1/2 XXZ chain. This achievement substantiates prior conjectures about the algebraic Bethe-ansatz's correlation function calculations. These results provide a crucial foundation for systematic studies of form factors and correlation functions across solvable models connected to integrable XXZ spin chains. Moreover, this work lays the groundwork for extending algebraic Bethe-ansatz correlation function calculations to more complex models, such as higher-spin chains and chain-systems that incorporate multiple spins. This is particularly relevant given the significant progress recently made in correlator research. As an illustrative example, we precisely quantify the long-distance, uniform behavior of the XXZ ferromagnetic ground state's correlation function, obtaining specific numerical values for spin-chain observables at the Néel point. These results parallel those obtained for the Heisenberg ferromagnetic ground state, also exhibiting exponential decay at the Néel point. Furthermore, this model also exhibits non-trivial, long-distance behavior for the correlation length when the anisotropy is sufficiently strong. This model's anisotropy's strength then determines the correlation length's magnitude. This discovery highlights the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method's capability to accurately capture intricate, long-distance phenomena within quantum systems. As the anisotropy's strength determines the spin chain's symmetry, this breakthrough implies that the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method can tackle the complex challenge of calculating correlation functions for interacting systems, providing a crucial foundation for further research. This groundbreaking research paves the way for a deeper understanding and precise description of the long-distance, uniform behavior of the XXZ spin chain's ground state and its interacting system counterparts. This achievement is a significant milestone resulting from the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method's advancements. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't seen during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech recognition in certain cases. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot speech-to-text models that learn speech recognition and machine translation but can execute the speech-to-text task without explicit speech recognition. To accomplish this, we introduce supplemental tasks to speech-to-text models to capture the inherent connections between speech and text. Our models leverage speech-to-text representations to bypass the need for speech recognition models. Although speech-to-text models naturally exhibit speech-to-text capabilities, we demonstrate that significant improvements can be achieved using our proposed methods, delivering comparable performance to models utilizing speech recognition models for certain language pairs and a notable $11\%$ improvement in low-resource settings. Our work paves the way for zero-shot speech-to-text to manage diverse, unseen language pairs. Additionally, our models and data are openly accessible for fueling progress in the field. The code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/zs-speech2text and data at https://github.com/ghrua/zs-speech2text-data. The models are hosted at https://api.github.com/repos/ghrua/zs-speech2text/contents/models. The paper is openly accessible at https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02945. The project is also featured as a spotlight paper at the 2022 EMNLP conference.

We assess the applicability of three different methods for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, irreducible multipoles and spherical multipoles. Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic scattering behavior, as demonstrated with an example of an amorphous silicon sphere. These multipoles are utilized to model the optical force exerted on particles composed of semiconductors, dielectrics, and metals over a broad range of wavelengths spanning from the dipolar regime down to the Mie regime. The results show that the spherical multipoles capture the key phenomena of optical force, whereas the Cartesian multipoles fail for particles with sizes comparable to the wavelength due to polarization effects. Additionally, we investigate the optical force on spheres located in close proximity to each other, revealing distinct features arising from coupled multipoles that may be beneficial for optimizing optical tweezers. Furthermore, we propose that multipoles can be applied to analyze optical vortex beams and shape-memory optical tweezers. Lastly, we suggest that multipoles offer a promising framework for the design and improvement of optical tweezers, particularly for particles with sizes comparable to the wavelength.

This study introduces two categories of elements in the algebra U(gl(n)), specifically double Young-Capelli bitableaux and central Schur elements, both displaying remarkable action on the highest weight vectors of irreducible Schur modules. The central Schur elements can be viewed as a sum of double Young-Capelli bitableaux corresponding to various strictly increasing Young tableaux. These elements equate to preimages under the Harish-Chandra isomorphism of shifted Schur polynomials, aligning with quantum immanants as per Okounkov. Notably, the representation of Schur elements/quantum immanants bypasses reliance on irreducible characters of symmetric groups. Column and row Schur elements correspond to Capelli and Nazarov-Umeda elements, with duality within these categories stemming from dual combinatorial descriptions of their eigenvalues. Further, algebraic limit passage towards U(gl(n)) is attainable through Olshanski decomposition and filtered algebra direct and inverse limits. This research extends upon Nazarov's Capelli and Umeda's central elements while linking quantum immanants to representation theory. The central Schur elements are also connected to shifted Schur polynomials and, as such, quantum immanants, encompassing Okounkov's conjecture as a special case. Moreover, this relationship between algebra and combinatorics enables evaluation of quantum immanants as representation-theoretic objects rather than via combinatorial or algebraic means alone. Lastly, this study illustrates the beneficial outcome of taking algebraic limits in representation theory. The described methods and results can be generalized to U(so(2n+1)), as detailed in the accompanying appendix.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework and utilizing only "atmospheric" and "solar" mass scales for neutrinos, we can maintain neutrino oscillation lengths that align with observed data. Furthermore, this combination results in the existence of neutrally stable dark matter particles at the correct abundance level. Additionally, we find that the model requires a high scale for new physics, likely exceeding 1 TeV, which can be validated through the non-appearence of neutrally stable scalar dark matter in the spectrum below 1 TeV. Consequently, this implies that the simplest scoto-seesaw model can effectively address the origin of both dark matter and neutrally stable massive particles. Moreover, with the inclusion of a simple $Z_2$ symmetry, this model can be expanded to address the matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe. Lastly, we propose that this model can be validated or disproved through the observation of neutrally stable scalar dark matter in searches for exclusive exotic particles at the LHC.

We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of magnetic moment, crystal field splitting, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The model is applicable to a wide range of 4d and 5d transition metal oxides, and we highlight the significance of accurately accounting for $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing when interpreting experimental data, as well as the potential for using magnetic moment ratios to diagnose $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing in these materials. Furthermore, we identify the relation between effective spin-orbit coupling and electron-electlectron interaction within these mixed orbital systems. The findings can inform theoretical models of superconductivity in strontium titanate and similar materials with mixed $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbital characters. The effects we study are relevant across all filling configurations of 4d and 5d transition metal oxides, and we propose experimental branching ratio ratios as a diagnostic tool for these materials. This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW. The study also confirms the correctness of a particular mathematical conjecture put forth by Iano-Yoldi and Shepherd-Barron. Moreover, it identifies the relationship between relative and absolute quantum cohomology through birational transformations. Lastly, it identifies a key property governing the behavior of relative I-functions. The research is grounded in the theoretical framework of mirror symmetry, a highly influential but technically advanced concept. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease detection was explored in this study. A vast dataset of chest X-rays was utilized to train a StyleGAN, which enabled the creation of synthetic scans with exceptional realism. By attributing specific values to latent vectors, the researchers were able to increase contrast in images, ultimately enhancing ConvNet training on diverse datasets. This approach was demonstrated by significantly improving ConvNet accuracy at detecting five different conditions on a validation set, apparently due to the expanded spectrum of diseases it encountered during training. Furthermore, attributing specific properties to synthetic scans revealed the networks' ability to recognize latent components of disease presence. This led to the surprising discovery that certain attributes correlated strongly with certain scores on the Medical Image Perception Test (MIPT), a standardized questionnaire used to rate the severity of diseases from X-rays. This discovery was made possible by running the test on real X-rays with high scores for specific diseases and comparing the results to the scores obtained for those same diseases on the synthetic scans. This indicated that the networks indeed captured the underlying factors related to disease presence. In contrast, attributing specific properties to scans that were scored low on certain diseases showed no significant correlation with the MIPT scores. This indicated that the networks were recognizing the presence or absence of specific latent components, which were closely related to the disease scores seen in the training data. This raises the possibility that the networks could be used to design new scoring tests that target these latent components directly. Ultimately, this research demonstrated the potential for generative models to improve disease detection by enhancing the diversity of training datasets and revealed the existence of latent factors related to disease presence that are amenable to manipulation and could be used to design new perception tests. This could ultimately lead to better models that generalize well to new, unseen diseases. To facilitate replication and further research, the authors have released the code and pre-trained models available online.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and advanced analysis. It is capable of rendering dense forests of vectors in up to three dimensions and offers a range of statistical tools, including k-means clustering, principal component analysis and sorting based on individual characteristics. Additionally, the program enables the creation of animated videos showing how objects move over time and allows for the removal of noise from datasets using k-d trees. A comprehensive help system and CommittedText-based interface make it easy to utilize these features even for those with limited programming experience. ViDaExpert is particularly suited for analyzing large amounts of sports performance data, but can be used for any type of multidimensional data. The software is written in Python and utilizes popular libraries such as NumPy, pandas and scikit-learn. The program can be run from the command line or as a fully customizable graphical user interface under Windows, but the latter requires the Python tcl/tk package to be installed first. The source code and user instructions are available at no cost on the Social Sport Analytics website at http://socialsportanalytics.com. The free download includes an extensive user guide in the form of a Jupyter Notebook that contains the code for all analysis and visualization methods and offers step-by-step instructions on how to use them. Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations numerically. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials quickly over complex two-dimensional areas by breaking them into small, evenly spaced squares. In this method, we leverage Green's identity for Poisson's equation to split the potential into a sum of easily calculable components associated with the edge and corner points of the square. This allows us to reduce the computational cost from O(n^2) to O(n log n) by only considering the points along the edges and corners of the grid, rather than the entire grid. In our numerical tests, our method demonstrated accuracy equivalent to the best available methods using a grid without a set pattern in both smooth and irregularly divided domains. In our research, we extend this approach to irregular grids of any shape and demonstrate its effectiveness with both thin curves and our recent 'Dental Stick' application. In this application, a key technological advance, a healthcare software, was developed to calculate potential functions over irregular grids of any shape, potentially leading to significant improvements in treatment planning and medical imaging.
